div.head: GERMANS 1111 BACK AT MR. PUNCH.
div.p: GERMANS 1111 BACK AT MR. PUNCH.
Enemy Imposture In The United States.

It is well known that the virile attitude of Mr. Punch on the War has given particular offence in Germany. The leading German newspapers have already solemnly warned the conductors of "Punch" as to what will befall them when the Germans come to London. Mr. Punch, however, goes on his way undismayed, and continues to deal faithfully and fearlessly with Germany and with the Kaiser. Some two or three months ago a fine volume of "Punch" Cartoons was published in New York, comprising some 150 illustrations, the object of which was to bring clearly before the citizens of the United States the arrogant atti- tude of Germany towards the European Powers from 1860 to 1915. _ .

This collection of cartoons showed the methods of the Teuton in such unflattering colours that Germany became nervous as to the stability of her influence in the United States of America. A counterblast must be issued at once, and a blow struck at Mr. Punch, and, through him, at the hated English. It was decided to produce a rival to "Punch.," one that should not only supplant the famous periodical in the favour of the American pub- lic, but should be full of the spirit of hostility to Great Britain.

div.head: Rival " Punch " On U.S. Bookstalls.
div.p: A Rival " Punch " On U.S. Bookstalls.

In pursuance of this plan, two or three weeks ago the Bookstalls of the United States were adorned with a plentiful supply of copies of a periodical which resembled " Punch " very closely, but was not "Punch." The front cover was embellished with Doyle's famous design, which has been known in all parts of the world from time immemorial- as the cover -design of "Punch." In size and shake the periodical was identical with "Punch," but purchasers who bought copies for the modest price of 10 cents. (5d.) were surprised to read above the cover design the legend "As England sees U.S. shown in "Punch," and beneath the design the words :- " Some Famous and Forgotten Cartoons that the present generation of Americans _ _ _
should see."
"Reproduced by The American Truth Society, 1,133, Broadway, New York."

The contents of the periodical were fifteen full-page cartoons taken from the issues of " Punch " from 1842 to 1870. These cartoons, which were mainly of the American Civil War period, when England was not in sympathy with America, had been carefully chosen as being those most likely to make Americans offended with Great Britain. Comments in red ink appeared beneath each cartoon, some of which ran :—" John Bull felt like thrashing us during our Civil War," "The wish of Bank- ruptcy was father to the thought during our Civil War," "John Bull's new Confidence Trick' calls for a billion dollars"; and on the last page, by way, of explaining why " Punch " had been selected for this attack on Great Britain, was printed: "The English mind is always shown in London ' Punch.' " That the cartoons had been deliberately selected in such a way as to misrepresent both the attitude of " Punch " and of Great Britain in relation to the Civil War, and also to represent the feel- ings of fifty years ago as those of to-day, is only ftirther evidence, if such were needed, of the Germanic origin of the publication. A " Punch " Produced By The Germans.

Fortunately, or unfortunately, depending on the point of view, a day or two after this precious publication was .placed on the book- stalls, the Secretary of "Punch" arrived in Nei- York. A visit to the publishers, The American Truth Society, proved, as was antici- pated, that. despite its name, the society was a German organisation run by Germans, and having direct connection with the organisers of the numerous bomb and other outrages in the States.

The police court is a place where can be seen tragedies both great and small, a daily living-picture film whereon are shown strong bad men or weak good men deliberately leaving or gradually being drawn away from the path of virtue. A court of law is not an ideal spot for jests and quips, but they do occur. More frequently are seen the strug- gles to escape the meshes of punishment or the matching of wit against wit and skill against skill. "Is this man a maniac ? " asked the ma- gistrate of the North London police court the other day, speaking to an applicant for a summons. I don't know," was the total- ly unexpected reply, "but I understand that he is .married." _ _

A prisoner at the sessions had been duly convicted of theft when it was seen, on "proving previous convictions," that he had actually been in prison at the time the theft was committed. " Why didn't you say so ?" asked the judge of the prisoner angrily. "Your lordship, I was afraid of prejudic- ing the jury against me." Did you consider the old lady to be in full 'possession of her faculties?" demanded a pompous lawyer of a country, witness. "I dunno rightly, sir, but she 'ad summat tied up in an old red handkercher," was another unlooked for response which raised a laugh.

WIT FROM THE JUDGE. An Irish advocate was pleading for his client, a poor labourer charged with tres- pass. My client is a humble individual. He lives in a hovel and his miserable dwel- lng is in a forlorn and dilapidated state. But, my lord, the labourer's cottage, how- ever ruinous is its plight, is his sanctuary and castle. Yes the winds may enter. it: the rains may penetrate it, but the king himself may not enter unbidden." "What ! not the reigning king ?" asked the joke-loving judge. The story is told of a sergeant-at-law whose leathern lungs were the object of a judge's jocularity. He practised on the Nor- thern Circuit, in a town where the civil and. criminal courts were some distance apart. One day a judge observed:—"l have not seen Mr. B. in court during the last two days. Does anyone know where he is ?" Oh, yes, my lord," said a learned coun- sel, "he is now speaking in the other court." "Dear, dear, I'm afraid I am growing deaf," was the sly response, "for I don't hear him."

There is a good story told of the days when Lord Halsbury was a barrister. He was ar- guing a case on behalf of a Welshman, and showed a great knowledge of the Principality and its people. "Come, come," said the Judge at last, "you know you cannot make yourself out to be a Welshman." "Perhaps not," replied the barrister, "but I have made a great deal of money out of Welshmen in my time." f` Well, then," replied the Judge, "suppose we call you a Wefshman by extraction."

div.head: Its Withdrawal,
div.p: Its Withdrawal,

Upon threat of legal procedure, these valiant protagonists of Germany promptly undertook to withdraw all copies of the publication from circulation, to hand these copies over to the true "Punch" authorities, and to enter into a formal undertaking not to re-issue "Punch" cartoons, at all events, in the misleading form in which they had been issued. The publication was scathingly reviewed by the New York Press, which has since noted. with pleasure its disappearance from the book- stalls, and with caustic comment on the reason for its withdrawal. The net result of the ad- venture is the still further discrediting of the fierman propagandists in America.

div.head: LAW COURT CRAFT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: LAW COURT CRAFT AND HUMOUR.
Jests And Quips In Tragic Surroundings.
HUMOUR OF THE UNEXPECTED.

A lawyer was defending a burglar accused of housebreakin,g. "I submit, your hon- our," he concluded, "that my client did not break into the house at all. He found a window open, merely inserted his arm and removed a few articles. Now, my client's arm is not himself and I fail to see how you can punish the whole person for an offence committed by one of his limbs only." "That argument," said the judge gravely, "is well put. Following it out logically, I sentence the prisoner's arm to twelve months' imprisonment. He can accompany it or not as he chooses." _

Whereupon, the prisoner smiled and with his lawyer's aid, unscrewed his cork arm and, leaving it in the dock, walko out. Another prisoner was charged with being drunk and pleaded "Not Guilty." A wit- ness was being examined and the following dialogue occurred : Lawyer.—" The prisoner spoke to you. What did he say ? ' Witnisss.-4 Re asked .to be called early, air." Lawyer.—" Indeed. That does not sound Like the remark of an intoxicated person. Did he give any reason for being called early ?" Witness—hesitating.—" Yes, sir, he said he was to be Queen of the May." The prisoner received sentence. CLEVER COUNSEL.

A. case was being tried in which one of the persons concerned was a dealer in condensed milk. The following passage between coun- sel and the dealer took place:— Lawyer.—" You sell milk, then ?" Dealer.—"l do." Lawyer.—" Then you know something about agriculture, I suppose?" Dealer.—" No, I . .

Lawyer (interrupting).—" I beg pardon—l forgot, of course—y(4 are one of those milk- sellers who do not obtain their supplies from agricultural sources." The witness tried hard to get in an ex- planation, but the clever counsel plunged in- to another side of the case and left the inci- dent to work its effect on the jury. In another ease, the plaintiff was suing the proprietors of a motor-bus for injuries upon his arm: these were alleged to have been so serious as to prevent him following his employment. Now, sir,' said the counsel for the de- fendants, "kindly show the jury how high you eatt lift your hand since this accident be- fell you." The man slowly raised the injured limb to the height of his shoulder. "Is that as far as you can get it ?" "Yes, sir."
"Well, now show the jury how high you were able to raise it previous to the acci- dent."
The plaintiff, to the disgust of his lawyer, promptly hoisted the hurt arm right over his bead.
A POLITE LAWYER.

It is told of an American lawyer who lost no opportunity of paying attention to the members of the jury, that on one occa- sion, when his voice was drowned by a loud peal of thunder, he turned to the jury and said solemnly, "Gentlemen, pardon this tin. seemly interruption." Another barrister was also gifted with ex- treme politeness, but he was often very prosy. He was pleading before a court' of four judges and returned to one point over and over again. "But, Mr. F.," broke in the president, "you have dealt with that matter four times already."

" Oh, no, my lord, only three times, I think," replied the offender in the gentlest tones. "it is a point very difficult to under- stand and as there are four of your lordships, I think I ought in justice to my client to dwell on it once again."

div.head: TELLING PAUSE.
div.p: A TELLING PAUSE.

There is a striking story told of a New Eng:and lawyer who hit upon a novel scheme to win his case. He was representing the people of a certain village which had been burned to the ground. The fire-engines from a neighbouring town had been held up by a draw-bridge which had been left open to al- low a tug to pass down the stream. The rail- road company to whom the bridge belonged contended that it had been open no more than five minutes and in that time, they said, the fire could not make such great head- way that the delayed engines would find it impossible to overcome it. The plaintiffs' counsel, when he came to make his speech simply said:—" Our oppon- ents admit that the draw-bridge was open five minutes. Now, gentlemen of the jury, will you take out your watches, please ?" They did so and held them in their hands. "Now will you kindly tell me when five minutes is over," said the lawyer ,and sat down. Silence reigned, it became oppressive and intolerable—surely the watches had stopped. There was a hurricane of sighs when the word " Time " was called. "Gentlemen, I leave it with you as to whe- ther five minutes is long enough for a fire to get out of hand." The jury brought in promptly # verdict for the plaintiffs. Silence was golden.
After man makes the opportunity the oppor- tunity may make him.
When you refuse to do a mean act your enemies think you can't.

div.head: WARRINGTON DISTRICT NURSES.
div.p: WARRINGTON DISTRICT NURSES.
1.-ligh Tributes To Ladies Who Do Splendid Work.

div.head: ANNUAL MEETINGS OF MONEY-FINDERS.
div.p: ANNUAL MEETINGS OF MONEY-FINDERS.

The Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) pre- skied over the annual meetliteof the Warring- ton District Nursing Association, which was held in the Town Hall on Thursday evening. In opening the meeting his Worship said he was sure that all present would be interested in and gratified by the excellence of the annual report which had been submitted to subscribers —and a summary of which appeared in our columns last week. Notwithstanding the many calls which had, of late, been made upon the charitable, both the General Committee and the Working Men's Committee .had to report 1 an increase in the ordinary subscriptions. That was just as it should be, for an institution that rendered such service to people—people_ who would not know how to go on without it—as did that association, deserved, and ought to have, war or no 'war, the sympathy and support of the generously disposed at all times. (Hear, hear.) During last year the nurses paid 15,256 visits, and to 606 out of the 664 eases attended upon they were sent by the local medi- cal men; a fact which spoke volumes as to the high opinion in which they and their work were held by those most qualified to know. Letters of apology for non-attendance, it was reported, were received from the Rev. Father Whittle, the Rev. W. T. Derry, Mrs. Fair- dough, Mrs. Broadbent and Messrs. F. A. Frost and W. P. Rylands. •

had di,ease and illness and disorders that were not caused by shells or shrapnel, but by gross ignorance, insobriety and indifference, and that in the long run those ailments were fatal to more than were the instruments of war. The proposition was carried with applause.

div.head: SUBSCRIPTIONS SATISFACTORY DESPITE
div.p: SUBSCRIPTIONS SATISFACTORY DESPITE
WAR.

Councillor Henry Robes, in presenting his report as honorary treasurer—a report which showed receipts totalling .{1369 9s. 4d. and a balanee at the end of the year of £B3 19s. 2d.— regretted that he had not yet got all the churches 'and chapels in Warrington on the list of 'subscribers. But he hoped that, in time, he might succeed in his endeavour to do so— a hope in which he was encouraged by reason of the fact that two additional places of wor- ship figured in the list this year. At. the same rate of progress his grandson—assuming he be- came treasurer of the association—might be .able to congratulate some future annual meet- ing upon having a subscription from every reli- gious institution in the town. (Laughter.) They were he was pleased to say, getting very near the time when the sum which he had suggested that it was desirable they should have as a stand-by would be reached. A few years ago they set out to raise £2,000 as a stand-by, in order that the income from that amount might be something to depend upon in case bad times ever came and subscriptions were, in conse- quence, seriously reduced. He was very glad to say that in spite of the tremendous demands made during the last eighteen months the sub- scriptions had held up remarkably well, and he ! sincerely hoped that they would continue to do so. It was nice to know that they now had an assured income of something between £BO ' and 0290 a year to fall back upon in case bad times came. A study of the list of diseases and complaints nursed by the nurses from that institution would carry to every mind a.wonder- ' ful exeitiplification of duty under circumstances that Were, in many eases, by no means pleasant and would serve to convince the reader that the nurses were rendering to the community L services of the highest possible character and value.

A HINT TO CHURCHES AND CHAPELS. The Rev. E. C. Brookes moved the adoption of the Treasurer's report, which She regarded as highly satisfactory, specially gratifying being the increase in the- amount of church offertories. However, he was still of opinion that in that direction there was yet room for considerable improvement, for out of 44 places of worship in the town only eleven contributed. That was a very poor proportion. If churches felt that they could not devote .a collection to the Nursing Association why did they not give some contribution from the proceeds of a sale of work, or something of that sort?

div.head: MORE FATAL THAN SHOT AND SHELL.
div.p: MORE FATAL THAN SHOT AND SHELL.

Mr. J. Rymer Young seconded, remarking that surely it was possible still to further in- crease the income of the Association in a town like Warrington. He was rather inclined to think that the Association ought to be a much bigger affair, with more nurses and covering greater ground. One way in which they could show their complete appreciation and approval of the nurses was by taking care that they were very well paid. They had read a lot lately of the heroic work of the nurses in the hospitals where the war-broken warriors were tended, but they must not forget that in Warrington they

div.head: ONE GOOD EFFECT OF THE WAR.
div.p: ONE GOOD EFFECT OF THE WAR.

Mr. J. -Upson proposed a vote of thanks to the Working Men's Committee for their suc- cessful efforts to swell the funds; to the Ladies' Committee for the care and attention they had given to the home and in superintending the work of the nursing staff; to Miss Milne and her staff for their unselfish devotion to duty and to the hon. secretary (Lieut.-Colonel J. D. Fair- dough) and hon. treasurer. In doing so he said that a new function had during the year been added to the many already performed by the nurses, for it had come to his knowledge that not only did they pay something like fifty visits a day to the sick—at a cost of little more than 9d. a visit—but that they also made a largte number of calls upon the wives and children of men who had fallen at the Front; and not only , ministered to their physical needs, when required so to do, but also ministered with words of consolation and cheer,to the wounded lives and broken hearts of those who had lost their loved- ones. (Hear, hear.) The war had had the effect of bringing into prominence such good works as were carried on by Associations like that, and he believed that those bodies would never again lose that tiewly-found promi- nence.

div.head: RE-ELECTIONS AND THANKS.
div.p: RE-ELECTIONS AND THANKS.

The Rev. Father Hind seconded, and the pro- position having been carried with applause, Mr. T. S. Steel moved the re-election of the presi- dent, vice-president and committee, with the substitution of the name of Father Hind for that of Father Neville Wilson on the last- named body. This was seconded by Mr. Harry Hope and also carried. The meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to the .Mayor for presiding, and an expression of best wishes and a safe return from the war for Lieutenant-Colonel Fairclough.

div.head: HOW WORKERS HELP.
div.p: HOW WORKERS HELP.
Last Year's Receipts Less, But Still Satisfactory.

During the year ended June 30th, the Work- ing Men's Committee, working in conjunction with the Warrington District Nursing Associa- tion—whose headquarters are at 21 Arpley- street—were able to raise no less a sum than £250 2s. 5d., of which £245 10s. 2d. has been handed over/to the treasurer of the Association. the balance of £4 12s. 3d. being absorbed by ex- penses. The previous—and: pre-war year—the total sum raised was £3Ol 16s. lid., of which £297 Bs. 10d. was paid over to the treasurer, but it has to be borne in mind that the total receipts for that year included £6O realised as the result of a special effort on the part of one of the large works in the town; an effort which was not repeated last year. On the whole, therefore, the total raised last year was a most satisfactory one, and that was the view taken of it by the delegates who, assembled at the annual meeting of the Work- ing Men's. Committee,, which was held. in. the Council Chamber of the Town Hall on. Saturday afternoon. The President (Mr. W. Peter Rylands) was in the chair, and he was sup- ported by the chairman (Mr. Geo. Walker), the vice-chairman (Mr. T. Wadsworth), the hon. treasurer (Mr. Henry 'Hope), and the hon. sec. (Mr. Henry Taylor).

div.head: "EFFORT BEYOND ALL PRAISE."
div.p: "EFFORT BEYOND ALL PRAISE."
At the outset letters regretting inability to attend were read from the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), Councillor H. Roberts and Mr. F. W. Monks.
iTis Worship's absence was due fo the fact that he was out of town.

Councillor Roberts wrote :—" May I express the gratitude and admiration which 'every member of the parent, committee feels for the great and successful efforts which have again resulted in such a substantial contribution to the funds of our Association from the working men of our town. . . . It points to earnest zeal on the pint of the officers and a perfection of organised effort which is beyond all praise. My work and anxieties as ,hon. treasurer of the parent committee have been greatly' lessened by
your splendid co-operation, and I am very grateful."
PRESIDENTIAL PRAISE.

The President said he thought the Working Men's Committee might lom back with con- siderable satisfaction to the work which had been done during the past year. There were many calls, nowadays, upon the charity of the people, but he did not know of one charitable object that they should think of with more sympathy than the Nursing Association. (Hear,. hear.) An institution like the Infirmary, appealed more directly to the eye, because they could see the building and some of the work which was being done in connection with it. They all heard also of the operations performed in that institution and of the accident cases taken there for treatment, but it was only those who had themselves been badly ill who could fully appreciate what it meant to have a good nurse to visit them and minister to them. When one recalled that last year the staff at the dis- posal of the Association paid no fewer than fifty visits every day, one could, in a measure, imagine the vast amount of satisfaction, pleasure, relief and help which they conveyed into the homes of the poor of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The reflection was one that should stimulate to greater endeavour all who had hitherto supported the Association, and should be the means of winning deserved sup- port from those who had not hitherto given it. Whilst the employes of many of the most im- portant firms appeared in thO list of contribu- tions, it was a matter for regret that there were ..undoubtedly some very noticeable absentees. He hoped that as the result of further effort the employes of those firms would figure in the list in next year's annual report. (Hear, hear.) The Working Men's Committee had been work- ing now for about ten years; it took a great deal of organising, but, since the day it was got properly going, the committee had never looked back. He believed that every year since the inception of the committee the subscriptions from the works had shown an increase. The total amount available had not always in- creased, but it had to be borne in mind that that amount was from time to time swelled by special efforts—something that was not done every year. For instance, the total amount col- lected last year was £245, as compared with £.297 in the previous year. Works Collections Increased.

That, of course, was to te regretted, but they must not omit to notice that the previous year's total had some extraordinary items in it, and that the actual ordinary works collections had as a matter of fact increased. They had, in- deed, gone up from .ClB2 to £203, and that in- crease was the more gratifying in that it had taken place despite the war. But it must be borne in mind that the funds were not yet quite large enough to enable the Association to do all that it would like to do. The cost of carrying on the Association was very heavy, and he could not help feeling that the working men's con- tributions should total at least £3OO a year. The more money contributed, the more the work that would be done, and here, perhaps, he ought to mention that the general accoulits showed a slight loss on the year's working. It was regrettable, but fortunately it was not a very serious matter. It, however, served to emphasise the fact that the Working Men's Committee, and the other supporters of the Association, must not relax their efforts. (Hear, hear). Mr. Rylands concluded by moving the adoption of the accounts.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDA f, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA f, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
THIRTY WORKS THAT DO NOT HELP.

The Treasurer said that the various works were still increasing their subscriptions year by year, and the Friendly Societies and the Trade Socilties were coming into line splendidly. (Hear, hear.) Five new societies joined the list of subscribing bodies during the year. Special subscriptions were down about £l7 on the year, but that was due to the fact that, of course, the previous year's special subscriptions of £6O from Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s works, was not again forthcoming. To counterbalance this there was a net gain of £4l on. the works and Friendly Societies' subscriptions. (Ap- plause.) Several works at which they had been pegging away for as long as nine or ten years still refused to come in; indeed, the employes of some thirty firms carrying on business within a two mile radius of Market Gate made no contributions at all. If the committee could only get £2 a year from the employes of each of those firms half of the money that was needed, over and above that already coming in, would be secured. The committee could not rely on special efforts every year.

div.head: " ArkM.ELS.OF_MERGNe!"
div.p: " ArkM.ELS.OF_MERGNe!"

Mr. Geo. Walker seconded. It was' he said,, gratifying that despite the absence from the balance sheet of the extraordinary gift of £6O from Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s employes, the committee had maintained their position and slightly improved on it. He would like the workers .to study the sort of cases that came under the care of the nurses, and then they would have4ome conception of the peculiar and arduous duties wlafch the nurses were called upon to perform, and did, in fact, so admir- ably perform. Not long ago he (the speaker) happened to be going home in a tramcar, when

Mr. Geo. Walker proposed the re-election of Mr. W. Peter Rylands to the presidency, dilating upon the known interest which that gentleman takes not only in the Association, but also in the Infirmary and in all local charitable and helpful organisations. Mr. F. Baker seconded, remarking that Mr. Rylands set an example for everyone in the in- terest he took in all good causes. _ _

• The proposition having been carried with applause, Mr. Rylands briefly returned thanks, confessing that he took a particularly keen in- terest in the work of the Nursing Association. He had many occupations, but he supposed it was always possible to put another straw on a horse without breaking its back. They might depend upon him to give them all the help that was in his power. (Applause.)

he noticed among his fellow passengers a man whom he knew had been serioit.sly ill for months. He complimented the man upon his improved appearance and the man said "Walker, those nurses of yours are angels of mercy !" That was the testimonial of a man who knew what he was talking about—knew what the nurses had done for, him and what they were doing for hundreds of others. Mr. Walker mentioned that the White Heather Day effori put forth by the Caledonian and the Works Bowling Associations, which last year resulte( in the addition of £6 to the funds, would, thi, , year, bring in £ls—which sum would figure next year's balance sheet. (Applause.) Those present were then constituted the General Committee, with power to add to their numbers.

div.head: PRESIDENT RE-ELECTED.
div.p: PRESIDENT RE-ELECTED.
THE VICE-PRESIDENTS.

On the proposition of Mr. Thomas Wadsworth the following were re-elected Vice-presidents : The Mayor of Warrington, Aldermen J. Smethurst and T. Burton, Major G. R. Cros- field, and Messrs. F. W. Monks, Henry Roberts, Wm. Carson, Walter Milner, C. E. Bunch, T. W. Fletcher. T. Atherton, J. A. Ransome, R Chadwick, Wm. Murray and 0. Lofthouse.

div.head: OTHER OFFICERS APPOINTED.
div.p: OTHER OFFICERS APPOINTED.

Mr. F. Cooke proposed the re-election of Mr. George Walker as chairman, observing that he was sure they could not find a better man for the post. (Hear, hear.) The proposition having been carried, Mr. Walker expressed his thanks. Mr. T. Wadsworth was re-elected vice-chair- man, and Alderman Burton and Messrs. G. Walker and Wm. Charnock were appointed trustees for the ensuing year. Mr. Henry Hope was again appointed hon. treasurer, and Mr. Henry Taylor hon. secretary. In proposing the re-election of the hon. secretary, Mr. Hope said that Mr. Taylor had now served the committee a little over a year and he was the best helper he (the speaker) had yet had on the committee. In returning thanks for his re-election, Mr. Taylor said that when he undertook a job he always endeavoured to do it properly. With a kind and considerate President and an excellent Treasurer to help, his duties had really been very light, and he had done what he had done with great pleasure. _ _ _
Messrs. Walker, Hope and Taylor were ap- pointed representatives of the committee on the Executive Committee of the Association.
THANKS TO THE NURSES.

The meeting concluded with votes of thanks. That to the Lady Superintendent and staff of the Association was proposed by Mr. Henry Hope, Mr. W. Kilduff seconding and remark- ing upon the educational value of the work of the nurses, as well as upon the service they rendered in the alleviation of pain and suffer- ing. When they went into the homes of the poor, the people noticed the work that they were doing, how they set about their task, SEc., and, by so noticing, they learned valuable lessons.

Mr. G. Walker, in supporting, said that there was a very great demand for nurses, on account of the war. However, the Association's nurses had stood loyally by that institution, notwithstanding the fact that they had had every inducement to enter other spheres of labour.

A delegate also spoke a few words in support of the proposition, observing that it was very largely due to the skilled attention of the Association's nurses that he was able to be there that day. He expressed a desire to help the Association, and said that although, being only in a humble position, he could not give as much money as he would like, he would be pleased to do any work for the committee that might be in his power. (Applause.) The proposition was carried.

Other votes of thanks were accorded the hon. auditor (Mr. Edwin Bradshaw), the President. the Chairman, the Deputy-chairman and all the other officials, and to the Mayor for lending the Council Chamber for that afternoon's meet- ing.

div.head: "INDELIBLE INIQUITY."
div.p: "INDELIBLE INIQUITY."
Rev. T. Parr And German Atrocities.

A special service was held at the Primitive Methodist Church, Legh-street, Warrington, on Thursday afternoon, the sermon being preached by the Rev. Theophilus Parr, of Bolton. , At night a lecture was given by the Rev. T. Parr on " The Rainbow in the Cloud," or, "The Bright Side of the War." There were present a good number of people, over whom Mr. Hy. Brocklehurst presided. The Dark Side -

After referring to the horrors or the war, the lecturer said that the fall of Germany to-day was the most colossal fall of a nation; it was a fall of morals. Germany had lost her soul. The horrors inflicted by that nation had stamped her with indelible iniquity. But horrible as all her deeds were, the most horrible fact was the silence of her ministers. Not a voice had been lifted up against the atrocities. - And the Bright !

Turning to the bright side of the war, the speaker mentioned the self-sacrifice of the nations, the brotherhood of the soldiers, and the bravery and devotion of Nurse Cavell. He de- clared that Belgium was being purified and that France was being transformed, and added, "May we hope that England is being also trans- formed." Men, he said, had been driven to the Church, and he spoke of the religious atmos- phere amongst the soldiers in France. He also referred to the impetuErthat the war had given to social reform, land reform, and Christian unity.

div.head: BIG FARM FIRE.
div.p: BIG FARM FIRE.
An Early Morning Outbreak At
Bewsey.

About seven o'clock on Wednesday morning, information was received at the Warrington Fire Station to the effect that a fire had broken out on the farm premises of Mr. T. J. War- burton, at Beney. With great promptitude, the steam fire engine Major and a full comple- ment of men in charge of Deputy-Superin- tendent H. Cook were dispatched to the scene of the conflagration, and on their arrival they found. that a large square brick building—used as stables, shippons and piggeries, and con- taining a. large quantity of fodder, hay, straw, mangels, potato-sets in boxes, corn-cutting machinery and an engine—were burning fiercely. The brigade promptly got to work from an adjoining pit, three powerful jets being used, and by dint of untiring efforts they were able to save about half of the building and contents, but a portion of the roof and the upper floor were destroyed. The firemen were engaged for some hours in turning over and removing the smouldering debris, returning to the station about 3.30 p.m. Prior to the arrival of the brigade about thirty head of cattle—in- cluding horses, cows and pigs—were safely removed from the burning building, and whilst helping in this task a labourer named T. Gerhity received burns to his hands and arms, which necessitated medical attention.
The damage, which is roughly estimated at a few hundred pounds, is covered by insurance.

Mackie and Co. Distillers Ltd. have intimated to the trade that the limit of supply of their "White Horse" Whisky has been reached, and in order to maintain the great age of the brand, they are unwillingly obliged to refuse orders from new customers, unless a small quantity is available after old customers' requirements have been met. Old customers will receivr quantities pro-rata according to requirements.

div.head: UNDIPPED SHEEP.
div.p: UNDIPPED SHEEP.
Burtonwood Dealer And Farm Hand Summoned.

At the County Police Court on Wednesday, before Messrs. C. E. Parker and H. P. Mortimer, Arthur Smith, of Forest Farm, Burton wood, was summoned for being in charge of seventy sheep and failing to dip them as required by an Order of the Board of Agricul- ture issued on April Ist; and George Dufton, of 2, Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath, was sum- moned for being the owner of the said sheep and for failing to have them dipped. Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for the defendants, and entered a plea of not guilty. Prosecuting, Superintendent Foster said that by the Order of April Ist the sheep were re- quired to be dipped between July 13th and August 31st, and between September Ist and November 15th. If the sheep were not• dipped both the owner and the person in charge of the sheep were liable. On April 25th a constable served Smith with a copy of the Order, and Smith knew perfectly well the condition of dipping. Dufton was a sheep dealer in a large way of business, and the seventy sheep were his property. Smith was the person who had charge of the sheep. " Thought All Restrictions Were Off."

On November 17th, Smith's farm was visited and the sheep were found there. He admitted that they had been there since September 11th. Smith said that they had not been dipped, and that he did not think it was his place to dip them. Later an inspector saw Mr. Dufton. who Said that he had not dipped the sheep because he thought that all the restrictions w-..re off. Superintendent Foster added that, sr on after the war broke out, certain restrictions were k taken off, but a fresh Order was brought out on April lst. The Board of Agriculture were doing their best to prevent scab amongst sheep but if sheep were moved about and duo pre- cautions were not taken, all their efforts would be wasted. _ -

Mr. Steel pleaded that Mr. Dufton had every desire to carry out the regulations, but he was misled by the auctioneers from whom he bought the sheep. Smith was fined 20s. and Duf ton was ordered to pay the costs.

Testing Eggs.

_ A person can test eggs to find out if they are fresh before breaking them by the following method r--Dissolve two ounces of kitchen salt in a pint of water. When a rresh egg is placed in this solution it will descend to the bottom of the vessel, while one that has been laid on the previous day will not quite reach the bot- tom. If the egg be three days old it will swim in the liquid and if it is more than three days old it will float on the surface and project above the latter more and more in proportion as it is older.

div.head: faters to titt2 (Oita
div.p: faters to titt2 (Oita
MUNITIONS AND DRINK.

Sir,—Your correspondent, "Citizen,' is only too evidently a " temperance " advocate of the extremist school, who prefer abuse and denun- ciation to argument. I hold no brief for the Trade, but when a teetotalist like " Citizen " talks about their spending money on full page Press advertisements, &c., in their own de- fence, and tries to pretend that such expenditure proves the anti-restriction agitation to be a sham—well, one can only stand aghast at his audacity! He must know perfectly well that the hundreds of professional " temperance " lecturers up and down the country don't live on love, and that the various teetotalist organisations spend large sums in maintaining their campaign against the licensed trade. One of these societies alone raised in a single year £10,486, of which £7,928 was spent on "salaries, offices, district superintendents and agents; grants to auxiliaries, cost of agencies, demon- strations, meetings, deputations, &c." In 1907, the "Temperance Record" estimated the annual income of the -teetotalist bodies totalled £382,700! I do not for one moment accuse " Citizen " of being an agent of this rich and powerful organisation; but I wish to point out that the favourite teetotalist trick of suggesting that-- any- body who disagrees with them is an emissary of the brewers cuts both ways, and that as regards propaganda expenditure the water-bottle zealots are well in front. _
J. E. SIMPSON.
November 30th, 1915.

div.head: DRINK RESTRICTIONS: TILLETT'S OPINION.
div.p: DRINK RESTRICTIONS: TILLETT'S OPINION.

Sir,—l have no wish to intervene or trespass upon the discussion proceeding in your columns between your correspondents, Mr. .1. E. Simpson and " Citizen " re "The limitation of drinking facilities," but in your issue of November 27th Mr. Simpson refers to Mr. Ben Tillett, voicing the opinions of the "Dockers' Union," in opposition to the further restrictions. I have seen something similar on large posters in some of our towns.

Almost immediately after reading Mr. Simp- son's letter I was reading the "Good Templars' Watchword" of November 27th, containing an open letter to Mr. Ben Tillett from Mr. Guy 'Taylor, " Courtfield," South Norwood Park, London, S.E., in which he reminds Mr. Ben Tillett of some utterances publicly used by him in the past, and giving him- the time and place when spoken. ' I thought it might be in- teresting to re-quote them just now : " After years of experience," he (Mr. Ben Tillett) found, "That Trade Union work con- ducted in public-houses was a positive failure:"

"Directly men began to spend money in drink, they took from the butcher, the baker, the furniture maker, and the carpenter and builder, and from every other form of industry —they took from these industries the legitimate and bona-fide portions of what they should claim of all Trade Unionists."

"Trade Unionists should' become total abstainers themselves, and absolutely veto the holding of lodge meetings in public-houses." Referring to what he had seen in Newcastle a previous night, a drunken British workman being led home by a bull-pup: "The dog was sober. If the dog had been drunk they never would have got home. I thought to myself at the time, 'Benjamin, there's some work for you to do while chaps like that are forgetting themselves.'" "The alcohol microbe was not half such a decent chap as the'cholera microbe. The latter enforced cleanliness, but the alcohol microbe was dirty, and lived amid squalor. If only for the loss of life caused, drink was a damnable thing. But it meant loss of honour among men, and of virtue among women—and chaps like me spending their heart and life in the work of reform, have to wade through the damnable gutter of drink to pull out many a man who ought to be on the dry land of tem- perance."

"Every man who spent a cent. in alcoholic liquors was a robber. Drink was deteriorating to the strength of brain, and of physioue. that would be more than ever necessary in the fiercer competition that was coming." "A man who neelected °the welfare of his child was a coward, a cur. a robber of his country, and a blackguard to his family, whether he drank much or little." I have no further comment to make. PATRICK O'BRIEN. 125, Wilderspool-road, Warrington.

div.head: DRINK RESTRICTIONS.
div.p: DRINK RESTRICTIONS.

"HOUSE FAMINE."
Cr. Pemberton Gives "Concrete
Facts For The People."

div.head: " REVELATIONS."
div.p: " REVELATIONS."

"The Liverpool Courier" of November 20th contained the following vigorous article by Councillor John Pemberton, of Warrington. The " Courier " printed it under the heading "Builder's Extraordinary Revelations ": I have read with the greatest interest the article on "The House Famine" which ap- peared in last Saturday's "Courier," and with which I entirely agree. The public mind is so obsessed with the war—quite right, I don't com- plain of it—that no thought is being given to the extraordinary situation that is arising all over the country. And so it strikes me that your article will serve the most useful purpose of warning the public, and, through them, the Government of the terrible dangers ahead.

div.head: Two Million Persons Want Houses.
div.p: Two Million Persons Want Houses.

A house famine! One can hardly conceive in our happy little England what that really means. There are close upon half a million fewer houses in this country than there ought to be. There are three million British soldiers on war service, and that number, is rapidly growing to four millions. A great many of these are married, and have homes of their own. Nearly a million of them married before they went to the war, and the marriages when the armies return will bring that number up to a full million. So that after the war this country will have two million people who cannot be housed under normal family conditions. Is this position actually realised in the land? I fear not.

The property-owners and the builders are such a favourite target for public odium and contempt that it is usual to find only, a lethargic interest being evinced in their affairs. But the present grave subject is one over which the public should bestir themselves. The ex- tinction of the house-builder may be only an incident in this crisis from the national point of view. It is certainly a very disagreeable incident so far as the unfortunate house-builder is concerned, but there are far graver issues at stake. What of the people who want houses and cannot have them? They will go else- where, which will be very bad for England. What of the generations still unborn? They will find palatial municipal buildings in which they may have the benefit of a very expensive and elaborate educational system, but when their early training is finished and they come to the age when they would like to settle in homes of their own they will in turn find that there are no houses for them, and those few that may be changing tenants will through the law of supply and demand show a rent which will-have a most serious effect on the matrimonial mar- ket.
Crippled By Legislation.

I have seen this crisis approaching for some years now, and I have myself warned several members of Parliament, Perhaps I may be per- mitted to give my actual personal experience as a result of the Finance Act, 1909-10. For 40 years I have been engaged in the building trade. I have always built under best con- ditions, and have had no advances or unneces- sary legal costs or interest to pay. Therefore I have been able to erect property as economic- ally as it was possible to do. In 1909 I was building houses suitable for the working classes, and I was able to get whatever financial accom- modation I required, both in the shape of advances from my bank and as mortgages. But as soon as legislation altered the conditions by taxing both the land on which-I built and the land on which I did not build by doubling the expenses a conveyancing and threatening fur- ther taxation and restrictions, I found myself faced with very serious difficulties. Mortgagees began to ask to have their mortgages reduced, the bank ceased to lend to the same extent as before, and buyers fell completely away. Property as an investment dropped flat, and my position as a business man became alarmingly serious in a few months. I concentrated all my efforts in cutting my losses. I drew all my jobs to a close, even going so far as to leave some of the work unfinished. I have two small villas with £l2O worth of work done towards their construction, and they are at this moment in the same unfinished condition as they were when I left thein four years ago. I kept my leading men in my employ as long as possible in the hope that the Government would, change its cruel policy and encourage building to go on again. It was a false• hope and cost me a further considerable sum of money.

div.head: Tax On Raw Material.
div.p: Tax On Raw Material.

-I possess 218, 000 To-day my position is this. worth of freehold land, which is my raw material, lying useless on my hands.. I AM will- ing and anxious to build upon it, but I cannot do so because of the fina,ncia I position and the red fear of investors to put their money in property; I am unable to carry on my trade, and over and above that fact I am incurring heavy .expenses by being compelled to hold on to my land. Is there any other trader who is thus taxed for possessing raw material which he cannot utilise? ,

Here is another illustration of the unfair con- ditions which hundreds of property owners in Lancashire are up against. I have some property on.which there is a mortgage of £5,000., It is exceptionally good property in a splendid, position, and was valued under its cost by the mortgagee's valuer. I have two-thirds of that value lent upon it, and I was able to borrow at 4 per •cent. It has :paid me these last two or three years at the rate of 51. per cent., because of the ever-increasing r,?te la the district. I 2.1 l P 9.5 -callea 'llPoii Ey thp inoligago to pay 1 ;;;ni Mt. xlra ititertht, So, you see, at one blow they take two-thirds of my. income from it. Besides that, I have to pay increased rates, increaSea taXation, increased wages for re- decorsitiMiS and repairs to the property, and in- creakiti. prices for Materials generally. At the sala time, I have to pay the higher cost of living as do my tenants. But they, on the other hand, have had their wages raised and are earn- ing through overtime 20 or 30 per cent. more than ever before. Where' is the justice of it?

div.head: Fool's Paradise.
div.p: A Fool's Paradise.

Property owners, for some reason or another, have become the favourite victims of the Government. There has been special legisla- tion passed in respect to property, taxing it, re- stricting it and making it more expensive than any other form of investment. Property is a drug in the Market despite the fact that the demand for 'houses was never so brisk; rents are better, and there are practically no empty houses. Yet a builder cannot get what it costs to build. Is there any other investment in the country in such an extraordinary position? I defy anybody to show me one. I venture to predict that when this war is over the housing question will be the most serious problem that tliis country has ever faced. It is not a question of politics; it is a matter of common justice. And politicians must cease to go on living in a fool's paradise. If they do not, there will be a rude awakening for them and, what is more important, for the , people of this country.

div.head: MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: MUSICAL SOCIETY.
Concert Version Of Edward German's "Merrie England."
A PATRIOTIC EFFORT.

The opening concert of the Warrington Musical Society's season given in Parr Hall on Saturday evening in aid of Local War Funds, merited a much fuller measure of public sup- port than was accorded it, many empty seats being noticeable amongst a somewhat scattered audience. A programme which comprised an orchestral performance of Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsodie (No. 2) and the presentment in con- cert font'. of Edward German's opera " Merrie England," was, necessarily, Of a bright and exhilarating kind, and one, therefore, that might have been expected to draw a large attendance, especially when it is borne in mind that the whole of the vocal music was sung by local and favourite singers. Alas! for the fickle- ness of Warrington's musical public. " Merrie England," robbed of its joyous sur- roundings, its May blossoms, its 'gorgeous pageantry, its ludicrous masque, and its inimitable Wilkins, was yet full of interest for concert purposes. Its wealth of melody in song and old English dance, its rousing choruses, and its finely-conceived concerted pieces, breath- ing freshness and gaiety, present an aggregation of attractions quite sufficiently connected to rivet attention and to banish all regrets. In quite an appreciative frame of mind, Satur- day's audience therefore listened to the "Merrie England" music, numerous encores serving to attest the keen enjoyment found in its perform- ance. Miss Helen Anderton's singing of the parts scored for Queen Elizabeth and Jill-all- Alone showed, in her voice as in the artistic use she made of it_ a marked improvement upon her past high achievements, , and it is scarcely too much to say that interest largely centred upon her cultured rendering of the songs and solo passages which fell to her lot in the portrayal of these characters, and 8f the very onerous declamations of the finale to Part I. of the programme. It was, of course, impos- sible that Miss Anderton could be expected to sing, just now, of a peaceful England smil- ingly slumbering. By some forethought, as happy as it was well-timed, she was Provided, in Queen Elizabeth's song, with a new set of words more in consonance with the strenuous times in which we are living. These two new verses are so noteworthy in themselves that no apology is needed for here interpolating them:
0 patient England! Still thou thy watch art keeping; Still in the future _ .

_ Lingers the hour for sleeping! Keep watch and ward awhile, Peace yet again shall smile, But now 'gainst force or wile, Be wakeful, ever wakeful! Sword and buckler in thy hand Guard well the shore of this fair land! War, like the ever hungry sea, Hewls,round our Isle; , But, if thou shalt steadfast be, Peace yet again shall smile!

England, fair England, Not yet the time for slumber; Still must thy bosom The breastplate harsh encumber! Let not thy fingers yield . Grasp of thy sword and shield! Thou shalt arise and wield Destruction when I call thee! Sword and buckler, &c.

In the music for Bessie, Madame Sara Silcock found Much that was suited to her voice and style. Best of all was her singing of the waltz- song, "Who shall say that Love is cruel?" ta which, though- her enunciation is not of the best, she was able to impart a brilliancy of vocalisation and a trueness of intonation that were entirely praiseworthy. Mr. J. W. Bibby sang •" The Yeomen of England" somewhat heavily, and somewhat too seriouslY, but with a distinctness of delivery that strongly brought home its patriotic appeal. He, too, was not constrained to adhere altogether to Mr. Basil Hood's text. Instead of inviting Spaniards and Dutchmen and Frenchmen and such men to curse as foemen the yeomen of England, we had in the second verse of this song an up-to- date idea rendered thus:

div.head: And Austrians, Hungarians And German barbarians As foemen may curse them The Yeomen of England!
div.p: And Austrians, Hungarians And German barbarians As foemen may curse them The Yeomen of England!

The song, "An English Rose," which offered to Mr. J. Rabbitt the opportunity of ingratiat- ing himself, with the audience, was received with clamorous applause, in response to which he repeated it. The suggestion may, however, be pardoned that the temptation to capture his audience by the display of well-rounded top notes should be restrained by Mr. Rabbitt in the interests of a more uniformly vocalised and more clearly enunciated rendering of this charming ballad. In the quintet "Love is meant to make us glad," as in Essex's song, with trio, "When Cupid first," some unsteadiness in the tempo,l and too great an eagerness on the part of tlie participants in them, detracted from a perfect ensemble. The two duets for Miss Anderton and Mr. Babbitt, and that between Mr. Bibby and Mr. Rabbitt, with chorus, were, on the other hand, given quite satisfactorily, "It, is the merry month of May" being so charmingly sung by the two first-named as to receive a well-merited encore.

The society's chorus sang easily and with great zest the choral portions of "Merrie Eng- land," but failed now and then to attack' smartly in one or two isolated entries. A small detachment of male voices, were put to it to hold their own, as they valiantly did, against trebles and altos who greatly outnumbered them, but, on the whole, the lack of balance in the choral voices was not unduly conspicuous. A number of minor solo parts were cUp.ibly sung by Messrs. J. Sephton, J. P. Huxtable, G. H. Smith and F. Fieldhouce. For the play- ing of the orchestra in " Merrie England" one need only qualify high praise with the remark 'that it was occasionally so loud as somewhat to handicap tie vocal soloists. In the_dance music and that attending the entry of the Queen and again in the finale to Part I. the fine body of the society's instrumentalists—almost entirely local players—acquitted themselves admirably. The performance of the Liszt Rhapsodie was remarkable, unfortunately, in revealing the orehestra's weakness in its inability, in the string section, to grapple with the difficulties of the second and larger portion of this work. The broad phrases of the earlier part of the Rhapsodic) were finely declaimed by the trom- bone, backed up later by other instruments, but the ever-changing mood of the livelier subject into which these_ merge—a subject which works up to a fine climax—presented pitfalls, to the 'players of stringed instruments especially, over which they did not, by any means, come unscathed. It is, of course, too much to look for that uniformity of executant ability amongst the society's numerous body of violinists in the abgence of which a finished performance of the Rhapsodie is well-nigh *im- possible. As. leader of the orchestra, Mr. R. H. Pearson is to be congratulated upon his brilliant playing of the violin cadenza occurring in course of the work. , _ _
Mr. F.ll. Crossley was at his accustomed post as conductor, and skilfully and painstakingly guided all concerned through the intricacieS, of the evening's music.

A Game Two Can Play. "Waiter," called the irate diner, there- seems to be a dollar on this bill I can't account, for." "Oh, that's a joke, sir," apologised the waiter—" just a bet the cashier and I have. I'll have it fixed right away, sir." "What do you mean about a bet?" asked the diner, detaining him. "Well, sir, I bet the cashier 50 cents you would see the mistake, and he bet you wouldn't; so I win, sir." , "Suppose I hadn't npticed it?" "He'd have gotten the dollar, sir," "I see. Give me your pencil," and he wrote a 'few lines on the back of the bill, folded it up, and handed it to the waiter. "Take that to the eashier.', The waiter leaned over the cashier's shouldir as he unfolded the paper. It read: "I'll bet you $5 that when you send this back you don't find me." And they didn't.

div.p: HOW WAR HITS THEM.
There was an unusually small attendanee at the fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, which was held under the chairmanship of Mr. A. J. Jolley at the Work- on Wednesday morning.
TRiBUTES TO MEMORY OF OLD'

div.head: MEMBER.
div.p: MEMBER.

Before the business was proceeded with, the Chairman moved a vote of condolence with the widow and family of the late Mr. Alfred Brooks, formerly a member of the Board, on which he sat as representing Rixton-with-Glazebrook. The deceased gentleman, the Chairman said, was an honourable colleague, and for many years served the poor and the public at large with a single-minded devotion to his duty that, could scarcely be surpassed. He was courteous to all, but, when he felt it his duty to do so, he did not shrink from expressing views that di4 not always commend themselves to his colleagues. Mr. G. Mather seconded, and Miss Broadbent and Mr. J. Billinge having added their tributes to Mr. Brooks's worth and service, the proposi- tion was carried in silence.
The late Mr. Brooks, it may be added, left the Board on March 15th, 1911.
WHITECROSS MILITARY HOSPITAL.

The Local Government Board wrote respecting the claim of the Guardians upon the Army Council for the military occation of part of the Whitecros,s Hospital for the period ended September 30th. With regard to the sum of £563 2s. 3d charged for remuneration of officers, the letter pointed out that the Guardians were only entitled to recover from the Army Coun- cil the remuneration of additional officers en- gaged in consequence of the military occupation and excess payment to the ordinary staff made in accordance with the 'instructions circulated on May 18th last, or sanctioned by the Board. The letter further inquired whether the sum referred to included any part of the normal re- muneration of the staff of the institution. If so, the Army Council should be credited with such amount. It was not clear to the Board that the sums of £265 is. 2d. for nurses' rations and National Insurance stamps, and £lBl 2s. Bd. for fuel, lighting, washing, &c., respectively, represented only the expenditure in excess of the normal cost of such services in respect of the occupied premises, and if those amounts in fact represented the total expenditure, the Army Connell ought to be credited with so much of the EUM as represented the normal expenditure. The Chairman thought that the points raised in the, letter were technical ones, with which the Clerk could satisfactorily deal. All that the military authorities wanted to be sure about was that nothing had been charged to them that they should not pay. As a matter of fact, noth- ing had been charged that they were not liable to pay. They had made a payment on account of £2,750. To a motion that the matter be left in the hands of the Clerk, Mr. J. Billinge moved an amendment to the effect that the Clerk be in- structed to reply to the letter from the Local Government Board, and that such reply be submitted to the Finance Committee. He made that proposal out or no disrespect to the Clerk, but because he thought that the members had a right to know all, and not only part, of the business of the Union.
Miss Broadbent seconded the amendment, which was carried by seven votes to four.

div.head: NO ACTION TAKEN.
div.p: NO ACTION TAKEN.

A letter from the Fareham Union asked the Guardians to support them in an apweal to the Local Government Board to allow Boards of Guardians to relieve old-age pensioners without disqualifying them for a continuance of their pensions, it being pointed out that since the ss. maximuni was fixed the cost of living had greatly increased. The Chairman: It is contrary to law; it can- not be done.
Mr. G. Mather: Most Boards of Guardians allow a little extra to old-age pensioners. The Chairm way? In what w _ _ _ _ •
Mr. G. Mather: In medical extras!

The Chairman: They are not extras in the ordinary sense. A person has to have a medical certificate before he or she gets those. Mr. W. C. Brooks proposed that no action be taken in the matter, and the proposition was carried.

"A GROWING FORCE IN THE COUNTRY." The Chairman made a brief report upon the 17th annual meeting of the Association of Poor Law Unions, which was held in London on November 25th and 26th, and which he and the Clerk attended, as representing the Warrington Union. "There was," he said, "a large at- tendance from all parts of the country, presided over on the first day by Sir John W. Spear, and on the second day by Mr. Beavan, of Cardiff. The main business was, as usual, the considera- tion of the report of the Executive Council, dealing with all the matters connected with Poor Law work, directly or indirectly, Parlia- mentary or administrative, which have arisen , during the year. These ranged over almost the whole alphabet, from Assessment at one end to Vaccination and Vagrancy at the other. The matters arousing most discussion were super- annuation, old-age pensions and the existing legal disabilities of recipients of Poor Law relief. Despite much heated, language from a few extremists and the moving of hostile amendments, the action of the Executive was supported by overwhelming majorities. The Executive is fairly representative of the best elements in the Association, and the subscribing Unions cover more than 96 per cent. of the population of England and Wales. Amongst so large a number there are, of course, some whose , zeal is not according to knowledge, and' not a few who are inexperienced; but, in most cases, Boards elect as their representatives members whose riper judgment corrects and subdues the indiscretions of the minority. The net result is that the association is a growing force in the country, moulding opinion and practice, and making for a more sympathetic administration of the Poor Law without departing from or losing sight of the sound sociological principles which must be adhered to if the relief which should be a blessing is not to degenerate into a curse."

Mr. J. Billinge said that, whilst he was muck obliged to the Chairman for his repOrt, he was rather sorry that the Board should have sent delegates to the meeting this year, in view of existing circumstances. He noticed that a large number of Unions did not send representatives this year, on account of the expense. The deputation from that Board- cost over .tl.l, and he was of opinion .that that money would have been better employed had it been donated to the Red Cross Funds. He knew that there were advantages that might be gained by attending these meetings. but he could not help thinking that they might have foregone them on this occasion.

div.head: \VAR BUDGET.
div.p: THE \VAR BUDGET.

"All the brhins, all the tKeasure and resources of our Empire are perverted—temporarily, we hope—to engines of: destruction and munitions of war. Fellows of the Royal Society are busy with gas problems.- Jt mind like Sir Stanley Von Donep's is optalto weigh and pronounce upon any and every diabolical, invention likely to kill men wholesale,. either. by land or sea, or from the air. VIS gun i just now our great- est industry; the high explosive that feeds it is the Work of giant intellects like Lord Moulton's, one of the most brilliant • Senior Wranglers whom Cambridge ever ..produced. This is how Ignatiu§ Phayre summarises the present topsy-turvy • Condition of the World's efforts at the present moment, in his interest- ing article in "The War Budget" just. out. His article is called "Testing Our New Guns," and tells many interesting things about the making of big .guns which have not been published before. The white-hot interest in the situation in Greece makes particularly valuable a further article by Edmund Dane, dealing with the plot at Athens. This is Mr. Dane's weekly "Story of the Great War." with which he has won such fame as a sure prophet. "The War Budget" tells also the story of the deeds which won the V.C: at Loos, cOntains its regular weekly feature concerning the Volunteer Training Corps, and is crowded With photographs and drawings and cartoons. "The War Budget"' is the ou4 Bd. illustrated war weekly.

"Duty and Discipline." The list .of annual subscribers to the Duty and Discipline Movement includes the name of Mr. W. R. Laws, the Police Court Missionary and Probation Officer for Warrington.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Brotherhood. An open meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Brotherhood will be held to-morrow, tinder the chairmanship of Councillor .3. T. Locker. The address will be given by Councillor B. J. Picker- ing, of Salford, and Mrs. J. Smallshaw will be the soloist.

div.head: To-day's Sale of Work.
div.p: To-day's Sale of Work.
The annual sale of work in aid of the funds connected with Christ Church, Latchford, will be held in the Parish Room, Grappenhall-road, to-day, the opening Ceremony being performed at 3 o'clock.

div.head: Women As Tram Conductors.
div.p: Women As Tram Conductors.

The minutes of the Tramways Committee to be submitted to the Town Council at their meet- ing on Tuesday contain the following item : " It was resolved that the manager be authorised to employ female conductors through the agency of the Labour Exchange, and that they be paid the fixed rate of pay."

div.head: Whist Drive for Russian Red Cross.
div.p: Whist Drive for Russian Red Cross.

A whist drive organised in aid of the Russian Red Cross Society took place on Thursday eVen- ing at Atkinson's Cafe, Bridge-street. A feature of the evening's entertainment was the serving of Russian refreshments in the Russian fashion. Immediately after, the refreshment.• interval Mr. Harold Maybury delivered an appropriate lecturette entitled "Russia and its People." The prize winners were :—Ladies: Miss E. Downing, Mrs. Williamson and Miss Houghton; gentle- Men : Messrs. C. F. Maybury. J. Scott and ,E. Wakefield. The catering arrangements were excellent.

div.head: Proposed Catholic Presentation.
div.p: Proposed Catholic Presentation.

A fund has been opened with a view to rais- ing money for making suitable presentations to the Rev. Fathers Neville Wilson and Basil Primavesi, who have recently left the church —St. Mary's—with which they were for long associated, and have gone to other and different spheres of labour. Both of the reverend gentlemen were well known and respected in the town. The Chairman of the Committee which is organising the presentation is Mr. J. Eckersley, and the treasurer is Mr. W. Duck- worth, of St. Elphin's-terrace, Manchester-read.' Subscriptions should be sent either to the Treasurer„ or to Father Wilson's successor— the Rev. T. A. Hind.

A Day of National Prayer. With the approval and cordial sympathy of His Majesty the King it has been decided by the representative heads of the Churches to invite everyone to join together in united national prayer as an act of humble homage to God and in public recognition of the national reliance upon -His ever-ruling Hand in the crisis through which the Empire is passing at the present time. The first Sunday in the New Year (January 2nd) has been appointed for this solemn occasion. We understand that the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) will invite the Corporation and public men to join him in attendance at public worship at the Parish Church on that day.

div.head: Local Life In Pre-Historic Days.
div.p: Local Life In Pre-Historic Days.

On Friday of last week, at the Museum, the members of the Warrington Shorthand Writers' Association and friends listened to a lecture by Mr. C. Madeley, who, in a highly- interesting manner, ' dealt with life in the locality in pre-historic times, illustrating his remarks by reference to the specimens on ex- hibition in the Museum. The President of the Association (Mr. T. W. Durant) presided, and, at the close, expressed thanks to Mr. Madeley. The interest of the members wa3 manifest in the fact that they lingered at the close for further inspection of the specimens, which had become much more attractive as a result a the lecture.

div.head: Co-operative Concert.
div.p: Co-operative Concert.

, A very enjoyable and well attended concert took place on Thursday evening at the Co- operative Hall, Sankey-street, many notable artistes giving their services. Brief speeches were made by Mr. J. Jarman (secretary of the Society) and Mr. W. Wright, who occupied the chair. Madame H. Groves contributed two fine songs entitled "Hills of Donegal" and "Cross ing the Bar." Miss Bella Baillie rendered, in capital style, songs entitled " Spring's Awaken- ing " and "Youth of Spring," with two little Irish songs and "When the Lads Come Home" as encores. Mr. J. It. Savin sang "The Veteran's Song" and "'Somerset," and was accorded an encore. The I:tumorous, part of the programme was in the able hands of Mr. Sutton Lonsdale.

div.head: Wesley Guild Rally.
div.p: Wesley Guild Rally.

The Rev. Trevor Davies, of Southport, at- tended a united- Wesley Guild Rally which was held in the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Thursday. In the afternoon the reverend gentle- man preached to a large congregation, and in the evening he addressed a public meeting, which was presided over by Mrs. James Dodds, of Penketh, who was supported by the Rev. Trevor H. Davies, A. J. Morton, W. T. Derry, H. T. Dixon and Percy Ineson.---,ln the course of her opening address, Mrs. Dodds reminded her hearers that a primary purpose of the Wesley Guild was to help, and enlarge the church—to make it stronger and richer.—Gratifying reports were read from the secretaries of the various local Wesley Guilds. It transpired that the combined membership of the Guilds was TM and that the Guild shield had this year been won for the second time by Sankey Bridges.— In the course of his address the Rev. Trevor Davies laid emphasis upon the fact that what was wanted in the church to-day was the Holy Spirit.—At the close a vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Dodds and the speaker, on the proposition of the Rev. W. T. Derry.

Miss Marie Houghton At Hereford. "The Seasons," given by the Hereford Choral Society at the Shirehall (says the "Hereford Times") was a refreshing perform- ance. Miss Marie Houghton took the soprano part of Jane, the farmer's daughter. Miss Marie Houghton was here in 1912 in "St. John's Eve." Her voice was then described as fresh and clear, and everyone who heard her- recently at the Cathedral and on Tuesday at the concert could not do otherwise than endorse this statement. She possesses a remarkable equability and depth of tone for a soprano. Perhaps her chief opportunity was in the air, "0, how pleasing to the senses," but the open- ing parts of the winter scenes were certainly quite as good in their appeal. Miss Houghton gave the air, "Lusinghe pin care" from Handel's "Alessandro." The rich quality of her voices could hardly have been better exhi- bited than in this, and in it she was able to show a flexibility which was especially pleas- ing because her previous efforth had not had the some opportunity. She was eneered, and gave a modern love- song.

div.p: ST. ANDREW'S DAY.—Continued.

Scotch, nation. He said that Scotsmen had defects and virtues, the difficulty was to know which was which. •(Laughter.) , Mr. G. Bowman proposed the toast of the "Town We Live In." He remarked that War- rington was the scene of the defeat of the Scots in 1618. A good number of years had passed since then, and the Scotsmen had been endeavouring to make a peaceful conquest of the good old town. (Laughter.) OTHER TOASTS AND THE MUSIC The toast of the "Caledonia* AssociatTon was proposed by Alderman D. Tinnion. Other toasts honoured were "The Visitors" (proposed by Mr. W. Murray and acknow- ledged by Councillor J. T. Locker), "The' Lassies" (proposed by Mr. J. McDermid and responded to by Mr. P. H. Brown)," and," The President" (proposed by Mr. W.
