div.head: Mine Host Councillor Chrimes.
div.p: Mine Host Councillor Chrimes.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday, the off-licence of 16-18, Greenall-street, was tem- porarily transferred to Arthur Fellows, of 202, Longford-street. The licence of the Ship Inn, Liverpool-road, was similarly transferred from the executors of the late, Mrs. Walker ,to Councillor John Chrimes.
What About A Plum Pudding For " Tommy " ?

Among the "special needs " at the Raddon Court Red Cross Hospital are plum puddings, and it is hoped that many will be forthcoming at the next Pound Day, which is to be held on Wednesday next. Blankets, mincemeat and groceries are also specially required.

Wood's College. The, following pupils of Wood's College sub- mitted Primary Theory Tests in Gregg Short- hand of sufficiently high standard to warrant certificates being granted them :—Kate Mur- tagh, Lily Bailey, Mabel Bagshaw, Ivy Shaw, A. lligham, Ethel Oakley, Mary Tanner, I. Grundy and J. Small. Miss Murtagh has been particularly congratulated by the examining body on the excellence of her paper. „

div.head: Spanish Teacher's Sudden Death.
div.p: Spanish Teacher's Sudden Death.

Senor Antonio Martinez, aged 54 years, who was for a number of years a teacher of Spanish in Warrington, died suddenly at his residence, 23, Hill-road, Mossley-hill, Liverpool on Satur- day. He was appointed Spanish teacher at the local Technical School in 1906, but later was transferred to the Commercial Institute in Arpley-street. He was- teaching in Warrington on the Wednesday before his death.

div.head: Motor Cycle On Fire.
div.p: Motor Cycle On Fire.

Through the explosion of the petr )1 tank, a motor cycle caught fire on Tuesday evening in Wilderspool-road. The cycle, which had a side- car attached, was proceeding in the direction of Stockton Heath. With the'aid of sacks, secured from a neighbouring works, the fire was con- fined to the mechanism of the cycle. In aboat five minutes a patent fire extinguisher was pro- cured, and with this the flames were soon put out.
Special War "In Memoriam" Service.

The Parish Church Magazine for this month contains the following :—" A special service in commemoration of our sailors and soldiers who have been killed or died of their wounds during the war, will be held at the Parish Church on Friday, December 17th, at 8 p.m. His Worship the Mayor has promised to attend, and has in- vited the members of the Corporation to accompany him. We shall ask the clergy of the town to co-operate with us, and invite their people to join."

div.head: "Tommies' " Tea.
div.p: The "Tommies' " Tea.

It is expected that a large crowd of people will be present at the Parr Hall on Thursday next, when the much-discussed " Tommies' " Tea will be held. But, if sufficient funds are to be raised to provide the Winwick Hospital wounded soldiers with a cinematograph and to give them a happy Christmas, it is necessary that not only scores, but hundreds, aye and even thousands, should be there. The proceed- ings will be opened at 3 p.m. by Lady Harmood Banner.

div.head: Daresbury Farmer Unsuccessfully Summoned.
div.p: Daresbury Farmer Unsuccessfully Summoned.

At the St. Helens Petty Sessions yesterday, John Thomas Fryer, of Kekewick Farm, Dares- bury, was summoned for selling milk deficient in fat to the extent of 4 per, cent,—Mr. T. S. Steel, for the defendant, stated that the reason for the deficiency was that the cows had, been out to grass during the summer, and as it was now the end of the season the nature of the grass bad deteriorated. The milk had improved on the cows going to the shippon.—lt being proved that the milk had not been tampered with, the case was dismissed. Musical Successes."'

_ At the examination of music held at tiver- pool on November 15th and succeeding days, pupils of Mrs. G. Mayhall, Associate of the Victoria College of Music, and certificates of Trinity and London Colleges, 148, Knutsford- road, Warrington,, passed very successfully in pianoforte playing, and the theory of music. Their names and grades are as follows: ASSOC fate.—Miss Janet Makin, Ellesmere street, Warrington. This entitles her to append the letters A.V.C.M. to her name, and to. wear the cap and gown of the college. Intermediate.—Miss Cissie Lamb, Ashwood- avenue, Padgate-lane; first. class pass with honours. Miss May Allen, Sutton-street, War- rington, first class pass with honours.

£72 Compensation for Loss of Son. At the Warrington County Court on Thurs- day, before His Honour Judge J. Scott-Fox, K.C., Patrick Dunn, a miner, of 3, Wood-street, Golborne, claimed, as next of kin, compensa- tion from Messrs. J. F. and E. Caulfield, Ltd.. of Newton-le-Willows, in respect of an accident which occurred to his son James.

Mr. W. Trenholme, of Bradford, appeared for the applicant, and Mr. J. Chapman, of Man- chester, for the respondents. Mr. Trenholme said that James Dunn, son of the applicant, was killed as a result of an acci- dent whilst in the employ of the respondents. The claim for compensation was on behalf of the father, mother and their two children, who were partly dependent upon the deceased, whose average earnings were 19s. 10d. a week. The parties had come to terms—subject to his Honour's approval—for the payment of a sum of C 72 to the applicants. This was agreed to by his Honour.

Fighting Mens' Wives Entertained. While "Tommy" and "Jack" are away doing duty for King and country on land and sea the question of brightening the lives of those they have left behind has been solved by the members of the Warrington Branch of the British Women's Temperance Association, who are holding a series of social evenings in various parts of the town. One of these gath- erings was held on Wednesday evening in the Working Men's Mission Schoolroom, Bank Quay, when a large number of wives, mothers and sweethearts were present. Mrs. W. Reid (wife of the Rev. W. Reid, Presbyterian min- ister) occunied the chair, and gave a short and homely address. The programme was -sus- tained by members of the Working Men's Mission Women's Bible Class, who rendered solos and choruies in a very acceptable man- ner. A Belgian lady who was present enter- tained the audience with two solos, both of which were sung in her native tongue. During an interval in the programme light refresh- Inents were handed round by members of the lassociation.

Gift for Old Railway Servant On Saturday eveniDg there was a large gath- erihg of the local employes of the Cheshire Lines Committee and friends at the Victoria Vaults, Mersey-street, the reason for the assembly being a presentation to ex-Inspector William Richard Smith, who has recently be- come the licensee of the house, and who for thirty-seven and a half years worked on the line, for twenty years in the capacity of Inspector. During his long period of service Mr. Smith not only earned the respect and esteem of his fellow-employes, but also his chiefs, and there was such a widespread desire to do him honour on the occasion of his retire- s. ment from the Committee's service that money enough was forthcoming to buy a gold watch for him, and another for Mrs. Smith, and to also hand over to Mr. Smith a purse of gold. On behalf of the subscribers, Mr. Darbyshire made the presentation, which Mr. Smith suit- ably acknowledged. During the evening songs were rendered by Messrs. McGregor, Stout, Young, Hornby, Ffannan, Holton and Lomas, Messrs. Roberts and Laivas being the accom- panists.

div.p: BIRTHS. MARRIAGES. DEATHS.

Notices of births, marriages,, and deaths, in memoriam notices, and acknowledgments of sympathy are inserted in "The Examiner" at the following rates :—Not exceeding 20 words, is. 6d: each; every additional seven words, ed.
Deaths. COOPER.—November 25th, at 163, Welifield-street, George Cooper, aged 28 years.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
MR. SONAR LAW'S OPTIMISM.
Mr. Bonar Law took a general review of the

situation. at the St. Andrew's .Day. dinner of the Royal Scots Corporation.. He frankly ad- mitted that from the East he looked for no good news for manly months. "We may have bad news long before we have good." But the tendency on the whole is that we are inexor- ably moving towards victory. ' We have over- come the munitions difficulty, and on.the West front we have nothing to fear and much to hope for. In Russia we see the same thing. Munitions are coming through, and the inva- sion has. been stopped., The :silent pressure of the Navy is telling, and the whole popula- tion of Germany is ceasing .to • believe that ,victory is in their grasp. • In regard to finance, which is largely the key to the situation, 'Mr. Bonar Law is,none the less Sanguine. "I do not pretend," 'he said, "that we can go on indefinitely on the scale at which we are going now, and I wish it could be reduced; but I do say that the wealth of, this country has. not been touched yet, and that .we shall stand the strain much longer than our 'enemies can."
LOCAL SCOTS AND THEIR V.C. PIPER.

The Warrington Caledonian Association were very fortunate. this year. On those ‘annual occasions when the clans foregather to honour Scotland and all things Scotch, a piper is usually engaged to grace the occasion. Piper Laidlaw, upon whom the King recently conferred .the Victoria Cross, was in great demand from all over the country. The War- rington Association beat off till rivals and secured the . hero for their St. Andrew's dinner—much to their own delight. and the envy of many brither Scots in other parts. The Manchester Caledonian Association, through its _hen. secretary, have shown that

no ill-will lingers in Manchester at any rate. Mr. Pearson, the gentleman in question, promptly wrote:— " Dear Mr. Davenport,—l presume you would be in the chair at your St. Andrew's dinner last night, and I desire to congratulate you and your Association on having had the honour of entertaining a Scotch V.C. hero in the person of Piper Laidlaw,. It is a unique experience to have the opportunity of thus honouring the wearer of the Victoria Cross just back from the scene of the fighting, and lam very glad indeed that you seized it. I see from the newspapers that Piper Laidlaw played you a tune or twa, and I am sure he would thoroughly enjoy your gathering." Of course, Piper Laidlaw was in our local Lord Derby Hospital, and possession is nine parts of the law.

div.head: MAYOR'S WHIST DRIVE.
div.p: THE MAYOR'S WHIST DRIVE.

Last year the Mayor and Mayoress gave a whist drive and dance in Parr Hall in aid of patriotic funds, and as wsuccess the event set up a distinct record. It is going to be re- peated on Thursday, the 16th inst., in aid of theSoldiers' Tobacco Fund and the Infirmary. Tickets, we are pleased to know, are being freely bought, and it is hoped that all who in- tend to be present will have secured their tickets in good time, so that provision may be made to meet everyone's comfort. Refresh- ments will be served at strictly moderate prices. The cause is so good and the event so -attractive that the drive and dance will un- doubtedly fulfil the expectations of His Worship and those working along with him.

div.head: FREEMASONRY.
div.p: FREEMASONRY.
"Lodge Of Lights" Century And
A Half Record.

The 150th anniversary of the "Lodge of Lights!" No. 148 wasP celebrated at the Masonic Hall, Bold-street, Warrington, on Monday even- ing. W. Bro. C. S. Smith, the Master fof the Lodge, presided, and was supported by a large number of Provincial brethren and Past Masters of that and all the other Warrington lodges. It had been intended to mark the occasion by a large Masonic gathering and banquet in Parr Hall. but the event was cele- brated..in consequence of the war, on very much more modest lines.

The Worshipful Masters of the other War- rington lodges were invited to take part in the ceremony, as follows: W. Bro. 11. Maddock! as Master of the "Gilbert Greenall " Lodge, which ranks next in seniority, to No. 148, occupied the Senior Warden's chair; W. Bro. W. H. Tickle (in- the'absence in France of W. Bro. the 'Rev. W. Bracecamp the Master of " Charity " Lodge), .occupied the Junior Warden's chair; and other duties were per- formed by W. Bra. J. M. Murray, Master of "Friendship" Lodge; W. Bro. T. S. Steel, Master of "St. Elphin's " Lodge; and W. Bro. Woods, Master of the "Lodge of Rectitude.", W. Bra. Herbert Woods read a paper on "The History of Freemasonry in Warrington. The paper, which was' of a most interesting descrip- tion, and was favourably commented upon, set forth the fact that the earliest record, of the making of a 'Freemason in this town as con- tained in the diary of Elias, Aehmole, who died in 1692, and concerning whom an interest- ing and instructive article recently appeared in "The Examiner."

A Lodge Of Freemasons was constituted in Warrington in 1755, but it had no connection with the Lodge iato which Elias Ashmole was initiated. . That Lodge of 1755 was ultimately transferred to Quebec, where it finally lapsed about 1822. The "Lodge of Lights" was warranted on November Bth, 1765, and had held its meetings regularly from that time to, the present day. During its existence the Lodge had, to a considerable extent, been connected . with public events in the town; such, for in- stance, as the laying of the foundation stone of the Museum and Library in 1855, and with St. Peter's Church and Orford Church, &c. It was also associated with the placing of the key-stone in Warrington Bridge in 1837, which key-stone is now being carefully preserved.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
AN OPEN LETTER
To The Clergy And Christian Laymen Of Warrington.

div.head: WEEKEND DRINKING.
div.p: WEEKEND DRINKING.

The Mayor, some months ago, stated that he saw no cause for restricting the hours of sale of intoxicants. I agree with your correspondent last week that the public he a right to know what representations he made last Tuesday week 'before the Manchester Conference. Did he express the same opinion? 'The following particulars of the drinking habits of a section of our townsmen are certainly of such a char- acter ,that they cannot be passed over lightly in view of the moral back-wash they represent. By the request of the Citizeps' Temperance League the observations of five public-houses were made during two bouts on a recent Sat- urday evening-8 to 10—and an hour and a half on the Sunday evening following-7.30 to 9—and the following persons entered:—

My purpose- in writing this letter is to call , the attention of the public of Warrington to ' a state of moral torpidity from which, in the view of a good many people, the good old town is suffering. We pride ourselves, and rightly so, on our glorious historyl civil and religious, and the eternal debt, we owe to the moral stal- warts of the past, who dearly won these things for us. We therefore, in the first place, look to all the Christian ministers, and, secondly, to the Christian laymen associated with them, to safeguard the moral welfare of our people. I think it is not out of place to say that we do not receive all the direction and guidance on public morals from the sources named that we have a right to expect. It is.all very, well for our mirtisters, as they occasionally do, to give expression to Christian platitudes and pious expressions deploring social 'evils, the enormity of which they are only indirectly acquainted with; if thew evils were burnt into their souls by first-hand knowledge they could not he satisfied with 'mere passive -utterance. Direct acquaintance would result in well- directed efforts to 'awaken the public conscience. I claim it is thtuty of Christian mintsters to be the leaders not only in moral thoirght, but also in moral aetion, and': that they ought to know the moral conditions which afflict the well-being of the community and, voice the Christian conscience thereon: If on questions of public morals they spoke with one voice,' with the Christian public behind them, I ask, who would stand against them? The holy vocation of the 'Christian Church is not to go "cap in hand" to any 'public authority begging attention, but in the name of the Christian Church to demand. that these things shall not be. Concerning the laymen, it is constantly remarked that. the town is poor indeed in representative laymen, taking any initiative and lead on public morals. It is not wit of place here to ask how many' are there who owe their present position to the thought and care bestowed upon them in early life by others who were really alive to their moral and spiritual interests. "They once ran well. What has hindered them?" tls it material prosperity and association? This general indifference is exercising the minds of the rank and file in the Churches. A few months ago the Citizens' Temperance League addressed a circular letter to every Christian Church in this town, asking their co-operation in a house-to-house canvass in the interests of the King's War Pledge. There were" six replies; only four were sympathetic. I cast no refleetion, 'except indirectly as indi- cating the indifference resultant on the moral aspect having no voice. Another 'case: A resolution was passed a short time since by the Citizens' Temperance League and sent. to the Watch Committee, call- ing attention to the growing evil of intemper- ance, especially amongst young men and women. Our local leaders, among them Chris- tian' laymen,. confessed they saw no reason for alarm, and yet at the very time they were admitting their ignorance one of the worst cases that have disgraced our town was before our Police Court. •

As a Free" Churchman I ain more acquainted with this section- of the Christian Church. They, at any rate, 'do not possess their former vigour. and. I am apprehensive lest the with- drawal of intelligent laymen from 'personal activity in Church work is responsible for some of the indifference. Lord Haldane, pro- bably the. greatest thinker we have to-day, recently uttered a note' of warning to the Churches "not to 'neglect spiritual teaching." I make no comment on the figures given above, except to say ,that the facts they reveal should give our religious leaders much food for thought. One striking fact stands out—that the people are neither in their homes.nor the churches—and if the clergy want congregations to preach to they will find them in the public- houses in their thousands. Other aspects of the grave conditions will serve for another letter. The moral -conscience of the people must be stirred.
Signed on behalf of the Citizens' Temperance League,
JOHN GRIFFITHS, Vice-Vresident.
Warrington.

div.head: GRATEFUL "TOMMY."
div.p: A GRATEFUL "TOMMY."
Ex-Whilecross Patient's Letter Of Thanks.

The Matron of the Whitecross Military Hos- pital has received a graceful letter of thanks from an ex-patient, Private S. Nicholson, ot the 6th Cameron Highlanders. Writing from 7, Bruntsfield-avenue, Edinburgh, he says: "I beg permission to accord my thanks for the con- sideration and kindness shown me at your hos- pital during my stay there from October sth to November 19th. I can hardly find words in which adequately to express my appreciation of the attention received, but I do not wonder at patients recovering so rapidly—as was the case with myself—when everything that is possible is done for their benefit. In truth, my sojourn in hospital was a source of great enjoyment that I shall not readily forget." This is only one of many similar letters re- ceived acknowledging kindly and successful treatment received at Whitecross Hospital.

div.head: TRAGIC STORY.
div.p: TRAGIC STORY.
SERGT.-MAJOR THOMAS DAVIES.
Shot While Returning From Trench Duty In Flanders.

The town was startled yesterday when the news rapidly spread that Sergeant-Major Thomas Davies, of the Warrington Territorials, serving in Flanders; had been killed while on duty. DetailS of. the tragedy are not to hand, but that, the Sergeant-Major has been shot lead is only too true. The first in- timation of the affair came to the km H. (Wen from Quartermaster-Sergeant William Tynan, also of the Territorials, who asked the reverend gentleman to break the sad news to Sergeant-Major Davies' wife and mother, at 7, Lexden-street, Lovely-lane, where the three formerly lived very happily together.

div.head: One Of The Cleanest Soldiers.
div.p: One Of The Cleanest Soldiers.

"He was shot," said this terrible message, "while returning from trench duty. I do not know the full, details. . . . One of the clean- est soldiers has been taken from the Army, cleanest in word, thought or. deed. Ile has lived and died a model to any man out here, always true to the Christ he professed at home, and never afraid of checking profanity wher-

div.head: ST. ANDREW'S DAY.
div.p: ST. ANDREW'S DAY.
Warrington Scotsmen Honour The Piper Of Loos.
DINNER, SONG AND SPEECH

There was a gathering of the clans at the Lion Hotel', Warrington, on' Tuesday evening, when the annual dinner of the Warrington. Caledonian Association was held. For years past the Association have met on St. Andrew's Day (November 30th), but last year the gather- ing Was not held owing to the desire of the members not to take part in soCial events during a time of stress and anxiety. This year, how- ever, it was felt that they should meet, not only for the sake of meeting, but also for the purpose of helping some good organisation that has arisen out of the war. And, consequent upon their gathering, a large sum will be devoted to the Lord Derby War Hospital Cinema Fund.
A most distinguished guest at the dinner was Piper Daniel Laidlaw, V.C, of the King's Own Scottish Borderers, who is still a patient— though happily convalescent—at the Lord Derby Hospital, Winwick.

div.head: PIPING IN THE HAGGIS.
div.p: PIPING IN THE HAGGIS.

After assembling in the hall, the guests followed the Piper into the dining-room, and whilst they were taking their seats were treated to a "skirl of the pipes." Later, Piper Laidlaw played in "the haggis "—without which national dish no gathering of men from " beyant the Tweed" is complete—and the "Drams a la Ecossaise "—which is a very nice way of phrasing "Wee droppies o' Scotch." But the chief event of the evening occurred when the Piper marched round the room play- ing the two tunes which he played- when he won the Victoria Cross—namely, "Blue Bon- nets Over the Border" and "The Standard on the Braes o' Mar." When the Piper con- 'eluded, the company rose from their seats, and after cheering him time after time, sang "lie's a Jolly Good Fellow." Referring to the Piper, the President of the Association (Mr. J. L. Davenport) said that they were greatly honoured by his presence, as he had been in- vited to a number of St. Andrew's Day gather- ings in almost every part of the Kingdom. He had, however, preferred to remain in Warring- ton, as he said the people here had treated him very kindly. After the dinner, the President submitted the toasts of "The King," "The Queen, Queen Alexandra and the Rest of the Royal Family" and "The Duke of Rothesay, president of the Association." He also read a number of letters of apology for non-attendance.

div.head: ABSENT FRIENDS.
div.p: ABSENT FRIENDS.

Writing from the House of Commons, Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., said "My. public duties take me away a great deal, and involve very arduous travelling. Had I been able to attend, I should have asked to leave to pay a humble Saxon's tribute to the undying glories of your Scottish regiments. One cannot' read of their gallantry and sacrifice without the deepest emotion." Sir Arthur Crosfield wrote as follows:

"I am greatly obliged for your kind letter of the 22nd, and for the invitation which indeed. is most tempting, and I wish with all my heart that I could accept. Alas, it is simply im.' possible for me to get to Warrington before December 6th, when lam due there. The whole of my time here is fully occupied. I have • much on hand here just now, and in addition am very shortly publishing a little book. I am anxious to get it into the printer's hands as speedily as possible, and therefore every minute of my time is occupied with• its preparation. Though not with you in the flesh, I shall be with you in the spirit, on November 30th—a date that Will bring back to one some I f my most cherished recollections of the truly delightful evenings I have had the privilege of spending with you previously on' St. Andrew's Day." Other letters were received from Colonel Moggridge. Colonel Mocatta, Dr. Hutton,. Mr. Martin Nicholls (chief constable), Councillor W. H. J. Jenkins and Mr. Malcolm Grant. In a short speech, the Preside/it remarked on the loss that Warrington had sustained by the death of Sir Peter Carlew Walker.

OUR GALLANT SOLDIERS AND SAILORS. Proposing the toast of. "His Majesty's Forces," Mr. J. Fulton-Smith said that the British were on their trial as a nation. They were constained to ask how it was that the country had been led into this terrible conflict with Germany, and that they as a nation were compelled, An self-defence, to exert every influence and all the resources they possessed. to prevent themselves being wiped off the face of the earth. As a nation they were compelled by a solemn compact to support Belgium in the event of that• country being invaded, or its rights violated. That compact required that a certain number of men should 'he sent to her aid. Re believed that the number was 120,000, but Britain had been able to do more for her ally than that, and to put 1,000,000 men in the field was a thing never accomplished before in the history of this countrY.; and a thing certainly never expected by a large number of people! That had been done by the indomitable energy and patriotism which inspired the heart of every true Britisher. The power of German organisation had failed; German plans had gone " a-gley "all along. THE INSPIRATION OF TRADITION.
Replying to the toast, Captain lWathams said that nobert Burns, • away back in the days when the .country was threatened by the might of the French, wrote a poem in which occurred the lines:
"While.we sing God save the King, Ne'er forget the people."

The National Anthem to-day was a prayer. People, soldiers and sailors were all embraced in one phrase, "His Majesty's Forces." Before the war the British Army was spoken of as a mercenary army, but it was composed none the less of men who had made soldiering a pro- fession, not so much because they loved soldier- ing, but because of the traditions. It was be- cause of those traditions that the original British Army, made history on the Mons-road: (Loud applause.) That was the example that the British people had before them on the out- break of the war, and there arose an army of men who joined, not because they loped to fight, but because their country called them and be- cause in some way they caught som of that spirit of sacrifice which animated the Army on the battlefields of Mons: (Applause.)

div.head: "A, Willing Race."
div.p: "A, Willing Race."

They had the traditions of the British Army and Navy in mind and the whole of their glorious history, with the result that to-day the nation were a willing race. They knew what their forefathers did at Waterloo, Blenheim ~ and Balaclava, and whilst they did not make gods of their ancestors, they felt that in their -veins ran the blood oft heroes. (Applause.) From the past they received the inspiration of their deeds, and they went forward into the future with a divine faith in the justice of their cause, Tie would like to say that in going into the future the nation had realised that it could not live on its ,Past, that it could not live in its present, but could only live by keeping alive in the hearts of the people, the spirit of deter- mination. That being so, they were .going, for- ward into the fight prepared to make all the sacrifices necessary. Concluding, Captain.' Mathams asked that whilst they honoured the Army, they should not forget the Navy: the debt that they owed to the Navy was the debt of the nation's greatness. (Applause.)

div.head: "SCOTLAND FOR EVER!"
div.p: "SCOTLAND FOR EVER!"
" Scotland " was proposed by Dr. J. S. Manson, who spoke on the characteristics Of the

div.head: LATE SERGT.-MAJOR T. DAVTEs.
div.p: THE LATE SERGT.-MAJOR T. DAVTEs.

ever it may have come from. The men of his Company ,realise their great. loss, and it is with heavy hearts that they lie down to rest to-night. I have lost a friend—a true friend— and you. sir, have lost a stalwart -in your Church."

div.head: Chaplain's Story.
div.p: The Chaplain's Story.
In a very sympathetic letter to Mrs. Davies, the Rev. F. G. Goddard (Vicar of All Saints', Stoneyeroft, Liverpool,- and-an Army Chaplain) writes:— s
" I Ara a Chapinin• to -to which the 4th South Lancashires are attached. I grieve to say that I have sad news to tell you about your husband.— i.'as killed last night

whilst on duty—being shot while leading- a detachment of his men---killed very distress- ingly, too, by a soldiewbf another regiment. The funeral was...to-day, and I officiated at it. We laid him /to rest. in the churchyard of -a little place—whose church is shattered—behind our lines, where lie - some: more of his regi- ment, The Battalion was very upset over it. I came over with an old friend of your hus- band's, and he spoke much of him. His death was so tragic and so unexpected that even for us it is hard to bear. But you must. feel that he, too, died for his country. I offered a prayer for you at the graveside, that God would be with you and' bless you with His presence in 'your great 'how; of trial. You must realise that now you are one of the noble band ,of England's 'wives and .children that have given up their very best and dearest for .a sacred and holy cause. May God, 'Who spared not His own Son, but freely gave Him for us,' be with you in this fellowship of suf- fering. You have our earnest prayers out here. There are so many in his Battalion who will miss him."

div.head: Served In SaOh Africa.
div.p: Served In SaOh Africa.

- The late Sergeant-Major was a water fitter in the employ of the Warrington Corporation. He had' seen considerable service, not only in the -Territorials, but in. the old Volunteers, with whose A:dive Service Company he went to South Africa, _ under the late Captain Appleton. He mobilised at once with the Territorials on the 'outbreak of war and went with the first contingent 'to France:
A Golborne-street Stalwart.

• Our late hero was connected with the Gol- borne-street Baptist Church frimn boyhood. He became a member and took an active part in the young men's class, while of the Institute he was one of the authors and became the life and soul of its existence. He was captain of the Free Church Boys' Brigade and was actually in camp with them twelve months last AugUst, when instructions to mobilise were issued.

He was held in the very highest esteem by the Church and congregation and the school at Golborne-street, •which was evidenced by the fact that on Thursday, when the sad news reached the Pastor (the Rev. H. Ogden), a children's concert that had been arranged for the came night was post'poned to some future date.

div.head: HOSPITAL SUNDAY "AS USUAL."
div.p: HOSPITAL SUNDAY "AS USUAL."
Collections To Be Made On March 19th Next.

A meeting of the Hospital Sunday Com- mittee was held at the Warrington Infirmary on Friday ,afternoon. tar. John Fairclough was in the chair, and others present were the Revs: Canon Willis (rector of Warrington), James Davies, W. T.. Derry and T. A. Hind, Mr. J. 11. J. Hampson (hon. secretary of the knfirm- ary and Dispensary) and Mr. A. J. Jolley (hon. secretary of the Hospital Sunday Committee). In his annual report, Mr. Jolley pointed out that two places of worship which contributed to the fund in 1914 . failed to do so in 1915. Nine others renewed their contributions or commenced contributing. „There was a net gain under this head of £7 13s. 6d. The total receipts were £277. 18s. 6d.,. an increase as compared with last year of £2O Bs. &I. Of the total re- ceived, £159 2s. was collected within the borough and £llB 16s. 6d. outside the borough. The ex- penses had totalled £l4 10s., as compared with £l6 Bs. 2d: last year. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by the Rev. Canon Willis, the, report was adopted.

The Rev. James Davies moved and the Rev. Canon Willis seconded that Mr.' Jolley be re- appointed hon. secretary of the committee for the ensuing twelve mcluths. The proposition was carried unanimously. It was also decided to send a word of thanks to the officials of the churches who had con- tributed.

div.head: HAVE YOU ATTESTED?
div.p: HAVE YOU ATTESTED?
Last Days Of Recruiting Under
Lord Derby's Scheme.
FINAL CHANCE NEAR AT HAND.
Come into the ranks and fight for your King and country. Don't stay in the crowd and stare.—Lord Derby's Recruiting Poster.

The canvass of the "eligibles" of .Warring, ton, undertaken under Lord Derby's Scheme, is nearing completion. The canvassers who .have BO far come forward and Proferred their services have worked splendidly, but the task is a big one, and still more voluntary assistants are sought, and if only another fifty will come forward—and it ought not to be a difficult matter to get that number in a town of the size of Warrington—the• task can be completed in three or four days. When the • canvass started over six thousand men had to 1* visited; at the moment of writing a little over a. thousand remain to be seen. During the past week, report the honorary officials at the headquarters in Horsemarket- street, every help has been received from em- ployers. Every firm approached hag granted the request that they would facilitate can- vassing in their works. The .idea in ,going to the works is to get at the man whom it is difficult to find at his. home; it is a sort of final round-up. At one large works in the torn the eligible men have been examined and attested On the spot, and other firms have applied to the -Horsemarket-street headquarters to have their men similarly dealt with, a 9 it saves time and trouble and obviates the 'risk' of canvassers missing the men for whom they bold cards.

div.head: MORE AND STILL MORE" CANVASSERS
div.p: MORE AND STILL MORE" CANVASSERS
NEEDED.

Special stress is laid upon the need for more canvassers by those in charge of the local recruiting office. Of course, only those who are physically fit can go to the Front and do the actual fighting on behalf of the country, but those above military age and those who have been rejected on medical grounds can iinportaat the War 'by ,giving some of 'their time tci the completion of this. all-important canvass. "Slackers" is a word that has been bandied about. much of late, and it has generally ,been applied to the men eligible for Army Service. "is. it now .to be applied," asked one of the local honorary recruiters, "to the Older men and women who, appreciating the difficulties" of the position, nevertheless hold aloof froth this canvassing. work? - Are there not fifty men and women in Warrington who will. come for- ward and help the ,eighty, who have already done so much, to finish their task? The offi- cials at headquarters feel that it ' will be a reproach, to Warrington if the canvass is not eatisfaetorily completed within the given .time 7--which expires on December 11th."
CANVASSERS WELCOMED AT THE HOMES OF THE MEN.

may be," continued the official inter- viewed, *" that ladies and gentlemen, .who would otherwise offer their services, fear: that they may be Met with insults or contumely when they call at the houses 'of the supposed 'eligibles,' but,' generally speaking, such is not the Case, and, in fact, the majority of the canvassers have come positively to like. the .work, feeling that they are doing a good ser- „vice to their country, to the person ,canvassed and to the employer. Moreover, they feel' that it is only fair to the presumed 'eligible' that he Should have the opportunity of stating his case, if he feels that he ought not to go. Should anybody, by oversight or through any other reason, be 'uncanvassed, he will be less than unpatriotic if he does not present himself A the Horsemarket-street offices and either 'offer bim self or give his reasons why he. thinks he should not go soldiering." •

div.head: "SATISFACTION AND RELIEF" OF THE
div.p: "SATISFACTION AND RELIEF" OF THE
CANVASSED.

"Some of the men who have been can- vassed," continued our informant, "have ex- pressed their thanks to the canvassers for call- ing upon them and explaining to them so lucidly the position of affairs. Many doubted as to whether or not they would be committing themselves by giving information to the can- 'v asser, but after they have had the talk with a canvasser they have expressed nothing but satisfaction and relief that they have been .called upon and that the ordeal has been got over." ) There are, it appears, some four hundred men in the town who have stated, apparently, good and 'valid reasons why they should be Placed in a later group for business reasons, bid who so far; have not attested. div.head: WOUNDED.
div.p: WOUNDED.
RIFLEMAN C. HOSE.
Hit After Rescuing Half-Buried Comrades.

Rifleman Charles, Rose, of the King's. Royal Rifles, has been wounded in two places with shrapnel—in his hand and. side. Writing from the Ist War Hospital, Rubery Hill, Birthing- ham, to his wife, who resides with her two children—aged five and two :year e respectively— at 357. Winwiek;.road, he says:— "We were in the trenches, up to the knees in mud, on Sunday. It was very quiet, which was a very strange thing; for there .is. generally more. fighting on a Sunday than on any other day. On Monday we 'had just finished breakfast and T. was off duty until ten o'clock. As it was quiet, I got in the, dug-out to read 'The Examiner,' Which, you ,sent me, but I had no sooner got in than the enemy started sending shells over. Two of them dropped close to my dug-out, so I thought I would be safer outside.
In the Nick of Time.
"So out I got! And none too soon; for I had

not gone ten yards .when h shell dropped on the dug-out. So I said good-bye to my- kit and kip'! I then went into .a traverse, along with four more privates, and a corporal, but the shells knocked half the traverse in. The' cor- poral and two others were buried, but I was at the other end -and so escaped again. I helped to dig my comrades out, and we were in full view of the enemy all the time. But we got them out. all .right, and they were only a bit shaken. Later fotir of us went behind the traverse, laughing, .110-joking and having a smoke. ;The enemy must have been following me, for a shell burst close to me, and a pieoe about four inches Jong hit inc on the hand, and another piece got we in the side. When I got up the other two chaps were on the -floor, both. wounded. I. ran off for the stretcher-bearer.," but I wilt tht wrong way and IjDet a Quartermaster-gergeaht of another.torapany, who wrapped my; hand up, and off I iveut the (Tr-eiiitiv station. I can thank lucky star for being in Rubery Hill • r-A,;,.•9ntal, Birmingham., at the present time. I am all right here, and could not be looked after better in Buckingham .Palace. But I should like to be a bit neareilein."
RIFLEMAN CHARLES ROSE. Wounded.'

div.head: LAST EEK FOR RECRUITING.
div.p: LAST EEK FOR RECRUITING.
Canvass Under Lord Derby's Scheme Nearing Completion.
HAVE you BEEN ATTESTED?
Final Chance For Joining Under The Group System.

The men of military age and fitness in Warrington, who .have not already done so, will, (hiring the next few days, have, their last chance- of attesting under the group system, which forms part and parcel of the great recruiting scheme initiated by Lord Derby. Unless they are attested by Saturday next they run a risk of being swept into .the Army at an early date, instead of being formally enrolled and then relegated, according to their ages, to one 'or other of the many classes into which the able-bodied manhood.. of the country is to be divided. •

Joining under the group system is simple and fair, and it relieves the eligible man of all responsibility. It is the duty of every man, within the age limits laid down, to enrol, and then let the local, Tribunal try his cause, should he feel that he has grounds on which he should be excused from active service. It should not be forgotten that the right to appeal depends upon a man having first enrolled.

13y the kindness of the Corporation. tile Public Baths (Legh-street. entrance) will be, next week, placed at the disposal .of the local Recruiting Committee, and every arrangement will be. made for there enrolling the suitable men who offer.

div.head: TO MUNITION WORKERS.
div.p: TO MUNITION WORKERS.

It might be of service to quote the 'following official notice which has been issued with re- gard. to the enlistment of munition workers by the Ministry of Munitions, and which is signed by Lord Derby and the Right lion.. D. -Lloyd George Any Man officially, 'badged' or 'starred' for munitions work may. be enlisted for immediate service in the Army. A man so badged' or 'starred' may be attested for the reserve on condition of returning...to civil employment. Such men will, receive khaki armlets and will not be called up for service unless at some future time the Ministry' of Munitions decides that they are more urgently 'needed in the Army than for munitions work."

div.head: LOCAL TRIBUNALS.
div.p: LOCAL TRIBUNALS.

• Functions And Powers As To Grouping And Referring. It may be of interest to the manufacturer :as well as to the workman, briefly to outline the duties of the Tribunal and how it can be made use of by the eligible recruit. It is clearly laid down that no appeal can be considered by the Local Tribunal unless the appellant has been enrolled in his class, and this enrolment mnst be 'made not later than December 11th. There are .fOur lists of trades which. are pub- lished, and men who are engaged on these need not, unless they choose,: join their age groups, but they must be attested. . List A.—Occupations connected 'with. the •.. manufacture - and transport 'of munitions. List B.—Mining. • List C.—Certain employment in agricultural work and with the actual running of railways,. . • . • List D.—Occupations in connection 'with the manufacture of the export trade.

div.head: CLAIMS BY ATTESTED MEN.
div.p: CLAIMS BY ATTESTED MEN.

• So far as men in these trades are Concerned they will have the right to appear before the Tribunals .whether, they have attested or , not, hut unless they have attested their positions 'Will: be more Of a defendant than an appliCant.: 'Should the recruiting officer consider, after consulting with the employer, that these men can be released for military- duty he may ask for their release. If he fails to arrive at an understanding with the employer the case or cases can • be brought before the Tribunal. If the case or cases belong to List A the Local Tribunal 'will send their report to Minister of Munitions.
If the matter at issue :concerns. Lists C and D the reference goes to the Central Tribunal, and with these the final decision will rest .

Relating to a man who has been attested, notice of a claim given by an employer, on the ground that a man is individually indispen- sable in his civil employment, shall be sent to the Tribunal for the area in which the place of employment is situated.

But notice-of a claim by it man on grounds personal to himself, shell be sent to. the Tribunal for the area in which the plan resides. With reference to the mining industry, the recruiting officer will have no right to inter- fere. The Home Office is 'the department for this section, and it will be-a matter for arrange- ment between the employers and the men as to who can be spared.

Except for this section all listed workers will be liable to have their list of workers scrutinised by the recruiting representative. and this procedure also applies where men desire to be relegated to a later class.

"LISTED MEN" AT DISADVANTAGE. Although eligible, men who are not engaged in these scheduled trades will be entitled to ask to be put back to a later gronp, for domestic reasons or on account of their employment. But this privilege will only be extended to men who have attested before the 11th Of December, or, to put it. another way- non-attested Men will be applicants for favourable treatment, whereas the listed men Will only be brought there as defendants to an appeal brought by the recruit- ing representative. Before a man can make an application to be put further back, the consent of his employer should be secured. There is no compulsion, and therefore no man can be compelled to join, nor can he be com- pelled to stay in civilian employment, except in certain essential trades where they cannot ,caliSt for immediate service with the Colours. The form of application and the treatment of appellants will be made as simple as possible, and the procedure as little formal as possible. A notice of claims must be sent by a person who wishes to bring a case before a Local Tribunal to thp Office of the .Council by whim the Tribunal was appointed,' and for the War- rington Rural District the' Office will be Bewsey Chia mbers.

' There are 46 groups, 23, for single , men (in- cluding widowers without children dependant upon them), and 23 similar groups for married men: the first group tonsisting of single i men age 18, and the 46th group of married .men age 40. Each year constitutes a separate group. Men married since the 15th August, 1915, will be tredted as single men. Men of 18 will not be called up until they attain the age of 19. years.

div.head: REALLY "INDISPENSABLE"
div.p: REALLY "INDISPENSABLE"

. There will doubtless be some cases of men employed in one or other of the occupations in List's A and C who have not been starred; it will be open to a man or his:employer in a case of this kind to make an application to the Tribunal on the ground that the man is, in fact, engaged in one of these• occupations. If the recruiting officer agrees to the application the man will be treated as 'though he had been starred, and the Tribunal will then need only to notify the man or the employer as the ease may be.

On the other hand if the recruiting officer does not assent to the application the Local Tribunal can investigate the facts and send their recommendation to the Central Appeal Tribunal who, if they agree that the man is engaged in an occupation under the above heads. then•the man is to be treated as though he had been• starred. It muSt be clearly- understood that the recommendation and the decision of the Tribunals must be given for nationa.; masons, not simply for the convenience of the

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
employer. Speaking. generally, the employer must be able to show

(1) Not only that the man is individually in- dispensable, but also (2) That every effort has been niatle to obtain a temporary substitute for the man, and (3) That the maintenance 'f :the business is of national importance either for war work, for other essential domestic re- quirements, or for eiport trade, and further • (4) That the employer has given reasonable facilities for enlistment to men in his employ.

" Indispensable must be strictly inter- preted. It is not enough that the employer should be able to show that he will be inconvenienced, even seriously inconvenienced. It is imperative in this time of critical nepd that employers should do all in their power to adapt them- selves to the changed conditions; that, by the employment of men not eligible fer military service, by the employment of women—(which must be extended) and by reorganisation they should do their utmost to release men for the forces.

div.head: SPECIAL REASONS.
div.p: SPECIAL REASONS.

There can be no question that much more can be effected in these directions than has hitherto been attempted. Some men for special reasons may require time before joining the forces to enable thein to release themselves from civil obligations. It is open to any man who has attested and been grouped to make an application to the Tribunal, who will have the power to put him in a later group—for instance, he may be in independent business or there may be other business, financial or domestic arrangements, which a than may Wish to make, and for which it is only reasonable that he should have time. Each case will stand on its merits. Another class is that of a man who has de- pendants • though not married. Each case of this kind will be considered on its merits. In any case in which the Tribunal have power to decide that a man be placed in a later group. they are not to place him back more than 10 groups; they should not, Of course, place him back the Maximum number of groups unless the merits of the case warrant this concession.

If, when the time comes to call up the group to which thi3 man has been put back the cir- cumstance continues to be such as to justify his being placed in a still later group, application can be made to the Tribunal by the man or his employer. The recruiting officer may in any case in which a man has been placed in a later group subsequently grant a further concession if he is fully satisfied that it is warranted by the merits of the case. No claim will be considered unless the group in which the man has been placed is within eight groups of the last which has been called up for active service.

div.head: FACILITATE RECRUITING.-
div.p: FACILITATE RECRUITING.-

As regards cases under D and k, the recruit- ing officer who is representing the interests of the War Office will be a party in every case. All appeals must be made to the Local Tribunal. It will be seen, as Mr: Walter H. Long, says, that their duties are of a highly im- portant character, and that in deciding cases which come before them they will be acting es custodians of the national interests.

It is for them to do all in their power on the one hand to facilitate recruiting, and on the other to secure that the vital industrial and financial interests of the country receive con- sideration. It is' imperative to bear in mind that those who are in control of businesses must endeavour, by reorganisation and in other ways to secure that labour is most economically used so that the largest possible number of men may be released for military service.
W. FURNESS, • Fern Lea, Great Sankey, Ron.. Recruiting :Officer under. the :Western Command.

div.head: RURAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RURAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE.

A request has been made from headquarters dealing with Lord Derby's scheme to the various joint Parliamentary. Recruiting Committees that Advisory Conimittees shall be appointed in the main centres of the various Parliamentary Divisions to deal with the appeals of recruits who, for various reasons, wish to be relegated to later groups than those to which their age automatically lallocates them. Such Advisory Committees will act in conjunction with, and will advise, the recruiting officer or other War Office representative in the various cases brought before them. Where an agreement cannot be reached in any case, such case will be. passed on to the local Tribunal.

_ - We understand, that an Advisory Committee is being appointed to deal with the districts of Appleton, Daresbury, Grappenhall, Stockton Heath and Whitley, and that the following gentlemen have been invited to join the Board: Messrs. H. J. Westbrook, J. Longland, V. D. Davies, John Rose, F. Fairhurst. C. E. Rumney and Segar Owen.

div.head: "THAT _UNCOMFORTABLE
div.p: "THAT _UNCOMFORTABLE
FEELING ! "

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council, held on Wednesday, the Clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton) reported that in reply to the Secretary of the Rural District Councils' Association re Clerical .and Commercial Ap- pointmepts Committee, he had written to the effect that the .Warrington Rural District Council had already pared down the labour staff from 65 to 17; and that of the 17 only two were .of military age, and neither of them could, having in view their particular 'work, be sep- arated from the older men. The members of the office staff within. the military' age could not be dispensed with. _ _

Referring to the report, the Chairman (Mr. W. Furness) mentioned that, as a recruiting officer, he was advising all men, starred or un- starred, to attest. If employer or employe thought they would suffer hardship by being called up in their group, or. otherwise, it was open to them to go before the Tribunal. and explain the position, and the Tribunal, it was expected, would take a lenient and charitable view and give all parties concerned every bene- fit that they could. Mr. G. Mather: What, preoisely, is meant by a Man Attesting? . The Chairman: He enlists. At present the authorities are not examining for eyesight and almost anybody can get through, but when the time comes" for Calling them up there will, no doutt, be an immense amount of weeding out. Mr.' Furness added that one of the principal officials of. the Council offered himself .some months ago and had ;got a certificate to the effect that he was unfitted for the infantry owing to ocular trouble. A very uncomfortable atmosphere- was being created for Isingle or married men of recruitable age. The only way for them to escape from that atmosphere was to go and 'get attested and thus procure their badge and certificate; after which they would have no further trouble.

div.p: One of The Rechabites.

A brother-in-law of Mrs. Dickin- son—Private William Smith, of the Warrington Territorials—was' accidentally killed in August last whilst serving with the Warrington Terri- torials; and her husband, another son, two brothers-in-law, and fifteen nephews are all serving with the colours.

div.head: DIED OF WOUNDS.
div.p: DIED OF WOUNDS.
PRIVATE ERNEST HOWARD
Shot In The Breast And Dies In Brussels.

Mr. Howard, ,Bewsey View, Winwick-road, Orford, received the following official intima- tion from Perth bn Thursday of the death of his son, who was reported missing since the advancl, September 25th, in last week's "Examiner" "it is my painful duty to inform you that a report has this day (December t) been received from the War Office notifying the death of Private Ernest George Howard, Seaforth High- la.nders, which occurred at No. 1, Kriegslazarett, Brussels, on the 3rd October, and I am to .ex- press the sympathy and regret of the Army Council at your loss. The cause of death was shot in the breast—internal hfemorrhage." Enclosed was it note as follows :
"The King commands me to assure you of the true sympathy of His Majesty and the Queen in your SOITOW.
" KrreaENER."
An Early, Volunteer.
Private Howard, who was a printer employed at "The Examiner" Office, was the first man in the office to volunteer on the outbreak of the
I'IZIVATE E. HOWARD. Died of Wounds.

war. With a true instinct he saw the needs Of his country, and considered it to be his duty, as a single :man, "to go first," and he went. The ranks of the married 'men in our employ have since been .broken by the. calls of the nation; but it will be the,glory,, in memory, if not, as in this case, in life, of, such single men as Ernie Howard, that they, recognising their duty, did it. He was 25 years of age when he died, like a true. soldier, from a shot in the breast. AS a bey he attended. the Padgate and Orford schoolp, As recreations he indulged in bowls and billiards, and so successful was he with the cue that he won ,a handsome Prize for prowess on'the green cloth. Fie enlisted in September of last' year, and went to the Front in July.

div.head: DIED OF DISEASE.
div.p: DIED OF DISEASE.
PRIVATE A. J. CLEAVER.
Old Soldier Vt-ho Re-Enlisted Last Year.

Private A., J. Cleaver, g soldier of many yew*" standing, suocumbed at Alciandria Hos- pital 'from enteric fever on November 16th. Prior .to re-enlisting, at .the commencement of hostilities, he -resided with his family at: 11; Raddon-place, Latchford, in which. neighbour- hood he-was .widely known and respected. Forty-four years of age,. he. was .for some con- siderable time employed by Messrs. Robinson, Son and eo., glass manufacturers, Bank Quay, and subsequently held a position at the Latch-

div.head: SINGLE MEN FIRST.
div.p: SINGLE MEN FIRST.
The Working Of Local Tribunals Under The Derby Scheme.

he engaged in his old trade. However, he soon abandoned wiredrawing and worked his way across the vast Dominion \to Vancouver, where he eventually settled with a large firm of clothiers trading under the name of Peck. Between leaving Hamilton and settling in Van- couver he "Toughed it" in true colonial style, undertaking, a variety of jobs, ranging from electioneering to road-mending. When he was 'Direr in the .Old country, comparatively recently, he laid it down as a dictum that anybody who hopes to get on in the Dominion must, be pre- pared to take the rough with the smooth and must, all the time, be prepared to work at whatever offers. Like most persevering emi- grants, Private Allen eventually "made good," and was doing well with Messrs. Peck when the war broke out and the call to arms was sounded, and he, at the time, being only thirty years of age and single, decided to offer his services to the Empire as a fighting man. He was, in fact, one of the first to join the Canadian Contingent, but it was found that be- fore he would be available for active service he would have to undergo an operation. So eager a recruit was he, that he did not let an opera- tion stand in his way, but, in order to fit him- self, not only cheerfully underwent it, but also footed the surgeon's bill—a -matter of £3O. The result,. of having to undergo the operation was I that instead of corning over to the war zone with the first contingent of the Canadian be made his debut with the second contingent—as a member of the 29th Canadian Infantry IBattalion. .
His Last Visits to Warrington.

Private Allen was in England on holiday at the beginning of 1914, and came to Warrington, staying with his only sister, who is the wife of Mr. E. H. Mann, of 35, Clarence-street; Mr. Mann being the assistant local superintendent for the Prudential Assurance Co. He had only been back in. Canada a short time after 'his holiday when war was declared. His last visit to Warrington was when became over with the Second Canadian Contingent; and when he spent a few days last September, prior to crossing to France, with his sister and her husband. Private Allen had only been in the trenches two, days when he was invalided on account of rheumatism and, on the very day that the Hos- pital Ship Anglia went down,: his' Warrington relatives received a letter from a nurse in a French hospital, saying that he was in the establishment to which she was attached, suffer- ing from a recurrence of the complaint for which he had been operated upon in Canada. Lest Friday, however, his eldest brother—Mr. Maurice Allen, who is engaged in the wire trade at ,Eeclesfield, Sheffield—received an official in- timation that Private Allen was on the Anglia when it went down, and that he was now reported " missing—probably drowned." The Anglia sank on November 17th. Skilled In SWimming.

As a boy Private Allen attended the Heath- side School, and both then and later on he was a member of the congregation of St. Paul's Church. As a young man he served in the old Volunteers—in the Cycle Section Private Allen was one of the smartest exponents of the natatory art in this district, and possessed a fine record of competition suc- cesses. lie commenced swimming in 1899 at the age of 13. In 1902 he was second in the W.S.C. 50 yards handicap, and was also second' in the 100 yards race at Rock Savage. The same year he assisted tjie Warrington Polo Team when they won the clftimpionship of the Third Division of the Liverpool and District League. In 1903 he swam third to J. Peers in the 150 yards championship of Warrington, and played with the polo team in a notable season, which ended in their becoming champions of the Second Division of the Liverpool and District League. In 1904 he was first at Balliol-road. Liverpool; first at Altrincham, and second in the Cham- pionship of Warrington contest. In 1905 he won that championship. The following year he was again second to his rival, T. Pemberton, and second in the 100 yards race at Rock Savage. In 1907 he was ,first in the 50 yards handicap at Ramsey,. Isle of Man. He also achieved the brilliant performance of carrying off the local 150 yards championship in the record time of imin. 50sec. He secured this championship also in 1908 and 1909, and in the latter year was first in the 100 yards and 200 yards handicaps at Douglas, Isle of Man, and first at Widnes. In 1910 Ile again carried off the championship of Warrington, and Was also again first at Widnes. Since going to Canada Private Allen won several prizes, the Most notable being the second in the 200 yards sea championship of British Columbia in 1912, and again in 1913. In the same contest in 1914 he received a sore disappointment, apparently having the first place well in hand, when upon turning for the last length, he collided with another competitor, a mishap 'which com- pletely put him out of the race. Won Prize As Long Distance Runner.

When the Stockton Heath iale6 was opened Private Aiken gave a.embibition of swim- ming, upon which he was highly complimented. In addition to being a swimmer of note he was a runner of no mean speed and staying power, and in leo3 he won the seven miles novices handicap promoted by the. Sankey Harriers. So excellent a swimmer as be, that it is thought' that *Flu% the vessel, on which' ,Jie was crossing, struck the Mai Mine he must have been rendered hors de °mutat by the explosion izave been confined between decks, for he was a tile " stayer " in the water, and could have kes affeiii for hours had he had his. liberty. It Allen, (4 6, Arnold-street, who is engaged at the WhitetrosS Wire Works, and who served with the of Volunteers in the South African War, being promoted to the .rank of Sergeant whilst :on .active service. div.head: HENRY'S CLAIM.
div.p: HENRY'S CLAIM.

The following has been written by Capt. B. S. Townroe, private secretary to the Director- 'General of Recruiting, in order to explain clearly, and in homely phrase, how the Local Tribunals will do their work).

Henry stopped on his way back from work; and read the poster, -headed "Single Men First," describing the group system introduced by the War Office. He went home quickly and at tea said to his mother, "Do you know, mother, I shall really have to go this time. They are going to take all single men first. I would like to go as a volunteer."

Mrs. Morris replied resignedly, "Very well, my dear, if you will, you, will. I don't see though that it is right to take a widow's two sons. Still, if they want you to go and help beat the Kaiser, I suppose you must." Mrs. Morris showed visible signs of tears, and Henry dropped the subject for the time being. Henry that night could not sleep. His mind kept revolving over his attempts to join the Army since August 4th, 1914. Since his brother, Robert, had enlisted, he had always wanted to join the local Territorials, but his mother, terri- fied at the idea of both her sons becoming soldiers, had always persuaded him that his place was in her stationer's shop, and that drills at night would interfere with his work. Then when war broke out, he begged his mother to let him go with his old pals. She explained that business in the country had to be carried on by someone, and that he was doing his bit be- hind the counter as well as if he wore khaki. Henry rolled over on the other side of the bed, as he realised now what a lame excuse that had been. Still he had been everything to his mother since his father died when he was three years old, and he had given way to her. For her sake he had received the cold shoulder from Maggie. He rolled over on the other side, as he thought of those winter months when Maggie refused to speak to him on the grounds that he was a "little slacker." Then came Mr. Lloyd George's demand for munition workers. After a great struggle with his mother he had per- suaded her to allow him to leave the shop and return to his former work of varnish-making to which he had been apprenticed. His mother had agreed to engage Maggie to help in the shop. On War Work.

Accordingly, in April, Henry went off to the Varnish Factory, and by October had assisted in the manufacture of many thousands of gallons of varnish which was used to cover high ex- plosive shells. Henry rolled over again as he thought of those hot summer months in the smelly factory,, and his qualms of conscience, as further friends joined the Army. At last, he decided to join the next day. With that de- cision he went to sleep. He went to the recruiting office the following morning, was found medically fit, received his 2s. 9d. pay, and was passed into Section B, Army Reserve. He was told that, as his age was 26 years and as he was a single man, he was in No. 9 group. 1916 had come. For three months Henry had walked the streets, usually in Maggie's com- pany, proud of the armlet with the red crown displayed on his left arm. He was so proud of the armlet that when he wore his overcoat, he always transferred it so that it could be seen, and Maggie usually carefully adjusted it .with the help of a safety pin. Then one day as he passed the Post Office, he saw in the window a notice with the Royal Arms on the top, stating that in a few weeks' time Group 9 would he called up for service with the Colours. The time had come, and he was face to face with the great opportunity; he would have to leave his mother and fight for her and for the other mothers- of Britain in the ranks ef the Army. When lie returner! I,erne he discussed the ques- tion with his mother whether he should appeal to the Local Tribunal to be postponed to a later group. She.ticlvised him to consult the Works Manager. The following day, the Works Manager asked him whether he was willing to appeal, as the firm must have his consent before they could send in a claim that he was required for the manufacture of varnish. Henry said. "I am ready to do whatever I am told and go wherever I am wanted."

"That is the right spirit," said the Works Manager. "Well. I think you are helping your country better here than anywhere else, but it is not for me to say. It is for the representa- tives of the country sitting on the Local Tribunals."

div.head: Passed to a Later Group.
div.p: Passed to a Later Group.

The employers, therefore, filled in a form. They stated that Henry was not only individu- ally indispensable, but that they had been try- ing for six months to obtain others also to do similar work. They said they were solely engaged on the manufacture of varnish for shells, and that they had already sent over 40 per cent. of their men to the Army or Navy. They were prepared to give half wages to any man who had enlisted under the group system, but asked that Henry should not be called up for several months. They stated further that they had just engaged six men invalided from the Front as unfit for further service, and were training them to take the places of Henry and , five other men.

The ease came on one Wednesday evening. It was held in a room in the Town Hall. The ex-Mayor was in the chair. He knew Henry well, for he was a superintendent of the Sunday school which Henry attended as a boy. On his right sat Admiral Caroe, who lived at the Hall just outside the town. Next to him was Joe Bartlett, who had organised the great strike in 1911, and whose reputation for fiery recruiting speeches was well-known throughout the whole of the country. Also sitting there were two members of the local Town Council—one a Free Church Minister, and the other a local shop- keeper. Henry expected to have to make a speech and, as a matter of fact, had told his mother exactly what he intended to say. The Chairman, however, asked the military repre- sentative present to state why he did not•agree with the claim. Captain Balfour made the followingTh av e s t talkedatem h e n this : s case over very carefully with my Advisory Committee. We fully under- stand how hard it would be for Mrs. Morris to have to give up her second eon, but we wish to point out that with the dependent's allowance and half wages from the firm, she will net lose a penny from the weekly allowance given her by her bdy. Her shop is not dependent on her son, and she has now trained a girl assistant to take his place. With regard to the claim made by the firm of Varnish Makers, we have consulted a representative of that industry, and we have come to the conclusion that .Henry 'Morris is not indispensable for any length of time—in fact; we understand that in 6 few I weeks' time it would be possible to replace him. I We, therefore, ask that he be postponed to a group which will probably be called up a little later. We would not urge this if the military necessity.was not so great, as you Are all aware." The Chairman then spoke. He said, "My tribunal las read carefully the requests set forth by Henry Morris and his employers, ask- ing for him to be postponed for several months. We shall not need to trouble the .appellant any further, as we have decided to postpone his call- ing up until Group IC In short, we have post- poned his calling up for five groups. We hope that that will be tai;4tuatery to him, and will I give time t 9 Arui to find a substitute for [hia4,"

div.head: The. I mpartiat lleeTtion.
div.p: The. I mpartiat lleeTtion.

This colithitieti hiS WO. TliairtS.Manageti !reported to the Managing ilifeaOr that even- ing, "-We shall have young Morris •with.ns for some time. That will get over our difficulties." The Managing Director replied, "This is an excellent system. It leaves the decision not to the individual conscience or to the individual employer, but to the representatives of the I•Tittioltv

Henry told his mother that night, "You don'f know, mother, what a relief it is to me not to have to decide for myself whether I should go, but to know that I am just in the hands of my country, and am doing my hit wherever I ara told to go." .

div.head: DISTRICT PI E. •\":-::•:''. 3
div.p: DISTRICT PI E. •\":-::•:''. 3

Skating on the Lake.—The skating public of Lymm and the surrounding districts again took advantage of the ice-covered waters of the lake during the last week-end. All classes of -skaters were represented, from the classic to the ama- teur, several of the latter receiving bruises, although not of a serious nature.

The Train Service.—Various rumours have been in circulation lately to the effect that drastic alterations are to be made in the train service beween Manchester and Lymm. These rumours were referred to at the Urban District Council meeting on Monday evening, and it was pointed out what a serious effect it would have on the district if some of the- trains— especially the last one from Manchester—were taken off.—The Clerk (Mr- W. Mullard) was asked to make inquiries into the matter.

Present at the Council Meeting.—The monthly meeting of the District 'Copncil was 'held on Monday evening, Councillor R. H. Gotobed pre- siding, Other members present were Coun- cillors J. H. Holt, W. G. Groves, A. Mclntyre, F. Ingham, C. E. Cowper, T. H. Warburton, F. Lockyer and G. H. Parker. The' officiElls in at- tendance were Messrs. W. Mullard (derk and collector), Cecil Mort (assistant clerk), D. Mort (surveyor), C. I. Barnes (water manager), and Dr. Leonard Thorp (temporary medical officer).

Recruiting Com m ittee.—Recruiting, with reference to the grouping and examining under Lord Derby's scheme has again been very brisk during the week, so much so that Mr. F. E. Evans, the local recruiting officer, and his assistants have had their hands full. So busy have they been that many who put in an appear- ance had to make more than one journey to the place appointed. Lymm is certainly answering the call in a manner quite up to the standard of other centres.

Dr. Thorp's Resignation.—At a meeting of the Lynim Sanitary Committee on November 22nd, a letter was read from Dr. Thorp (the temporary medical officer) informing the Coun- cil that he had written to Dr. de Jong inform- ing him that he wished to resign his position as deputy medical officer of health at the end of the quarter, and, if possible, to be released earlier.—lt was decided to ask Dr. de Jong for suggestions in the matter.—At Monday night's meeting of the Council Mr. Mallard (clerk) re- ported that no reply had yet been received from Dr. de Jong.

Skating Precautions.—At a recent meeting of the Lymm Water Committee a letter was read from the Rev. G. H. Thurston, calling attention to the fact that people—especially children— had been skating on the Lake. In his opinion the ice was not safe at the time, and he asked that provision should be made in case of acci- dents. The Urban District Council decided to purchase a stave ladder, and this, with some rope, is now at the waterworks.—The Council further decided to put up a notice at the Lake to warn the public that they go on the Lake at their own risk.

Cheshire Volunteers.—The Lymm detachment of the Cheshire Volunteers cordially invite all recruits of the group system (Lord Derby's Scheme) to join their ranks as temporary mem- bers, when they will be instructed in the pre- liminary stages of a soldier's duties, which will be advantageous for the future. Recruits desir- ous of availing, themselves of this opportunity will kindly, report themselves at the Drill Hall any Tuesday or Thursday at 8.30 p.m. It may be stated that this offer is being made at the express wish of the War Office by all Volunteer Corps in the country, and recruits will NOT be under military law. Any further information can be obtained from the Commandant (Captain Williamson) or his assistants—Sergeants Moston and Farrar.
