div.head: RECENT EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE RECENT EPIDEMIC.
Councillor Gives Good Advice To Parents.

The recent epidemic of infectious disease in Lymm has practically been stamped out— thanks to the energetic measures of the Council and its medical and sanitary staff. The Sanitary. Committee, who had the matter in hand, were informed on October 26th that .owing to the number of diphtheria cases in the hospital it was necessary, to open the second ward and to remover a patient into a separate building. Arrangements were made ivitlx the Altrincham District Council to take three cases into their Isolation Hospital at a charge of £5 ss. per week. A further arrangement was made with the Altrincham Council to take farther scarlet fever cases at a fee of £2 2s. per week for each patient. Precautionary Measures.

At a meeting of the committee held on October 27th, acting on the advice of the medical officer, it was decided to close the Lymm and Statham schoels, on account of diphtheria, for fourteen days. The committee met again on November and, when it was decided to close the Oyghtring- ton and Sandy-lane schools for a like period, and that the Lymm and Statham schools should be closed for a further period, from November 14th. The committee alp made other arrange- ments, all of which were carried out. Diphtheria Outbreak At An End.

At the meeting of the District Council on Mon- day evening, Dr. Thorp (temporary medical officer) reported that he was pleased to be able to report that the epidemic of diphtheria had ceased, and that it was now three weeks since the last case was reported. In all there had been 23 cases. All the patients had done well, and there had been no deaths. If it had not been that, unfortunately, two cases of scarlet fever were discovered in the girls' ward (41 November 14th, and later on in the same week (Fdtiiday, November 19th), three cases of chicken pox, the hospital would have been closed. A few cases of chicken pox occurred during the month, but the outbreak appeared to have nearly run its course. There were still three nurses engaged. One was nursing the two scarlet fever cases at home; and the patients could scarcely be asked to return to hospital. 4nother nurse was attending two scarlet fever eases in the hospital, and the third was nursing the•children who had had diphtheria. The nurse who had been doing night duty had returned to Manchester. At present there were two cases of scarlet fever in the east ward, and in the west ward were five patients who were convalescent after diphtheria. The west ward would be closed during the present week. The east ward would be required for the two scarlet fever cases for at least another five weeks. That would necessitate keeping the nurse for that period. The nurse looking after the two scarlet fever cases at home would, probably, return in about three weeks. Both the Oughtrington and Lymm schools had been reopened.

div.head: 'Doctor's Thanks—And Hints.
div.p: 'Doctor's Thanks—And Hints.

The doctor added: "I must thank you for providing me with the very necessary articles I requested for the hospital, for they added not only considerably to the comfort of your guests, but rendered the work of the nurses much easier. But, at the same time, I trust you will shortly be able to devote some attention to the hospital and permit very necessary altera- tions in the structure to enable the proper isola- tion of infectious cases and the dealing with more than one disease at a time, especially when the disease is divided between the two sexes. I should like to express my great appreciation ,of the valuable work done by Mr. Mort and of the very prompt manner in which he removed the various cases, and afterwards speedily disin- fected the premises, bedding, &c. Imported From

The Chairman (Mr. R. IT. Gotobed) said that the report was a very satisfactory one., Happily, they were coming to the end of the epidemic, and he trusted that there would be no further cases. He wished to bear testimony to the Coun- cil's appreciation of the work done by the Medical Officer and Mr. Mort, their sanitary inspector. He felt sure that no Council could have been better served by two officers than the Lymm Council had been. With regard to the fever( cases he would like to say a word, though he might get into trouble for doing so! They were pretty near a large town where there had been raging for some time, a rather serious epidemic of scarlet fever. He was of the opinion—and he thought that he was backed up in that opinion by the doctor—that the cases which had occurred in Lymm had been im- ported from outside. He would like to utter a note of Warning to the parents of Lymm. They should be most careful at a time like this of going into thronged places, and thus to avoid, for their own sakes and for the sake of the com- munity, the risk of bringing epidemics into their own particular community. He could not be- lieve that the cases reported had originated in the Lymm district, and he hoped that in future the people of the township would take proper precautions and not put themselves in danger. Incidentally, he, thought that the doctor and the Sanitary Committee were amply justified in closing the schools. Medical Officer Eulogised.

Councillor Cowper expressed his appreciation of the' "magnificent way Dr. Thorp had brought the cases through without a death." Dr. Thorp was both clever and energetic. Great thanks were due to him, and to Mr. Mort and the members of the Sanitary Com- mittee.

Dr. Thorn and Mr. Mort expressed thanks to the Council for the assistance that had been given them. A resolution was passed thanking the Altrinc- ham authorities for taking patients when the Lyrum Council's hospital was overcrowded.

div.head: CORPORAL BEN ELLIOTT.
div.p: CORPORAL BEN ELLIOTT.
Wants To Pay _Off Old Scores To The
Germans.

Mr. and Mrs. B. Elliott, Canterbury Cottage, New-road, Lymm, have this week received news from their son, Corporal B. Elliott, 2nd Scots Guards. who is at present an inmate of the Beach House Hospital, Bitton, near Bristol. He writes:—" I am feeling much better, but tho doctor says it will be some time before I am all right. You see all the nerves in my neck and in the back of my head have had a shaking up, and the only cure is to lie and rest. I have

dreadful pains in my head at times, for which 7 take medicine, but anyhow my rest treatment is doing me good. Unfortunately, I am afraid I shall be here over Christmas, which is aggra- vating, for I schOuld dearly have liked to spend the holidays at home. However, sooner or later I shall be able tolhave a few days With you, but I cannot say how long off that will be. I expect I -shall go out again at the - beginning of the New Year. I -want to go there again, for I have not. had enough. by a long way. There ,are old scores to pay off, and I must have revenge for this, !my injury." Corporal Elliott, it will be remembered, joined on September 7th of last year, and was wounded in action, October 16th, 1915.
PRIVATE S. PERCIVAL. •
ChriStmas Wishes From "Somewhere
In Egypt."
Mr. William Moston, 20, Newfield Cottages, Lymm, has this week received a communica- tion from Private S. C. Percival, of the Che- shire Regiment, "somewhere in Egypt." He writes as follows

"Just a line to inform you that I am keeping in the best of health and regret not -having written -sooner, hut, as .you know,, at a time like this it must be duty 'first always. We are having some very nice weather ,out here and the scenery is beautiful. Egypt is a fine place and at nights you can hear the boatmen singing their crooning songs as they pass up and down tie river. At present we are stationed at the seaside. We go bathing each (lay in the sea, and you can't tell how refreshed and fit we feel afterwards. I shall be giad when this awful war is over and we are all at home- again with our wives and children." • Private Percival concludes with the hope that his many ." pals " in Lymni will have a good Christmas.

div.head: SAPPER PERCY CLARE.
div.p: SAPPER PERCY CLARE.
Ready For Winter Campaign.

Sapper Percy Clare, of the Lymm Terri- torials, who, a few months ago, became attached to the Royal Engineers, has this week forwarded to his mother, who resides at Booth's Hill, the unique and interesting photograph which is here reproduced. As will he seen, Sapper Clare looks hale and
LANCE-CORPORAL J. DANDY.
in the summer months, his injuries consisting of shrapnel wounds in the knee and shoulder.

It seems that the above Private was just about to make himself comfortable for the night prior to snatching a few hours' sleep, when a shell burst overhead and he was hit as mentioned. He soon recovered from his injuries and subsequently took part in the British advance of September 25th to 27th, luckily without misfortune.

The subject of our photograph was attached to the Manchesters and is well known in Lymm and the surrounding districts/ As a youth he attended the Lymm Schools and was a chorister of some repute at the same church, prior to his leaving Lymm to take up residence at New- ton Heath. He was also a bellringer at the above church and was employed for some little time at Messrs. Robertson's Works, Latchford. His age is 31 years and is married, with three children.

caused by the rendering of a sketch entitled "Jackets," by members of the Warrington Temperance Guild Sketch Party. The children sang several melodies very sweetly. Miss Elsie Whitfield was the accompanist.

For The Prisoners Of War Funds.—A most successful and enjoyable whist drive was held in the Church Rooms on Thursday evening. It had been promoted by a number of ladies and gentlemen in the village and, it being .tid ul both the Lancashire and Cheshire Prisoners of War Funds, it was only natural that there should be a good number of players present. As a matter of fact thirty tables were required. The prizes—which' had been kindly given by the Vicar (Rev. James Collins), Mr. J. H. Clarke, Mr. James Richardson, Mr. J. W. Crossley and Mrs. Gordon Roberts—were won by the following :—Ladies: 1, Mrs. H. Littler; 2, Mrs. Jowett; 3, Mrs. Hallows; gentlemen: 1, Miss Butterworth; 2, Miss Knight. The last two ladies played "gentlemen's hands." During the evening refreshments were provided by the committee.. A musical programme was con- tributed to by Miss N. Moores and Mr. R. H. Pearson . (violin duet and violin solos), Miss Mclntyre (pianoforte solo), and Miss Blackburn, who, for her song "My- fanwy," was heartily encored. Another feature of the evening was the recitation of the poem "The Hell Gates of Soissons," by Mrs. Garnett. She was encored.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

Overturned Wagon.—Whilst proceeding to Taylor's Farm on Wednesday, a wagon with a heavy load of hay overturned near the Red Lion Hotel, at a point where the road dips on one side. Fortunately the horse was able to keep its feet, and as nobody was passing at the time no bodily damage was done.

Adult School Whist Drive.—A whist drive was held at the Adult School on Saturday evening, when a goodly number were present. Whist was played at fifteen tables, and the prize win- ners were:—Ladies: 1, Miss W Norbury; 2, Mrs. Jerams; gentlemen: 1, Mrs. Isherwood (playing as a gentleman); 2, Mr. J. Holt.

Sanitary Inspector Offers to Enlist.—Mr. G. W. Lloyd, 14, Pike-street, Stockton Heath, the assistant sanitary inspector to the Runcorn Rural District Council, has applied to the Council for leave of absence in order to join the Army. He said that if , accepted by the Army authorities, he intended to serve in the Sanitary Section of the Royal Medical Corps. The Coun- cil gave Mr. Lloyd their permission to submit himself for enlistment.

Death Of An Old Resident.—The death occurred on Thursday, November 25th, of Mr. James Miller, who passed away at his. residence, 31, Mitchell-street. Mr. Miller was in his 75th year, and has been failing in health for some little time. The funeral took place" on Monday at the Hill Cliffe Graveyard. Among the mourners were Mr. John Miller, Mr. Thomas Miller and Mr. Richard Miller, brothers of the deceased.

Recruiting Boom !—As we announced last week, special arrangements are being made to enable Stockton Heath eligibles .to enlist. On Saturday last a Recruiting Office was opened at the Red Lion Hotel and i/t is gratifying to know that nearly 30 men offered themselves as recruits. Some of these will join the ranks immediately, but the majority have attested under Lord Derby's group scheme. The Recruit- ing Office will be opened at the Church Rooms at 2.30 this afternoon, and it is hoped that the result will be as good as last week.

• Temperance Work Amongst Women.—The monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Branch of the British Women's Temperance Association was held on Tuesday evening in the- Providence Schols. Mrs. C. W. Hallows was in the chair, and a most interesting lecture was given by Mrs. Tanner, of Warrington. ,The lecturer spoke of the work that had yet to be done amongst the wives of soldiers. She gave many illustrations of the necessity of the work, and also spoke of her experiences as a temperance worker. During the evening Mr. G. Whitfield recited, and a pianoforte solo was played by Miss Deakin. Mrs. F. Gandy was the accom- panist for the hymns. Refreshments were pro- vided. the helpers who dispensed them being under the charge of Mrs. Grounds and Mrs. Whitfield.

United Band Of Hope.—ln the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Monday evening, the Rev. George Curtis presided over a large audience on the occasion of the first public meeting of the session of the Hill Cliffe and Stockton Heath United Band of Hope. An interesting lecture entitled "Water versus Alcohol," illustrated by chemi- cal experiments, was given by Mr. Peter Taylor, scientific lecturer to the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope- Union. An ex- cellent programme was afterwards submitted, and included 'songs by S. ,Gamble, A. Rams bottom ar.d George Walton. The audience were delighted with an action song entitled "Blue Bell Farm," which was performed by a number of small girls, who had been trained by Miss Isherwood. M. Ramsbottom, E. Travis and Arthur Spencer gave recitations, and Miss L. Jones a pianoforte solo. Much amusement was

div.head: PATRIOTIC FAMILY.
div.p: PATRIOTIC FAMILY.

Three Sons And Their Soldier-Father. Private Thomas Kirkpatrick, of the Cheshire Regiment, on Thursday night landed home on short leave from the firing line looking hale and hearty, and feeling in the best •of health after his recent stirring engagements in France. A local "Terrier," he was mobilised with his corps at the outbreak of war, and was eventually drafted to the Front ten months ago. Eighteen years of age, robust and well knit, he attended the Lymm Grammar School, and was a chorister and worshipper at the Parish Church, where he has many friends and admirers. An athlete of some note, he participated in all classes of sport, and played on many occasions with his school football team.
He is the son of Mr. William Kirkpatrick, for
many years proprietor of the Bridgewater Arms

In- the course of conversation with an "Ex- aminer" representative it transpired that Mr. W. Kirkpatrick, the young man's father, is an old Army veteran. He joined the Army so long ago as 1869, and served with the colours for the long period .of 40 years, when he retired on reaching the age limit. At the close of his military career he had obtained the rank Of pioneer-sergeant, with full rank, honours and dress. A possession 'which he highly cherishes is the Queen Victoria medal, obtained for long service and meritorious Conduct.
The father of Private T. Kirkpatrick was until a short time ago captain of the local fire brigade, and on his retirement was •warmly commended by the Council for his faithful ser- vices.

A brother of Private T. Kirkpatrick, Sapper Douglas Kirkpatrick, of the Royal Engineers, is at present in a military 'hospital in Cairo, Auffering from jttundice, although happily on the road to recovery.

Sapper Kirkpatrick was in Egypt mobilised when the war broke out, and was in the. skirmish at Ismailia, Egypt, and engagements in the Dardanelles. Writing to his sister some little time ago from the Dardanelles, Sapper Kirk- patrick states that his battalion have slept in holes dug in the ground, with wood floors. All around, stretching as far as the eye could see, were the blue wafers of the ocean.

The booming ot the guns and screech of shells overhead were awe-inspiring. "In the distance," states Sapper Kirkpatrick, ."-cotild 'be seen the hill 'of Acha Baba, which lOoked fine as the shadows of night fell over the scene. Every Friday matches and tobacco were hand?a round, and every now and then we went Tor a 'bath, which left us very much iefreshed.

"- I u-sed to boil my clothes in an old tin can, anil it was very amusing. for the dye out of my socks used to run into the other garments." The writer of the 'above, before joining .the Army, was a musician of some repute, for he

hearty, and quite prepared to weather the storms of approaching winter in the trenches. The dog shown is the mascot of the regiment and is a great favourite with the men. In a letter to his mother, dated November 23rd, he writes that snow fell on the two preceding days in that part of the country, but at the time of writing it had all gone and they were having better weather. Sapper Clare is very optimistic and hopes to be back in Lymm before many • more months have passed.

played the clarionet in Mr. Down's band on many occasions, and whilst in the Army with the regimental band. Another brother in this patriotic family is at present stationed at Ches- ter, under Major Dickson, on home service.

Stockton Heath Detachment. Orders for the week commencing 6th Decem- ber, 1915 :

BATTALION ORDERS. By Lieut.-Colonel Alan J. Sykes, Commanding Knutsford Battalion, The Cheshire Volunteer Regiment.
Wilmslow, 26th November, 1915.

I.—Training. The Central Association Volunteer Training Corps have received a letter from the War Office, dated November 19th, welcoming the proposal of the Association to train the men enlisted under Lord Derby's scheme for one day with the Colours and then passed on to the Reserve, before being called up. The War Office notify that the recruit on enlistment will be informed as to the address of the nearest Volunteer Training Corps to which he can be attached, if he so pleases. It is noted for the information of Com- mandants that such men will join the Volunteer Corps as ordinary members, but it is suggested, wherever possible, requests for subscriptions or entrance fee should be waived, and they should not be asked to purchase uniforms, but should be provided with the G.R. Armlet. The Khaki Armlet should be woin in civilian occupation, while the Red Armlet must be worn when on parade or on duty. The former is a proof that the man has enlisted under Lord Derby's scheme, while the latter is a substitute for a uniform, and a sign that he belongs to I recognised force, and is entitled to take part in the defence of his country.
By Order,
W. M. FORD, Adjutant.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Wesley Gui I d.—The usual meeting of the Wesley Guild was held on Monday evening, when a paper on " Browning " by given by the Rev. A. J. Morton. He pointed out that Browning was a difficult poet to understand; in fact he. doubted whether Browning himself understood all that he wrote. Nevertheless Mr. Morton gave his hearers sonie of the best of Browning's work, and thus made ,the lecture a very interesting and successful one. Mr. W. Newton occupied the chair.

div.head: FOULED BROOKS.
div.p: FOULED BROOKS.
Rural District Council Discuss A
Knotty Question.
I STOCK OWNER'S' COMPLAINT.

At their monthly meeting on Wednesday the Warrington Rural District Council discussed at length the question of sewerage in Padgate. The Local Government 'Board had If,rwarde4 a copy of a letter which they had received from Mr. Walter Bennett, Bruche Farm, Padgate, and requested to be furnished with the Council's observations thereon.
"A Cause of Serious Loss."
Mr. Bepnett's letter read :

-`-` willte you in 1913 re fouling of the brooks in this district, which rim through my land here, and are a cause of serious loss to me through the cattle drinking sewer water run- ning. along the old water courses. I have re- peatedly had cases of dysentery among the stock through this cause. They are cutting a drain on this farm to relieve the smell and cut off the sewerage from the ponds on this farm, with the exception of a short length, running the south side of Padgate-lane—that being the only possible drinking place for stock (mostly dairy stock) on this land. I have a cow only a fort- night since almost died on this land through dysentery. Luckily, we have been able to Pull her through. My chief cause of complaint, how- ever, is a ditch running through Tidy-lane Farm and through the only drinking pond there for all the stock in the yards and sheds in the winter time. „ This is nothing more than a cesspool. The sewerage runs down this ditch from Padgate village.. If my cattle and the farm are to be ruined for stock-keeping at the expense of property owners in the district (and my father is one of them) I consider it a great injustice to me as tenant, and a disgrace to the county in causing loss to any individual and in having a public nuisance allowed to go un- noticed. I wrote our District Council and they disputed any liability. The cattle will not drink the water until almost choking, and if this can be allowed I don't understand it. It
is an easy matter for them to fence the sewer- age or to pipe the drain and put the town's water in for the cattle to drink."
The Surveyor's Opinion.

The Surveyor (Mr. B. S. Newcomb) said that he had inquired into the matter and he folind that the field in which the cow was placed was in the borough of Warrington. At the time of his visit the water from which the animal was said to have drunk appeared to be quite good. He added: "I am of opinion that this Council is not causing serious pollution; at least, there is nothing to see at the presetit time." The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: May not the water look pure and yet be contaminated? The Surveyor: That remark might apply to every ditch in the district. The feeling of the Council at the last meeting was that a letter should be sent to the effect that we do not accept responsibility, and expressing the view that if the ditch were piped and the water sup- plied in this case, the Council might have to do the same in a great many other cases in the district.

div.head: " Ditch After Ditch Fouled."
div.p: " Ditch After Ditch Fouled."

Mr. G. Mather reminded the Council that they are the health authority for the district, and that they passed the plans for new houses and, further, that water closets had been "put into houses galore "; the result being that ditch after ditch and brook after brook had been fouled until, now, they had hardly a drop of clean water for cattle in the place. Numbers of those who were responsible for the present condition were going scot free, and the inhabi: tants had to suffer, in the way of paying rates. lie did not know whether the Council could remedy matters or whether they could put the cost of keeping the ditches clean on the owners. generally; or, further, whether they could go to the owners of the property causing the nuisance and get from them the money necessary to carry out Mr. Bennett's sugges- tion?
Mr. Ball: If we have allowed houses to be put up and closets put in I say that we and the rate- payers of Padgate are terribly to blame. •
Mr. J. W. Knowles wondered whether it was not a matter in which the Padgate people Amuld proceed against the parties who had fouled the brook.
A Proper Drainage Scheme?

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: Does not this emphasise the need for a proper drainage scheme for Padgate ? I was under the impres- sion that a modified sewerage scheme had been adopted for the parish and that something like £2OO was to be spent. Mr. G. Mather: We are going on with that now, but that does not touch a case like this, The Clerk said that the law on the point was was very simple. It was the duty of the Coun- cil to remedy all matters of the kind at the cost of the ratepayers. Mr. G. Mather: Not at the cost of the property owners, unfortunately! After prolonged discussion it was left to the Clerk and Surveyor to formulate a reply to the letter from the Local Government Board.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

War Working Party's Successful Effort.—ln- vitations sent out by the members of the Pen- keth and Sankey War Working Party to an American tea from 3 to 7 p.m. in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Thursday, met with a hearty response from all quarters. •The members of the party took charge of the various stalls. The proceeds, which will be devoted to providing comforts for our soldiers, exceeded all expecta- tions, as they amounted to no less a sum than £43.

Two More fdr the Highlanders.—The Penketh Roll of Honour continues to lengthen. .The latest recruits from the village are Fred Hall and Richard Gregson, who have joined the Sea- forth Highlanders. Grouped in various classes under Lord Derby's scheme are: Smith Tunstall, Ernest Darlington, Daniel Matthews, William Higham, Robert Higham, Joseph Dean, David Houghton, Harry Rhodes, John Barlow, William Cash, E. A. Murphy, Harold Ambler, William Watson, Harold Goulden. The " twa braw laddies," Hall and Gregson, left early on Friday morning for their depot at Fort George.

Home From the Front.—Corporal Herbert Molynepx had been home for a short spell straight from the trenches "somewhere in France." Feeling well and looking well, he is decidedly a good advertisement for the care taken of our men at the Front. Having-taken part in several engagements, he has had his share of narrow escapes, but fortunately has not received any serious injury. The nearest ap- proach to one such was when a piece of shrap- nel struck his rifle and, glancing Off, travelled up the front of his boot, tore through the laces, and left a scared foot, which caused him to limp for a few days, but did not put him out of action. .He returned to his "little clay home in a trench" on Friday.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.
Skating.—Skating was in full swing last week- end on Mr. William Smith's meadow at Long- ford. Many hundreds made the journey from the town and found the ice in excellent con- dition.

Concert For Sunday School Funds.—The Church Sunday School Funds should benefit Materially as the result of a tea and cow-eft held in the Schoolroom on Friday evening of last week. Much amusement and interest was caused by several competitions, included among which were smelling and candle-lighting con- tests. The • Rev. G. Vale Owen (vicar) was heartily applauded for his rendering of that fine old song "The Veteran," and "When Richard the Third. was on the Throne." Miss Ida Wilkinson sang "Dear Heart," and Mr. J. Gibson gave in fine style "The Skipper." Hearty thanks *ere accorded those who sent in private subscriptions and trays, or helped in any other ways to make the evening a success.

Death of an Old Inhabitant—The death took place on Saturday morning of Mr. Daniel Massey, of Orford: Park. The deceased gentle- man was in his 80th year, and was one of Orford's oldest inhabitants. Mr. Massey had suffered from heart trouble for the past two years, and for several years had led a quiet and retired life. A native of Macclesfield, he took a farm at Burtonwood when 23 years of age. Later he went to a farm at Middleton. He purchased Orford Park 25 years ago, and has lived there ever since. A Churchman, he was, up to a few years ago, a sidesinan at Orford Church, and a manager of the Day Schools. He leaves a wife, two sons and two daughters

to mourn their loss. As a young man the de- ceased went up for his fortnight's annual train- ing with the Earl of Chester's Yeomanry. The funeral took place, on Tuesday afternoon at Winwick Church. The service was conducted by the Vicar of Orford (the Ray. G. Vale Owen), assisted by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn. The chief mourners were: Messrs. William and Daniel Massey (sons). Mr. John M. Smith (grandson), Messrs. Isaac Howard and William Smith (sons- in-law), Messrs. William Sant and J. Dakin (cousins), and Messrs. W. White and J. W. Knowles. The carriers were Messrs. David Howard, 'Thomas Howard, J. Norman, John Dakin, jun., S. Walker and W. Hill. Wreaths were sent by the widow, "Will," "Danny," " Aggie and family," "Isaac and Lizzie," "Will, Polly and family,'" Mr. J. W. Knowles, Mr. and 'Mrs. Norman, Mr. and Mrs. W. Y. Smith, Mr. and Mrs. Hill, Mr. and Mrs. Dakin, and "All at Moat House Farm."

div.head: GRAF PENHALL.
div.p: GRAF PENHALL.
A BAKER'S FAILURE.
How Outside Competition Hurt His
Business.

The public examination of Samuel John Woodcock, baker, of Grappenhall Bridge, took place before Mr. Registrar Ridgway at the War- rington Bankruptcy Court on Friday. In his statement of affairs the debtor estimated his gross liabilities at £612 llis. 2d., of which g 597 2s. was expected to rank. His assets he estimated at £9B is. 9d., the deficiency being £499 Os. 3d. He gave as the causes of his failure, "Shortness of capital, severe competition, losses by horses, and the present war."

In the course of his examination 'the debtor said that the business was founded by his father in 1860. He took it over in 1896, on his father's death. The business'. was then about solvent. For the first five years he was in .firtnership with a brother, but in 1901 the 131 her went out of the business. At that time the concern was slightly insolvent. He had be m his own , baker and his own vanman. He h.d lost four horses in succession. To-day he as no more ago and insolvent than he was three yes 0 .during that period he had been fiOng effort 4 to pay off his debts. The prOi. niafrom the business last year were £lOO, and, an Joinestie expenses were about £7B. One of .V i•easons of his failure was that the bakers of the town had started sending . vans out into Grappenhal/. Branches of the Co-operative Sot ety had also absorbed a number of his customers.

div.head: • 3 WORLD,. 4.• •._
div.p: whose industries were threatened with extinction turned their attention to something required for the new armies, the fleet, dr the country, and their employes, men and women, loyally sup- ported them. Thus lace-blouse makers made canvas holdalls for Territorials, furriers sup- plied the War Office With fur and skin coats, toy factories sprang up as !if by magic and gave employment to idle' actists, and to thousands of women. Carpet looms turned out army blankets, Irish blouse and apron factories con- tracted for Government mattress and bolster covers and pillow cases; pen. makers went to surgical dressing factories, in all these changes women loyally co-operated, and many or them made, unselfish sacrifices for the country. Work for the V.A. Detachments.

A new class of employment will shortly be opened to women, for which they ought to be specially fitted. It has been found that the methods of supply improvised for the first year of the war, are far from perfect, consequently there is a very serious wastage in military hos- pitals, camps, d:c. More men are wanted in the armies, and thousands might be released at once if women of superior position, energetic and businesslike, filled administrative positions in the hospitals. The War Office has instituted a new scheme for the employment of members oi the V.A. Detachment of the St. John Ambulance Association and the British Red Cross Society These will take the places of quartermasters, clerks, housekeepers and storekeepers, and it is hoped that a more economical system of deal- ing with stores will be inaugurated by the women., The Government have already ar- ranged for a course of lectures as training for the work, which should be attended by all who desire to take up these duties. • . Braid for Tailor-mades.

Tailor-mades of all kinds remain one of the most important items in a woman's wardrobe, for every woman wears them. They were in- vented by British tailors, and when French- women adopted'the mode, they found the style scarcely to their taste, nor did it suit them. Consequently French designers devised the elaborate and decorated tailor-made, and every now and again, when change is demanded, the French style is adopted here. This winter, however, severity is a characteristic of all tailored suits, :braid and fur being the only decoration Permissible. The latter is extensively used. - It binds coats; pockets, buttonholes awl belts, and is used in various widths. It is often laid on fiat in 'rows to represent tucks, and is even made into sashes, finished with tassels. When it forms belts it is drawn through a buckle which is used in many forms and shapes,

and made of horn, pearl, galalith, and of course silver, or oxydised metals. Sometimes the buckle is covered with the material serving for the suit. The backs of this winter's coats are broad, and the sleeves long. Some coats fasten to the chin, others hare open throats and long Fevers. This Year's Ribbons.

Ribbons are the most wonderful of all this winter's productions. They enter into every department of women's attire, and play an im- portant part in each. They are made in variety that is absolutely bewildering, and are as beautiful as they are varied in colouring and design. Wide and narrow, plain, brocaded, shot and stitiped, all are artistic, and both Milliners and dressmakers, equally with the manufacturers of lingerie, vie with :each other in employing them tastefully and artistically. Milliners manipulate ...them with Marvellous skill, and the most 'delicate and beautiful flowers seem to grow from their clever 'fingers. This season's handsome wings and cockades are of ribbons. Picot edges are as- popular as 'ever, whilst the glittering tinsel ribbons, under soft , veilings, are largely used to give relief to sombre evening dresses. The material sets, that that are quite a feature of this season's fashions, owe their charm entirely to the rib- bons so lavishly used in their decorations. Hats, ruffles and the pretty frilly muffs are often made of ribbons only and trimmed with marabout ar a narrow edging of fur. Veils Various in Length. - Veils are again claiming attention, and form an important part of the millinereacheme with regard to the headgear of the moment. Variety and contrast are their chief characteristics. At one end of a wide choice. is the impertinent little veil that just reaches to the tip of the nose, and at the other the long flowing draped affair that falls almost, or quite to the waist, and imparts a note of mystery to the wearer. Between these two extremes are veils of many lengths and kinds. Decidedly ugly is the curtain-like arrangement that is, fastened to the top of the crown of the postilion hat, reaching the base of the :throat. This veil is very full, and its .folds stand out in front and behind. Completely enveloping the head it ap- pears to be circularl- in shape, the ends being apparently sewn together. All veils have fine meshes and borders Of chenille dots or velvet ribbon. Lace veils are much in evidence, and those of Chantilly are beautiful. produc- tions, being light and fairy-like with delicate borders of lace or chenille. There is something quite bewildering about these lovely accessories, but they are not for the million, their price being prohibitive.

div.head: CHAT and GOSSIP.
div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.

Christmas for the Children and the Soldiers. When nations lived more or less permanently in a state of war, a truce was always proclaimed, at Christmastide. Last year the Pope essayed. to bring about something of the sort, but with- out success, perhaps because it would seem that the more highly civilised the nations become, the more uncivilised are their 'nodes of warfare. The soldiers, however, on some parts of the Front, made their own truce, which, although informal, was real enough. There is irony in the sidea of celebrating Christmas in war time; nevertheless, for the sake of the children—and the soldiers—the festival must not be allowed to lapse. Sadness may reign, but in ministering to the happiness of others, an atmosphere of love and peace is created. The soldiers in France, Flanders, Mesopotamia, the Dardanelles, and the Balkans, will be far away on Christmas Day, but will expect to be remembered by all at home on the name day of the Prince of Peace.

French Religious Guilds. Probably in times of peace more men attended religious services., in iFrance than in this country. Since the war began churches in French towns and rural districts have been crowded daily with worshippers, and in Paris, . Notre Dame iS filled from morning until night—but chiefly with women. All the men of military age, together with the old, and even the slightly infirm—if they can render the least service— are at the Front. No special efforts are made to attract the Men in the barracks and trenches to the services held by ,ecclesiastics and soldier- priests, nor are special revival meetings a custom as in these hies, but there appears to have been, an awakening to the need for religion, due probably to the many religious Guilds founded on lines similar to those adopted by the late Count de Mun. These Guilds numbered before The war nearly one hundred and forty thousand men.

Changes in the Industrial World. Wonders have been achieved in the industrial world since the war began, and in these women have taken an iinportant 'and conspicuous part. In Lancashire and in the Midlands there was one dreadful fortnight in August of last year, when the whole industrial world seemed paralysed, and stagnation "seemed inevitable. But soon the -position changed, for manufacturers

That figure, he said, was a rather low one; very much lower than that reported by the majority of education authorities. Nowadays they were all .anxious to save money' and to economise, and if that average attendance could only be ificreased by one per cent. it would mean .about £3OO a year in additional grants. If the attendance could be raised to 90 per cent.— which was by no means an impossible figure-- the grants would be sAlelled by a really sub- stantial sum, and one \Obeli would be very wel- come. div.head: "SCARCITY OF SHIPS."

The following facts concerning market prices are taken from the report of Sir S. W. Royce and Co., Ltd., Manchester, dated _l\tovembegi

div.head: CHEMICALS,
div.p: CHEMICALS,

During.' this month there is little change in the general position. There is a continuance of the active, consuming, demand, which is with difficulty met by manufacturers and importers; Supplies available are readily taken up, and many articles have again increased in value and show a further upward tendency. Sulphate of Copper is scarce through a shortage of vitriol; price has advanced rapidly, and-the luarlcet is very,strong. Green Copperas is badly wanted, and shortage of wagons is making mat- ters very al,,:kwjard. Acetates of Lime very firm indeed, and only limited quantities available. Acetate of Soda is again dearer. Lead Salts also are higher, through scarcity and dearer metal: Acetate of Lead is in good demand; Nitrate of Lead is in short supply, Nitric Acid being difficult to obtain: kLitharge and Red Lead have just advanced 3.05. per ton. , Carbon- ate vf Potash is only selling in small lots, but supplies are quite limited, and prices very firm. Montreal Potashes are...scarce, and are dearer. Ammonia Salts are very firm all round. White .Powdered Arsenic has latterly less inquiry, but continues very firin. Cream of Tartar is easier, but the reason of this is not clear: Tartaric Acid is, very short on spot, and in better de- mand for forward delivery, and the market firm. Citric Acid is lower. Yellow Pnissiate of Potash is dearer, and is very scarce. Yellow PruSsiate of Soda is in good demand for near delivery and up to June. Birchromates of Potash and Soda are difficult to obtain. Oxalic Acid has advanced further. In Tar Products there is latterly little change. Benzoles con- tinue very firm. Solvent Naphtha is in good demand, and prices somewhat firmer. div.head: HOME NOTES.
div.p: HOME NOTES.
Profitable Recipes And Useful
Suggestions.

, Mixed Vegetable Soup. • Wash a small cauliflower or broccoli, pull it in pieces and place in a quart of water ;took till tender, but not brOken. Have ready (cut small) 1 carrot, 1 turnip, 2 onions, half head- of celery, 2 or 3 potatoes', 4 skinned tomatoes. Cut these vegetables up and ithice- in a ' frying , pan with .2oz. of butter, coo ring till a light brown, then add these to the eauliflOwer broth. _ Let the whole simmer. for 3 hours; add t pint of milk or pint` of water or more as preferred; ,put in the pieces of boiled cauliflower, also salt and pepper. Chicken Timbale..

Take a basin that will hold about a pint and a half, and grease it carefully. Boil some macaroni in salted water until tender, taking care to break it as little as possible. Line- the basin with the macaroni, winding it round and round the inside. Now prepare the following: Take the meat of a cold chicken, mince it, add to it sufficient cold ham to flavour nigely, add to it the Crumb Of :thick slice, of bread soaked in .milk, popper and salt to taste, a little grated lemon rind, and two well-beaten .eggs. Stir this all together, and with it fill the basin. Tie over with greased paper, and stelam for an hour. Serve with a good Bechamel sauce, to which has been added a flavouring to taste. How Not to Save. •

Ways we may save. Plenty of them, ,are there not, when you come- to .face the matter fairly and squarely? But do be rational, and tackle this business of retrenchment in a sensible and practical way. Don't try to save on essentials such as warm clothing and nourishing food. If you do this You may make 'yourself very ill and have a doctor's bill lo pay. It is wiser to deny .your- self such unnecessary things . as expensive,

elaborate, lace trimmed and embroidered frocks and under Wear, or the dainty delicacies that you have been accustomed to on the daily menu. For instance, you cannot go without bread, but you can do quite well without fancy biscuiti and rich cakes. You must _11,41V0 warm under- _

clothing and cosy gloves and 'socks, and sound, comfortable, well soled boots, but you will be none the, worse without a satin blouse and a string of pearls round your neck. A silk petti- coat may be chti'rming, but it is a thing one can easily do without. On the 'other hand, a woollen underskirt or a warm overcoat is .almost a necessity.—" Good Health."
Children, Join This Corner! Enter The Competitions! Write Your Best! Always Be Glad! Uncle Jack, " Examiner," Warrington.
HINTS TO SANTA CLAUS!
MY DEAR CHILDREN,-

One. would have thought that you would all , have been keen on telling inc what you ivoikld prefer, above everything else, for a .Christmas present, but, to my great surprise, I have, u'p to the time of writing, received fewer entries for this competition than .I have got for any One I have arranged 'since our mutual friend—Uncle Ned—went away to be ii,''soldier of the King. 1 This is a matter that must be seen into! Instead of my letter box being cram full with your efforts on Tuesday morning, I found but a handful of attempts. Generally am faced with scores of your essays;..this week I only get dozens. Can it be that you are not thinkin,, about Christmas presents this year? Perish 1-the thought! I never yet knew , a nephew or a niece who did not—war or no war! —look for Santa Claus (or the persona who do duty for this jolly, white-whiskered old soul) more ;and more each day as December 25th approaches, until, on Christmas Eve expecta- tion has reached such a piteh that the long- looked-for old gentleman—or those who help him in his work—is nearly kept away by ;the fact that the youngstexs for whose delight he is going round with his reindeers and sleigh will persist in keeping awake when they ought to be asleep. UNCLE JACK.

div.head: Love.
div.p: Love.

Love, wrote Robert G. Ingersoll, is the only bow on life's dark cloud. It i the morning and evening star. It shines on the babe and sheds.its radiance on the quiet tomb. It is the mother of art; inspirer of poet, patriot and philosopher. It is the air and light of every heart; builder of every home; Icindler of every fire on the hearth; it .was the first dress of immortality. It fills the world with melody, for music is the voice of love.. • Love is the magician, the enchanter that changes worthless things to joy, and makes right royal Queens and Kings of common clay. It is the perfume of that wonderful flower, the heart, and without that sacred passion, that divine swoon, we are less than beasts; but with it—earth is heaven and we ,are gods.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information In Popular
Language.
The Hands in Winter.

A very good wily of eleaniag-the, hands when they are very dirty, more czpecially in cold weather, is to rub a little pure lard well in all over them, then wash with eoup and water in the ordinary way. If this is done, the hands will not be nearly so likely to crack.

Thorns and Splinters. , When a. splinter has gone very deep into the flesh, try extraction by steam method. Heat a wide-Mouthed bottle, and make it two-thirds full with Very hot Water, and place under the injured spot. The suction draws the flesh down when a little pressure is used, and, the steam in a few moments removes both the splinter and inflammation. This method is par- ticularly good when the splinter has been in for some time. Causes of Headache. .

Too late going to bed, and anything that pro- mote& want of sleep, are fertjit causos of 'head! aches. .Brain repair goes on during sleep. People often don't know, or forget, :his. If you arc wort y lug or workint, hard all shy, t hen go IA itud get up curly. you aro like!y to be a "martyr to headache." More sleep is what you -need to cure you. For all nerxous head- aches hot fomentations are comfating and curative. They are far better than cold appli- cations. Want of exercise, living in badly ventilated rooms, indigestion, or anything that lowers the health, predisposes to headache. When headaches are not cured by simple means a doctor should be consulted. When hot fomentations are used application to the nape of the neck, as well as to the forehead, will give more relief than if used to the forehead only. The heat to the spinal cord soothes the brain.

div.head: BRUIN DECEIVED.
div.p: BRUIN DECEIVED.

The bear is very fond of honey, and when he hears a telegraph-post humming in the wilds of Siberia, he says to himself, "Au !the bees ,are humming up there on the top of that post! Good! I'll go up and get some honey!" Up he climbs, but only to find ,that he has made a little mistake. 'lie breaks down the telegraph-post, and, instead of honey, gets a nasty 'fall!

div.head: BRAVE Boy.
div.p: A BRAVE Boy.

At Whtersham, in Kent, there is a well which is 51 feet deep. ,One bitterly cold night a cat fell down this well, and she. would have died had it not been for a brave boy, named Archi- bald Burt. There was nobody to help him, for no one was at hand except a small boy, who was too young to be of any use. Archibald „ got . a bag, slung it over his shoulders, me fast the well rope, and climbed down it. He was in time to save the cat from drowning, and he put her into is bag. But the worst part was to come. His clothes were drenched with the icy-cold water at the bottom of the well. The cat and the bag were drenched too, and this made them 'much heavier than they otherwise would have been, and Archibald had to climb hand-over-hand up those 51 feet of rope with this weight on his back. When he reached the top he was half dead with cold, and exhaustion. The Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals have given him their medal for bravery, which 'he certainly well deserved.

div.head: PARISH CHURCH SALE OF
div.p: PARISH CHURCH SALE OF
WORK.
How The Proceeds Have Been
Divided.

"The sale of work this year," says the "War- rington Parish Church Magazine," "was in every way, except one, a very great success, and we owe a deep dept of gratitude to our visitors, and to all our workers awl officers for the most kind and generous help. The first day we made £lOO, the second • £7O, and the third £74, in all £244. The expenses only amounted to about £7, leaving us £237 to distribute, and this is the way the profits have been apportioned: Church Repair Fund, £9O; -Working Parties in 1916, £4O; Day Schools for use on Sunday, £2O; Re- payment of Loan from Fairfield Day School Funds to Church Institute, £52 10s.; the two Missions, £24 10s.; Organ Fund, £lO. This we consider a most satisfactory result. The one exception to which we have referred was the absence of so many of our regular congregation from the sale, leaving the burden of raising this large amount of £240 to rest upon the shoulders of a comparatively small number of devoted helpers in our midst, and a few most generous friends from without. This should not be the case. Everyone should bear his share and take his part. Even the poorest, who, can- not afford. to -buy, could pay the small charge for entrance, and show his interest by his pre- sence. . We earnestly hope that all our people will lay this to heart, and determine that nothing shall keep them away from the sale of 1916."

div.head: BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYANS
div.p: BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYANS
Former Pastor Re-Visits His
Old Church.

The anniversary services of the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church were held on Sunday, the spbcial preacher being the Rev. C. Hale Hocken, a former pastor., Preaching in the morning from the text "The secret of the Lord is with them that fear him" (Psalm xxiv., 15), the Rev. Mr. Hocken said that we were familiar with many things of which we did Vot know the secret _meaning— the hidden ,purpose. He instanced that though many were familiar with English literature, the majority of readers could not enter into the secrets of Shakespeare, Milton, Taylor, Charles Lamb and others innumerable. In the same way people were familiar with God—so familiar with God that they had lost all fear of Him. Answering the question "What are the things that impress us and that move us to the very centre of our being?" the preacher said that one of them was " Magnitude." They thought of the slowly wandering traveller over thei Himalayas—the backbone of the world. There amidst a vast solitude the traveller saw moun- tains—range upon range—until they thrust their huge shoulders right \tiP into the blue dome of Everest, 29,000 feet above the level of the sea.

div.head: Forces That Strike The Imagination.
div.p: Forces That Strike The Imagination.

The display of pier impressed one. The recent earthquake in Japan manifested incal- culable power of bursting with one swoop and destroying a whole city, thrusting aside of a mountain and great waves of lava into a boiling sea. That impressed them as an ex- hibition of power. Distance was another of the things that impaissed us; not only the waste distances of the .desolate -deserts, the vast seas, the fields of ice iii the Arctic regions, but beyond the planets and -the fixed stars was that un- thinkable distance. The thought of space so vast touched them all with awe. Surely the wonder and variety of life on this earth im- pressed them. The traveller amidst the tropical

forests of Central Africa or of South America— where there was teeming life—saw the beasts, the birds, the reptiles, the insects, the trees, the plants, the flowers, of all sizes and shapes and colours.

div.head: What Is Wanted To-day.
div.p: What Is Wanted To-day.

But, went on the preacher, there was a God whom men did not fear; there was His name which men mumbled over over a soiled Bible in the Police Courts. Men had lost their 'grip of God, tind that was the reason for all the super- ficialities and indefiniteness of modern civilisa- tion. What was wanted to-day was a due sense of fear and wonder and awe of God. Charles Wesley had it, and it could be found in his hymn, "Where shall my wondering soul be- gin?" The secret of a Christian life, concluded the preacher, was the surrender of the will to God.

At the conclusion of the sermon the Rev. C. Hale Hocken expressed his pleasure at being able to visit Bewsey-road Church once again. In the afternoon a musical aervial was held, and was very, well attended. Ths? soloists were Madame Sara Silcock. and Mr. Arthur Pearce, and both sang with their usual artistry. Mr. T. B. Duckworth was in the chair, mid the Rev. Ineson (of liold-street WesioFat: (ipir::11) gave a short address on "The -Mission of the Church in War Time:"
At the evening service the choir rendered the anthem "If You Love Me, Keep My Com- mandments."

div.head: FORE IGN.rM ISS lONS.
div.p: FORE IGN.rM ISS lONS.
Effort Must Be Maintained
Despite War.

The cause of Foreign Missions was pleaded at the Parish Church on Sunday by the Rev. C. Finch White, of the Diocese of Chota, Nagpur, Central Provinces, India. In the course of a sermon to 'a large congregation the reverend gentleman said that missionary effort could be considerably enlarged by the aid of medical work, and that "the thin end of the wedge" of Christianity was often driven in by means of the splendid service rendered by the hospitals and dispensaries. A big task confronted the missionaries, and the people should on no account let their interest in the work of the foreign field slacken, not even though the war was on.
The reverend gentleman also spoke to the Church-street and Fairfield Sunday School scholars in the afternoon.
The collections -throughout the day were de- voted to Foreign Missions.

div.head: "AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER ? "
div.p: "AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER ? "

The usual weekly gathering of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Brotherhood, held on Sunday, was pre- sided over by Mr. Ben Farrar, and was addressed by the Rev. A. J. Morton, the Wesleyan minister from Padgate. The reverend gentleman, in the course of his remarks, com- batted the fallacy that the only things that could be believed were those which could be seen. Life was full of things which were very real and yet were unseen. For instance, there was electricity. 'rhey could not see the life in electricity; they merely saw its effects and the instruments through which those effects were obtained. Did a man ever really see his mother? No, they saw but the form and were able to admire the attributes; but the soul, the life, the sympathy and the love which Were all summed up. in the word " mother " they never really saw, and could but feebly comprehend. An oft asked question was "Am I my brother's keeper ?" They were, and they could not escape the responsibility; for each life affected the lives around it for good or for evil, and conse- quently,it behoved each tne of them-to be true to the highest that was innate ix all. Mr. Payton presided at the organ, and Mr. C. Cotton read the lesson.

div.head: SPECIAL SALVATION SERVIcE.
div.p: SPECIAL SALVATION SERVIcE.

There was an increased attendance at the special service at the Picturedrome on Sunday evening. Staff-Captain Mann (the secretary for the young , people's work in ,the Liverpool division) was the leader, and gave an address on the text, "Jesus Christ. the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever." He touched upon the subject of the war and recounted some thrilling instances of courage and heroism on the part of British and French soldiers. The United Senior and young People's Bands led the singing. The Senior Band also gave a selection entitled "The Heart's Closed Door," and a male voice party rendered " Heavenly Mansions."
