div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

The Price of M;ik. lii these parts milk is now 41d. per quart. have been inquiring as to the price of this in- disPonsable article of diet in places in which I have formerly resided, and in none of these is it as high as .it now is in Warrington and dis- trict. The people of Halifax are reported to be very wroth at having to pay 4d., and even 34d. is in some places considered too high. My correspondents tell of communities on the East Lancashire border who strongly resented a recent increase from 3d. to 3W. The Labour Councils held protest meetings at which 'the advance was declared to be quits unjustifiable: It is only within the last fortnight that the extra halfpenny on the 3d. has been put on in the case of one 'place at the western extremity of the West Riding of Yorkshire, and there consumers have cut down requirements, so that the farmers and retailers have-much milk left on their hands, and have so far gained nothing, but rather the contrary. lam surprised at this. I 'certainly consider 31d. a quart a vary reasonable price for milk in these times; tilt when it gets to 41d., well • Receiver Worse Than Thief.

The local case of receiving stolen prcperty put me in mind of one occurring in ,a district in which I used. to live'. A pig butcher who had quite a large establishment and did a good trade could not resist the temptation to do a little illicit business on the lines now indicated. He arranged with a former employe who had gone into similar service in a neighbouring town systematically to rob his new master for their mutual advantage; and he regularly drove over and himself conveyed the stolen goods to his own premises. He was heavily filkoid on con- viction, but that was slight in comparison with the punishment he received in other, ways. His dishonesty led to his ruin; his customers left him, and he was obliged to give up business and seek a situation elsewhere.

An Attftil Dodger. Writing of dishonesty, I think of the absentee soldier who at Warrington produced an old rail- way ticket with the date erased, and that in turn:recalls the story of the supposed absent- minded traveller who, when a ticket collector entered .his. compartment began feeling in one pocket' after another, muttering the while that he must have lost it. "Why, what's that in your mouth?" exclaimed the amused official. Eh! well of all !" returned the apparently stupid passenger, taking the bit of pasteboard from between his lips and handing it to the still laughing railway man. But when some of his fellow passengers began to chaff him respecting the incident, the simple one with a knowing wink confided to them that he " wor nobbut sucking th' date off th' owd ticket!"

Furious Motoring. Last week's Borough Police Court. case re- ported under this heading brought to my mind that of a young colleague of my own who was much given to scorching by motor bike. ".Going home?" said he once to a passing innocent afflicted with "nerves "; don't trouble about the train—jump into the sidecar, and we'll have a nice gentle run." The gudgeon rose, to the bait, and on, being set._ down at his own door some half-dozen miles from the start- ing point, escaped in the condition generally described as "more dead than alive." "Obliged to you, of course," he gasped; "but no more for me, thanks." That young motorist is now dispatch riding "somewhere in France." When last I heard from him his letter was dated from hospital; he had damaged his knee as the result of a sideslip while going at.the rate of 35 miles an hour—seemed rather proud of it, too. Some fellows are .built that way; but all such should .enlist in the country's service and get on to the Continent, where constables cease from troubling if the weary are not at rest.

A Painful End. The death of the unfortunate Wm. Graham In an ice-bound pit, "his head being above the water," set me thinking of ii distressing fatality the victim in which was for years a colleague of my own. We set out to "do " one of the Parliamentary divisions in which an election was proceeding. Wa6 went in different direc- tions, and met late in the evening and com- pared notes. We parted in the high road near a polling booth which had just closed, and after leaving me he must have decided on a cut along the canal bank. I have never been able to understand what could have possessed one so habitually cautious to take so dangerous a path in the dark, a stream running on the side away from the canal. The poor fellow slipped into the latter at an unfrequented spot too far from human habitation for his cry of alarm to be heard. The water was not deep enough to drown him, yet it was impossible for one in such a situation to scramble up the steep bank to the towpath several yards above. His dead body was discovered at daylight, the hands still clinging to the grass at the side and the head above water. My lamented friend had evidently died from exposure, and one does not like to think of the agony he must have suffered before he became unconscious.

Instrumentalist's Compensation. The transfer of a 'local bandsman to the , Welsh Guards reminded me of the' experience of a young acquaintance in whom I have been r,articularly interested since he enlisted for war service. He was just completing training in the North when he met with a rather serious mishap. ,Ife was vaulting over a fence near the camp, when he fell and sustained infernal injury, netessitating prolonged hospital treat- ment. Meanwhile his regiment left for France, where they participated in historic engage- ments, achieving considerable distinction, but losing heavily—in fact, as my young friend mournfully expresses it, they have been practi: I.lly wiped out, their identity being lost. And' what of himself? Well, 'he happens to be a versatile musician, playing the trombone well and the piccolo splendidly. His ability in this latter respect Oommended him to the favour- able consideration of the conductor of a Scots i,egimental band having a vacancy for, that ing,trument. and he is now accompanying them on _peruiting service. He is "doing his bit" in a totally different direction from that nnticipatsd a few months ago.

The Soldier Boys. In a reference in last week's " Examiner " to the phrase "Lancashire lads," a rude couplet is quoted to show that it has been in use some hundreds of years. The term "Minden boys" as applied to Lancashire Fusiliers dates _itself. We know, too, about the "Death and glory boys," and how the name originated,—and so of various reginaents tlitt have performed exploits destined to live in history. When I was in Halifax the 33rd West Riding Regiment Lii ba'rracks there were called—and of course wherever they are they are still calieg—" Th' havver cake lads," the oat bread of which Car- mer generations of Northerners especially were Fond; and which- is still baked and hawked in Lancashire and Yorkshire distrtAts, having be- come their, symbol through an incklent occur- ring in the long bygoues,

A Plucky Old Astronomer. Mention of Councillor Dale's lecture on "The 'life and death of worlds" reminded me of an interesting nonogenarian whom I knew on the border of the sister counties. Although now in kis 91st year, he is apparently still going strong, or I. see from a -local paper that he has just "been 'lecturing in the Bronto country, with a scollege professor in the chair. Some years ago— ho would to upwards of 80 then—l heard him *peak for a osuplo of hours or to on "Other -worlds than ours," and about ten o'clock that -night, as was his ws on. such occasions,' he 'tramped back alone over the Fripors to his solitary 'dwelling some seven Or eight mates away. As a , :young Tan he was a shepherd, awl, he studied :astronomy aS he " watched his float; by night." I have had many adventures in his company, 'but possibly L ;13.4.10 'W4070 to. F.torne' of these 'things kbefor.c. •

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
ORIGIN AND MEANING OF WORDS.
Our Indebtedness To Early English Literature And

div.head: Bible.
div.p: The Bible.
ILLUMINATING DERIVATIONS.
BY C. E.

In my last paper I referred to rivers us-eful preservers of one of our earliest tongues —the Celtic. I have also incidentally referred to dialects as valuable in a similar way. We are also indebted to all early English' litera- ture, and coming down to later times, we owe much to the Bible and Prayer Book. There are several words in the Scriptures we under- stand because of their association, which if used apart would appeai to be either out of place or wrongly used. Take the -.Word Prevent. This comes from the Latin pre, before; ventum; to come; liter- ally, "to come before." Hence it may imply a person coming before and acting as guide, or it may imply coming before to hinder, to pre- vent as we use the word in the modern sense. In the Bible it is used in both senses. We have an example of its use in the first sense in the petition in the Prayer Book—" Prevent us, 0 Lord, in all our doings," also in the Psalms, "Thou preventest him with bless- ings," and again "I prevented the dawning of the morning." We find it used in the second Sense in the dospels, ". And when he was come into the house Jesus prevented him; saying," that is, He prevented Peter from speaking, by coming in or speaking before him.

The word Collects applied to a portion of the Prayer Book means that which collects the teaching of the Epistk and Gospel, gathering them together and presenting them as peti- tions. The origin of the word Heaven is of interest. It is the grammatical perfect of the verb to heave, so called because it is heaved or heaven up. The firmament is described in a similar way in the Scotch, and spoken of as the lift or lyft, what is lifted up.

div.head: RELATIONSHIP OF WORDS.
div.p: THE RELATIONSHIP OF WORDS.

The use in two different senses of the same word suggests a possible relationship, but the meanings often give no duo to such. Then, as we do With folk, we Must trace, the words back to their beginnings. We must unravel their pedigree. For, example, the word Canvas, cloth made from flax or hemp, and the word Canvass, meaning the soliciting of votes- No two meanings could appear to be farther apart, but let us see. As originally employed, the word canvas• meant the laborious work of sifting the hemp. When we realise that the word canvass means a sifting, we can readily see that the same idea is contained in the Word canvass when applied to voters, and so the mystery vanishes. The word canvas suggests Candidate. This springs from a Latin adjective signifying white,, shining. The competitors for offices in Rome were obliged to wear a white toga when going round the city soliciting the votes of the people. From this sPrang a number of words with no 'apparent connection unless we have the clue, such as candle, chandelier, eandonm Candlemas, cannel-coal, and the white candi- dum lily. The word Canter, as applied to the action of a liorst, does net at first sight appear to have any connection with the town of Canter- bury, hut such is the case.. In olden times the pilgrims to that shrine travelled on horse- back, and generally used ambling nags, and the easy pace at which they travelled was called a " Canterbury gallop," which was afterwards contracted to canter, and used generally to denote a particular horse action. There appears no connection between the word Cannon, a piece of artillery, and the Canon of a church, or the Canon of Holy Scriptures. The root of the word is Greek, canna, and meant a reed (hence cane), which was selected as a rule for measurement. Thus in,\Revelation xxi. 15 and 16, we read of the measuring reed, corresponding to the car- penter's rule. The Holy Scriptures are the rule or cannon of life. But what has this to do with the heavy artillery piece called a cannon? Probably this, that those who first used these engine S of war, requiring a name, in recognition of the straightness and hollow- ness like a reed, gave to them the Greek name for reed, canna or cannon. We have the Canna group of reed plants. Several of these are in the Park.

div.head: FAMILY WORDS.
div.p: FAMILY WORDS.

Some words are members of large families. Each has its own individuality and meaning, while a family likeness runs through all the group. The word Stock is a case in point. We have live stock, stock-in-trade, the village stocks, stock of a gun, _stocks on which ships are built, stocks that tie • ropnd the neck, family stock, Stock for soup, stock in public funds. The common idea in the whole is that of fixedness. The stock of a gun is that in which the barrel is fixed; village stocks are those in which the feet are fixed. Stock-in- trade is fixed capital also in the funds. The same idea is in the cognate words in the Scotch to ateik, to sneck, to fix a door. " Sticket the eon of the corps." Closed or fixed the eyes of the dead. The word Share is also one of a large family, and has among its relatives shire, shore, shive, shore, shrive, shred, shed (v), and sherd. The Anglo-Saxon Root signifies to separate or divide. Shire' is a district in England separ- ated from the rest; shore is a place where the continuity' of the land is interrupted or separ- ated by the sea; shred is that which is torn from the main piece. Sherd, as in potsherd,

div.head: ARKER.
div.p: ARKER.
is that which is broken off from any vessel, etc.

div.head: WORDS THAT HAVE DEGENERATED.
div.p: WORDS THAT HAVE DEGENERATED.

While some words, like some people, have risen in the world, others have fallen. A Villain is now an evil-disposed rascal. Originally a villain signified a countryman or, peasant, the hamlet in which such persons dwelt .being called a village. The term vil- lain,. before it became demeaned, was asre- spectable as its relatives, villa and village, which spring from the same stock. The word Blackguard has also fallen in the world. It was originally applied to a scullion, that is, a menial servant, who cleaned the pots and pans in the scullery; also in war in connection with an army. This, of course, is dirty work, and those who performed it, from their usual appearance, were called as a by- name the black-guard, but this only applied to their outside appearance. Now we apply the word to the inward and moral character of the individual. Knave meant once no more thaili lad. A Boor was a farmer, and a Varlet a serving man.. Crafty and Cunning did not at first imply crooked or underhand work, but only knowledge and skill. When we speak of a man's craft, or of a cunning workman, we get back to the original meaning. Retaliation signifies giving back as much as we Have received, but is now used entirely in respect to injuries, and seldom if ever to benefits. Were we to hear one speak of "re- taliating kindnesses," I doubt if we should Understand what the speaker meant. •

div.head: WORDS THAT HAVE BEEN ENNOBLED.
div.p: WORDS THAT HAVE BEEN ENNOBLED.

I have spoken of the degeneration of words. There has been a parallel process 'going (Ali in the opposite direction. Certain words have been ennobled, and this has been specially so in words employed in association with Chris- tianity. The word Humility in Greek sug- gests meatiness of spirit, now it has acquired a far more worthy meaning. Angels were at first only earthly messengers, 'and a Martyr simply meant a witness. Christianity appro- priated these, and angels arc now exclusively heavenly messengers, and a martyr is ono who witnesses to the truth with his blood. Para- dise meant some royal park or garden of de- lights, then it came to be used by the Jews as the abode of our first parents, and afterwards was claimed by Christianity for the state of heavenly blessedness.

Paper derives its name from the plant. papyrus, which grew in ancient Egypt, and its leaves were used as we now use prepared paper. The word Style in Connection with writing is traceable to a small iron instru- ment called a stylus, with which the ancients used to write on waxen tablets. Gradually the term was extended beyond the mere writ- ing to the character of the composition. " The word Field carries us back to the time when England was covered with wood,. and when to make a clearing it was necessary to fell it ho wood, so we have the wood-land and the fold-land, possibly also the veldt, although of this 1 am uncertain. The letter i in the modern field is. an addition, and did not' exist in the early English writers. . The word Attorney refers to an ancient custom Of conflict and signified one who ap- peared at the tourney and did. battle in the place of another. An Attorney engages in a tournament of words' on behalf of a client.

The meaning generally attributed to the Word Husband is doubtless right, honse-bond, the bond that holds the house together. In the old English the word is spelt husbonde. We speak of husbanding our resources, that is, holding them together. We have an expression which used to be in -Very common use, "It's all in my eye and Betty Martin." This and similar expres- sions are said to have their origin in theH popular ignoranco of Latin. It is supposed I to be an English corruption of an invocation to St. Martin by mariners, " Ah, mihi, beate Martine." (" Ali, me! blessed Martini") I should not like to pledge my verity on this origin, but more unlikely things have hap- pened in our. speech. Stipulate is derived from the word Stipula, the Latin for a straw. In buying or mortgaging land, to complete a transaction straws were once used or exchanged, and this act was called stipulation. It answered the same end as our modern prlactice of complet- ing a document by signing and sealing. This corresponds to an ancient Hebrew custom we find in the Book of Ruth, in which Naomi's nearest relative abandoned any claim to the land in question by plucking off his shoe and handing it to Boaz as an evidence of the sur- render and transfer of his right to put his foot upon the land as the buyer and re- deemer of the land of his dead relative. "And this was the manner in former times in Israel concerning redeeming and changing, for to confirm all things a man plucked off his shoe and gave it to his neighbour, and this was testimony in Israel." I see a certain author considers the origin of stipulation doubtful, but .surely the privi- lege might be accorded to an amateur anti- quarian to insert at least one doubtful origin. Antiquarians are described, somewhat un- fairly, as people who make something out of nothing and add sauce to it. I think, how- ever, that, of the words given, the last is the only one abota which there is any doubt.

div.head: SCHOOLBOY ABROAD.
div.p: A SCHOOLBOY ABROAD.
Reminiscences Of Childhood In Rangoon.
LAND AND SEA, EXPERI- - ENCES.

We were waiting on the qua 7 at Calicut— my father, a younger brother, a battalion of soldiers and I. We two boys, aged six and four respectively, were the only children of th. 3 party. Our fellow-travellers. were soldi?rs waiting to be carried to the troopship which was about a couple of miles out at sea. Durin.; the night we had travelled by train from Bangalore, a sraall garrison town in the centre of Mysore. The journey had made us terribly tired, for though, in some respects, India is an ideal country, its railways were at that time (1899), slow and cumbrous. At Bangalore 1 attended school for about 18 fil'onths, but the only striking went that occurred during that period of my life, was that I played truant and received a sound thrashing. ,After a miserably long wait on the quay we were placed in a boat which resembled a huge oyster shell. There were about thirty of :these boats and they were in charge of natives, who had to pilot us out to the transport The soldiers' wives and children, with the exception of my brother and I, had left Bangalore the day previous and were already embarked. At length we began to move in the direction of the transport, but, we had counted our chickens be- fore they, were hatched. Thanks to our native pilots and oarsmen, I had a novel experience.

div.head: LOST AT SEA.
div.p: LOST AT SEA.

As our very unseaworthy boats were making for the transport they were caught in a current and carried miles out to sea. For hours we could see nothing but sky and sea and a battalion of soldiers in open vessels lost at sea. Our pilots were helpless. First they sent us in one direction, then in another, till at length, the majority of the troops fell victims to sea- sickness. Our disgust May .easily be .imagined, but it was no use grumbling, and we simply had to trust to luck. Towards evening the trans- port, still waiting patiently for its passengers, was sighted. We made towards it and soon were on board, but the eight hours in a rocky boat under a tropical sun and without food is an 'experience that will be fixed permanently in my memory. Our destination was Ranoon, the capital Of ,Lower Burma, and we vrived there without further adventure.
Itangoon is a city bf about 180,000 inhabit Ants, and is situated on the eastern branch of the

. Irawadi. Visitors usually remember it on account of its terrific heat. At that time it was terribly behind the times. The " cars " from the town to our house were steam cars, big, ugly, clumsy-looking things that' used to go puffing up and down the main streets. The place we lived in was a huge wooden bungalow far away from "anywhere." Near by was a tree, more massive than I have seen elsewhere, under Thich I spent many hours watching lizards, &c. Rangoon seemed to be a hotbed of reptiles and mosquitoes. Often when walking about the house we could see scorpions, centi- pedes and other deadly insects crawling about the floor.
Rangoon possesses_ a fanious pagoda where

thousands of the Burmese—who are chiefly Buddhists—worship. It rises to a tremendous height in the -shape of a spire. From about half-way •up, it is covered with something that looks like gold. I was told it was gold, but I doubt it. Whether gold or not, however, it looks magnificent in the brilliant Sunshine. • -At each side of the pagoda is a huge and ugly figure of an animal. immediately inside, before the idols are reached, is a sort of bazaar, where fancy goods are sold by the
THE SLEEPING BEAUTY.
Inside the temple itself are thousands of

idols, but the one that is worshipped most is a figure of "The Sleeping Beauty." This is saply an image of it sleeping lady, but the Burmese say that when " she " wakes up, they will throw off the yoke of British rule and re- gain their independence. • School life in Rangoon was a very tame affair. Nobody seemed interested, and things went along in a very casual way. We had not lived there long before I was transferred from the infants' school to the senior school, and I was very proud of myself. I remember very clearly that it was one Friday afternoon that I was given a seat in Standard VII. of the Senior School. I was presented with three books—a Bible, a reading book and an exercise book. My opinion of myself rose considerably, and as I went home that night, I don't think that there was a schoolboy who felt prouder than I. But pride always goes before a fall. Our house, as I have already said, was a huge wooden bungalow, which was used for' the Officers' Mess.. Here were stored the regimental silver plate, the regimental colours and a number of silver trophies, the total value being estimated at £30,000.

The day after I had -received. my school- books, mother took me to visit one of her friends, who lived in a bungalow about half a mile away. We were sitting on the verandah having tea, when we noticed flames leaping to- wards the sky in the same direction as our home. I left the tea table and commenced to run towards home. Half-way over the Maidan (Common) a friend of mine cried out to me: "Your house is on fire."

Terribly excited, I ran home as hard as I could. Here I found that a laige crowd had already gathered and the fire engine was at work. Curious as it may sound, my only, thoughts were to save my three new school- books. •I attempted to break through the crowd in order to save them, but I was held back by my schoolmaster; and, it was not until he promisono give me another set of books on the Monday morning that I became quieted. Young as I was, I reflected on the awful consequences of die fire. I knew that being old and of wood, not all the fire engines „in the world could save my home. Nor was I wrong. I went out of the. crowd and, sitting in a quiet corner of the grounds I wept as tl)ough my heart would break. Everything went in that fire. All the "treasures" that I had accumulated, my books, my games, my money box, my clothes, everything. Within two hours that massive wooden building, with all its valuable contents, including the regi- mental colours, was one mass of ashes lying on

the ground. Not a single article was saved. How the outbreak occurred has always been . mystery, but it is the common belief that it was the work of a careless Indian servant who had charge of the paraffin lamps. Shortly after this disaster, the regiment, and our family with them, left Rangoon for Calcutta.

div.head: ' DAY OF REST.
div.p: ' DAY OF REST.

Increase In Pleasure-Seeking And • , Unnecessary ‘Vork. The committee of the Lord's-Day Observance Society feel that the present disregard of the Lord's Day in various ways, more especially in the providing of entertainments, calls for sin- cere protest. They fail to see how Gods help can be expected in this 'time of crisis so long as his will is so widely disregarded. The following resolution has just been passed by the General Committee of the Church Pastoral Aid Society That this committee, having special sources of information from clergy and lay agents, supported by the society throughout the country, deeply deplore the kgreat increase.in pleasure-seeking and also un- necessary work on the Lord's Day, and urge all who have influence in either direction to make all possible effort to discourage the provision of Sunday amusements, and to preserve to all workers their heritage of Sunday rest so far as is consistent with the national safety and .pub- lic -welfare."
A mother i alwaya ,ontwardly proud of her baby if it look like it's father, but inwardly §l.te way regret it.

div.head: ALL SOULS AND ALL HALLOWS.
div.p: ALL SOULS AND ALL HALLOWS.
Another Chapter Of Curious Survivals And Ancient
Customs.

div.head: INTERESTING LETTERS FROM READERS.
div.p: INTERESTING LETTERS FROM READERS.
BY ARTHUR

By word and letter we have received valued evidence of the appreciation which is felt to- wards this page of "The Examiner," and of the interest which has been awakened among our readers in matters antiquarian. Before quoting some letters on " Souling" habits, we propose to set forth some further literary dredgings of our own on the subject of our last article. November Ist and 2nd in the Church calen- dar are All Saints' and All Souls' Days. In the Middle Ages the custom arose of spending the eve of All Souls' Day in prayer for souls in purgatory, and the watchers in some places spent the entire night in church in vigil and intercession. The custom changed in form after the Reformation, and the popular habit of "Souling" arose. As was pointed out, this has lingered in our own neighbourhood in the form of souling songs and the gifts of soul Cakes. In other districts it has survived in more curious usages. Here is a rather remarkable instance frpm the Fylde district, as described in Thornber's " History of Blackpool." The last evening of October was called the Teanlay night, or the " Fast of All Souls'." Until recent years it was the custom to light bonfires on the hill tops on that evening, and from hills which encircle the, Fylde and the mosses of Marton fires sparkled ,brightly. The rustic idea was that the fires- in sonic way succoured those whose souls were detained in purgatory. As to the exact manner in which it was supposed to help no one was quite clear, but the belief was very firm, and the habit was evidently a survival of something which their ancestors had done through preceding cen- turies. A field near Poulton, where fires were lit, is still called " Purgatory " by the old inhabitants.

div.head: BONFIRE SUPERSTITIONS.
div.p: BONFIRE SUPERSTITIONS.

The association of the bonfire with All Saints' Eve is found also in Wales and Scot- land. In Pennant's book on Wales, written in 1777 he tells us that there was a custom upon All Saints' Eve .of making fires called Cod l Cooth. Each faniily. made its own fire in a conspicuous place near to its own house, and when the fire had burned low each one threw a white stone into the ashes, having first marked it with their own sign. After that they said their prayers turning round the fire, and went to bed. In the morning, as soon as they rose, they went to search out the stones, and if any were missing they had the notion that the person who throw in those that could not be found would die before au- other festival of All Souls'. Owen's History 'of the Welsh Bards has also an allusion to the fire. ,

"The Autumnal fire Is still kindled in North Wales, being on the' eve of the first day of November, and is 'attended by many cere- monies, such as running through the fire and smoke, and each casting a stone into the fire, and all running off at the conclusion to escape from the black short-tail sew; then supping upon parsnips, nuts and apples; catching at an apple suspended by a string with the mouth alone, and the same of an apple in a tub of water; each throwing a nut into the fire, and those that burn bright betoken prosperity to the owners through the following,- year,. but those that burn black and crackle denote mis- fortuno. On the following morning the Stones are searched for in the fire, and if any be missing, they betidek ill to those who throw them in." , In close resemblance are the Scotch Hal- loween fires kindled on, the same evening. A minister of Callander wrote some years ago: "They set up bonfires in every village. When tho bonfire is consumed the ashes are carefully collected into the form of a circle. There is a stone put in near tho circumfer- ence for every person of the several families interested in the bonfire; and whatever stone is moved out of its place or injured the next morning the person represented by that stone is devoted or fey, and is supposed not to live twelve 'months from that day." In other parts of Scotland the fire takes the form of a fire of faggots kindled and carried round the village upon the top of a pole, the bunches of faggots being renewed as they burned out. The people kindled faggots or rush lights of their own from the flame and received it as a sort of consecrated fire, from which they lit their household fires, the vir- tues of which would last for a year. _ _ _

Students of folk-lore will n-ot need to be told that there has been a mixing of ancient symbol in these usages. The idea of sacred fire belongs to a remote past; it .has evidently become grafted upon a Halloween ceremony.

div.head: ANOTHER PAGAN USAGE.
div.p: ANOTHER PAGAN USAGE.

The same process may be seen in a Hallow- tide ceremonial practised in Scotland on the Isle of Lewis. The people assembled at the Church of St. 11fulvay, from where they went to the sea shore. A brew of ale had been previously made, towards which each family had contributed a peck of malt. One of the men, carrying a large vessel of this ale in 'his hand, waded out into the sea until the water reached his waist. He then addressed himself to some deity whom they called Shong, and poured out into the water the ale which he carried. They then returned to the church and observed a minute of dead silence. At a given signal the candle on the altar was extin- guished, and the crowd proceeded to the vil- lage or field, where the night was spent in revelry. This is a very curious instance of the blend- ing of what is pagan and Christian. The propitiating of some deity who may send storms or spoil crops is ancient pagan usage, yet it is blended with a visit to church and a drunken revel, in the fields. It is, more- over, observed on the eve of All &HIM'. •

The introduction of a horse's head into the "Sotiling " custom shows that in some way the festival has been mixed up with hodening, or the bid English hobby-horse used by Mor- ris dancers, and common in Wales at Christ- mas under the title Mari Lhwyd.

div.head: REVELS AT LYMM.
div.p: REVELS AT LYMM.
Upon this we may write a separate chapter next week.

And now a few lines supplied by our readers on some modern aspects of " Souling." From Lymm we learn that " a horse's head, which formerly went from door to -door; might still be dis- covered without much search. It con- sisted of a genuine horse's skull with jaws that could be closed with a terrible snap, and went the round Of the village as recently as six years ago. • What the ceremony may have been years ago I can- not guess, but all through my own remem- brance it has been an occasion for horse- play and drunkenness. A gang of young; men decked themselves in showy dis- guiscp. The head was carried on •a • pole and drapings hung down to cover the man who carried it. He had a horn under the drapings, from which terrible sounds were emitted. The ' horse ' could rear, kick and bellow in a manner that was truly terrible, and which drove the children of the house to the shelter of the pantry or bedroom. The decorated gang went from door to door after dark on October 31st and November Ist. They haid Set speeches, one of which referred to Lord
Nelson, 'the Admiral with bluo ribbon's and white buttons, being impersonated by one of the visitors. A demand was made

div.head: lOUNFIELD.
div.p: lOUNFIELD.
for liquors and half a crown, and as the evening wore on and the effect of tho liquors began to be manifest, peace-loving folks had a bad time."

div.head: SOULING INDEED!
div.p: SOULING INDEED!

The following takes us -farther back, and shows an even rougher side of things : "In my grandfather's younger days--- from seventy to eighty years ago—the souling festival was celebrated in a very remarkable way on the Lancashire and Cheshire borders. From the neighbour- hood of Croft, Risley, Glazebury and Cul- . cheth, a batch •of young follows were chosen as soulers. They were not picked because they could sing, but because they could fight, and crossed the river to the Cheshire side. A full fortnight was spent in drinking and fighting. Set fightsitook Place between the picked champions of each county, and all the days finished in a general spree and carousal. This was souling ' with a vengeance, and though it suggests nothing of the religious fes- tival or centuries ago, it represents our great grandfathers' ideas of having a pro- fitable time. There are more ways than one of Reeping up a good thing."

Yet against "I am a Cheshire -lad who has gone souling ' many a time, but I have had to wait until last Saturday to be told what souling meant: I confess lam won- derfully interested. To show you bow little We understood what we were sing- ing about, we, or somebody else, altered 'Soul F Soul! for an apple or two,' into 'Solo, sole, sole of my shoo.' We had a verse, The roads are very dirty, . My shoes are very thin, And if I had a penny I'd get some nails put in. • "We also sang in Warrington sonic hopeless doggerel: Christmas is coming, Geese are getting fat, Please to put a penny In the,old man's hat. If you haven't a penny, A ha'penny will do, If you haven't a ha'penny, God bless you. ANOTHER SOULING SONG.

div.head: MESMER AND MESMERISM,
div.p: MESMER AND MESMERISM,
Personal Magnetic Powers Applied To Curative Purposes.
CURIOUS TREATMENT.

It is not generally known that the wbicl " mesmerism" is derived from the name of the founder (or, more properly, re-discoverer) of the science. This man, Frederick An- thony Mesmer, was born in Vienna in the year 1740, and the delight of his early years was the study of the works of the medieval alchemists and astrologers. At the same time he was studying medicine, and in 1766 he took his degree and began to practise. Six years later, after prolonged and careful reading of his favourite authors, he an- nounced his discovery of a universal - fluid, which he spoke of as "the immediate agent of all the phenomena of nature, in which life originates, and by which it is preserved." This idea was by no means new. As early as the sixteenth century philosophers had agreed that there must exist "a . universal magnetic fluid, independent ,of, tho Ugh prin- cipally acting through, the medium of the mineral magnet" The notion of using the magnet as an agent .for transmitting this universal fluid, and thereby effecting cures, originated in the writings of Paracelsus and Van Helmont (1577-1644), who derived the idea front the mystic philosophers of Arabia. Paracelsus, who, as all know, has been immortalised by Bromning, flourished from 1493 to 1541. He maintained that he had cured dropsy, gout, jaundice and other diseases by the use of the magnet. Mesmer at .first, in accordance with the old theory, used magnets, but after his quarrel with his master, the Jesuit Hel, who attempted to arrogate all the glory of the dis- covery to himself- he discarded them, and neneeforth used his fingers—or at most au iron rod.

div.head: MESMER'S PHILOSOPHY.
div.p: MESMER'S PHILOSOPHY.

Mesmer maintaimed. that "the universe was steeped in a fluid which produced all the phenomena around us, and served as a medi- um for the influence which the heavenly bodies, the earth and animated nature exer- cise upon each other." He believed that the properties of the human body were analogous to those of the magnet, that it also possessed poles and could operate upon the universal fluid By this means the physician ought in- stinctively to know the cause of the disease, its nature and its course.

In the year 1776 while practising as a phy- sician in his native town, Mesmer was called to the bedside of a patient who, as the cus- tom was for every complaint, was being bled. Ile noticed a remarkable phenomenon: when ho approached the sick man the flow of blood stopped, when he withdrew it recommenced. He wiallked backwards and forwards several times, and each time the same thing hap- pencd. Ile then became convinced that he was himself endowed with magnetic powers, and that he could use this wonderful influp. euce for curative purposes. After a series of successful experiments ig the hospitals of Switzerland and Bavaria he announced that "there is one health, one disease. .ste remedy and one physician, and that pAysician am I." Naturally his de- claration aroused much opposition among the orthodox medical men of the day, . and as his metir.+.ds were not always above suspi- cion his enemies seized the first opportunity that offered to persuade the Empress Maria Theresa to banish him from Vienna for fraud.

div.head: HE VISITS PARIS.
div.p: HE VISITS PARIS.

Driven out from his birthplace Mesmer went straight to the city where everything; that is new is welcomed, and there he was re- ceived with open arms and attracted so much attentiOn in the highest circles that some years later a royal mandate wag issued order- ing the medical faculty to enquire into his theories and his methods. Though the report of this cOmmission was "4 not favourable, people socked to him in crowds to be cured, and the overnment of- fered him a pension if he wcn experiments under certain edulitions. This he refused to do, preferring i lc udependent hand, though later on when 'the lovelty of his treatment was wearing oeff an his popu- larity consequently on the iivane, a applied to the Government again, brat bein' reusd began to sell his secret to chosen PuP,li!" With-the money thus obtail ed, and cPuoile subscription raised in his mour in :ranee, e he retired to Spa, where le lived fcr. some time, until the oppositioUti to his Evstem reached such a height he shred: from the virulence of the atta •ks made .?pon him, and returning to Switzerland he dwelt 19 peace there until his de2,th in the vear of the battle of Waterloo, drcl-otni sth, 1515.

div.head: HIS lairl 22.11ENT
div.p: HIS lairl 22.11ENT

Mesmer's methodf cu-COring mrious diseases seems to us childislind P. paubmimic in the extreme and we cant ' lorbar smiling when we read of the theatq,a,l as he used to im- press his patients. These were shown into a darkened room whose wails were covered with mirrors. In the middle of the floor stood igreat tub with two lids, through which passed iron rods whose ends the patients held. The tub was full of bottles of magnetised water, ar- ranged in rows one upon another, so that the neclis of those in the first row pointed to the centre, while in the second row the bottoms pointed inwards—and so on iu alternate rows. There was also some water in the tub, and usually, some. magnetised iron filings, ground glass, sulphur, manganese and other articles of a like nature. All this para- phernalia was considered essential to disen- gage the magnetic agent. The patients stood round this tub and di- rected the end of the rods to the parts of their bodies that were diseased. Sometimes a hoop suspended from the ceiling encircled their waists. At other times they formed the "chain," as it was called, i.e., they stood in a circle holding each other by thumb and forefinger in order that the current might circulate freely throughout the ring. Meanwhile the magnetiser, armed with an iron rod, presided over the meeting and ap- peared to sway the current at will. Occa- sionally he would step forward and gently touch he parts of the body affected with the end of his rod. And all the time soft and languid music would float through the cham- ber, in order to heighten the effect of mys- tery !

div.head: SENSATIONS OF • THE PATIENTS
div.p: SENSATIONS OF • THE PATIENTS

The sensations of the patients were varied. They felt spasmodic pains, especially in the head and stomach; they perspired freely; they suffered from palpitation of the heart; sometimes they seemed on the verge of suf- focation; at others they experienced a vast mental -exaltation and a sense of comfort and Vell-being. Their nerves were much affect- ted, a tingling made itself felt in their ears, they became dizzy and exceedingly sleepy. Them sensations always culminated in convulsions, though this effect might not be produced for hours after the treatment &- gran. When one patient succumbed all the ipst followed almost immediately. This was known as the "magnetic crisis," and Mesmer believed that this was Nature's way of effect- ing a cure. The convulsions usually lasted a long time and were very violent, but direct- ly they came on the sufferers were removed to the "crisis chamber " and carefully tended. It is said that on their recovery the patients felt but slightly exhausted and very greatly relieved both in mind' and body. When Mesmer died he left many disciples, the most distinguish of whom was the Mar- quis de Puysegur. This nobleman revolu- tionized the art by . showing that many of the phenomena might be produced by gentle manipulation causing sleep, and without the mpteritous surrottud%ing6. and violent • !means resorted to by Mesmer. The , gentler method was followed by Deleuze, Bertrand, Georget, Rostan and. 'Foisr-ete in France, and by Dr. John Elliotson in England up to about 1830.

div.p: Will-power.

Everything pivots on the will. Will-power is courage. Will-power is backbone. 'Will-power is stability. Will-power is determination. Will- power is character. " I will" conquers every difficulty. " I will "'succeeds in spite of re- peated failures-. "-I will " crushed in the night begi BS again in the nit tin i ug. 1 will "light on when everybody else has given up. div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.

Said a member of the Petersfield Rural Dis- trict Council recently, "My brother and I have 14 women working for us, and by next spring we might have 60 or 70. All these women will be trained by us, and personally I would rather train them than have them trained under the -County Council."

div.head: ROOT CROPS.
div.p: THE ROOT CROPS.

The figures just issued by the Board of Agri- culture show remarkably little difference in the average yields of roots, and though there is an actual falling off in the supply of turnips to the extent of a million and a half tons, this is due almost entirely to the decrease in the acreage. On the whole the report is more satisfacfory than it seemed likely to be earlier in the year, says "Farm and Home," though the lower totals will, of course, accentuate the. difficulties Caused by the high price of concentrated feeding stuffs.

div.head: WINTERING STORES: A GOOD COAT.
div.p: WINTERING STORES: A GOOD COAT.

By stores are meant strong steers, heifers or cows that are for next year's grazing, to go either direct' to the butcher from grass- or to be done up a bit at back-end of the year for ordin- ary, markets, or, as regards some of the prime sorts, to be finished off for the Christmas market in the stalls. Such cattle may be brought in any, time between now and Christmas, or even later, but it is decidedly advantageous to lay in the stock in good time, so as to be able to see to the winter treatment from the beginning and give the animals as long time as possible to grow and improve while on hand. Now, is the. time to begin to pick up some well-bred thrifty stores or good crosses that may, other things being equal, materially help to pay the rent. Many a herd has been ruined for want of warm hair to give protection in a rigorous sea- son. There is only one way of getting the com- forting garment, and that is to expose the herds at this .season onwards, and, to a certain degree. all winter. Temperature really, rules the growth of the coat, and it is promoted by per- mitting the stock to rough it pretty much ,in the open fields, at back-end, at all events.

div.head: FARMERS' "BIT."
div.p: THE FARMERS' "BIT."

Fourteen motor ambulances of the latest pat- I tern, approved of by the :War Office, were on view on Tuesday last week in St. James'-square. They were the last of a convoy of 50 presented by British farmers to the British Red Cross Society and the St. John Ambulance Associa- tion. The cars have accommodation for eight sitting patients, together with one attendant and a driver, or for four' patients when stretchers are used. The complete convoy has cost 02,500, the price of ea,a car being 3350, and with each has been given a sum Of £2OO for its upkeep for six months. During the day many farmers and land- olOners from the country who had contributed to their cost inspected the cars, which came from the counties of Wiltshire (4), Warwick- shire (2), Hereford (2), Stafford (1), Yorkshire (1), Northampton (1), Somerset (1), Monmouth (1), and Cheshire (1).

div.head: DEMAND FOR EGGS: A GREAT OPPORTUNITY.
div.p: THE DEMAND FOR EGGS: A GREAT OPPORTUNITY.

Never within the memory of man, has the de- mand for eggs been so enormous as it is at the present time. There is moreover every indica- tion that it will increase in the infmediate future, while prices, of course, are in no. way diminishing. This applies to all parts Of Great Britain. Eggs are higher in price than ever, and profit, despite the increase in the price of feeding stuffs, is very considerable. It is neces- sary that the food supply shall be maintained, and the person who endeavours by all the means in his power tq add to the supply is rendering a service to. his country. Up to the time of the outbreak of war the annual British consumption of eggs .amounted to the. gigantic sum of up- wards of. £24,000,000, nearly two-thirds of the supply coming from abroad and Ireland. These imports are now enormously, reduced, and thus. the poultry keepers in this country should rise to the occasion and do all that is possible to Meet the growing demand for eggs. That there are great possibilities of very largely increasing the output no one can deny. Everything seems at the present time to favour development. Our climate is all that can be desired for poultry; we possess the finest table fowls, and the most profitable layers that are to

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.
Another " Warrington " Club Enters" Soccer " Arena.
GREAT SANKEY RE-CIIRISTENED.

At a recent meeting of the Management com- mittee of the Great Sankey Football Club, it was decided .after some discussion to alter the name of the club, and henceforth it will be known as the Warrington' Association Football Club. It is felt that the new name will more adequately describe the nature of the club, and that it will give the committee more influence with other clubs in the. future when they make

----- their application for membership to the con- trolling bodies of the competitions in which they wish to join. If the committee can only retain the players they have now got together they would be successful in holding their own with the majority of the teams in the Lancashire Combination.

The Warrington A.F.C. were disappointed in their fixture with the Hindley Central Club, but the committee succeeded at the last moment in arranging a fixture with a team representing the Thelwall Club. The Thelwall team included P.. Kite (who keeps goal for Accrington) And Bromilow (of the St. Helens Recs.) The rest of

the men were locals. fleywood (of Manchester United) made his first appearance for the home club, who, however, were short of the services of Brindle, G. Whitfield and Ditch4eld. They called 'upon Fearnley, of the Warrington Rugby Club to keep goal, and he performed very creditably, and was loudly applauded for several saves. The first portion of the game was evenly contested, and the score at half-time was in favour 'of the home team by two points to nil. In the second half the visitors were completely outclassed, and but for the good custodianship of Kite, they would have suffered a more severe , reverse.

In the Warrington and District League on Saturday, the Paddington and Warrington , Central teams met to play their return fixture. Owing to the frost-bound nature of the ground the game was only proceeded with after consul- tation between the referee and captains. The opening half, as indicated by .the score, was evenly contested, and • each side was Credited with one goal. In the second half the United were seen to more advantage, and it was owing to an appeal for hands against Gilbert that they gained the lead. The appeal for -a penalty-kick .was not accepted by the referee, owing to the penalty area lines not being distinguishable, and he was quite justified in awarding a free- kick. The finaltscore was in favour of the home team, who deserved their victory on the general run of the game. They were best served by Derbyshire, Sherratt, Holden and Hardman, and the visitors were best represented by Knight, Gilbert, Stevens and Williams.

The Warrington and District Junior League games were in full- swing again last week. Probably the fact of having had a week's rest had a great deal to do witii the keenness which was displayed in the games that were decided. -

Howley United, in their game against Mersey Juniors, showed that they had maintained their recently improved form. The score at half-time was one goal each, but in the second half 'the United proved their superiority and ran out winners by 3-1. -

TA Cadets and the Scouts opposed each other in Victoria Park, and although the Scouts were not able to play their best team they had in mind the defeat of the previous week in a sham fight, and they were determined to reverse the result on the football field. They were suc- cessful in gaining the lead in the first half, but in the second half they were chiefly on the de- fensive, and it appeared as if their goalkeeper ' was helped by some kindly disposed power for, although the Cadets saw:some of their shots hit the uprights and the crossbar, they could not put one past the Scouts' goalkeeper. zones, had a splendid chance of equalising for 'the Cadets, as he had only to shoot past the goalie, but he hesitated and allowed himself to be easily robbed of the ball.

The match of the day was at •Arpley between the two top clubs of the League, St. Elphin's and Fairfield United Reserves. The ground was in a shocking condition for such an important game between these juniors. The United have shown much improved form recently, and brought their best available team, which in- cluded " Dobbie " Woodhouse'. The "Saints" were successful in retaining their unbeaten cer- tificate. Gleave and Buckley were very safe at back for the "Saints," and Hough and Boyle were the most dangerous forwards. Woodhouse, Tunstall, England and Lockhart were the pick of the United.
The match for last Saturday between Emmanuel Institute v. Penlieth Friends' was
cancelled owing to the ground being in an unfit condition.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
STEWING PEARS.

We hear but very little of these, yet they are in demand in some households and are highly valued. Properly cooked in a pannikin and served, stewed pears are a form of sweet that is appreciated at the dining table, and as the true stewing varieties of pears keep much longer than the dessert sorts there is very good reason why more attention should be paid to them. It is strange that but few of these cooking pears are planted nowadays, but in most gardens healthy old trees are to be found, showing that in the olden days store was set on them. I fail to see why stewing pears should have fallen into neg- lect, as they can be turned to good account in , most gardens while in many Oases they would I prove as profitable to. market growers as the better known dessert varieties. Some may say

that many of the dessert varieties are only fit to be cooked, and this is quite trup, but what we. want are pears that will keep for some time and herein lies the value of the true stewing pears, a dish of which is particularly welconie when the dessert varieties are exhausted.

div.head: WATERING ROOM PLANTS.
div.p: WATERING ROOM PLANTS.
Many who grow plants in rooms find a diffi- culty, as regards watering. Though the days are now short and the sun has but little power, yet

all too often the plants receive their usual supply of water, no thought being given to the fact that the demand on the roots is far less than it was in the summer. At this season it is always advisable to tap the side of the pot, and if a hollow sound is produced then it may he assumed that the plant is dry and in need of water. The best way to water is to stand the Plant or plants in a tub or bath until the air bubbles cease to appear.

div.head: PRUNING GOOSEBERRIES.
div.p: PRUNING GOOSEBERRIES.

In country districts where birds are numer- ous it is often advised that the pruning of these be deferred till the spring. It is, however, I think, better that the bushes be pruned as soon as all the leaves have faller', and dressed with something that will make the buds distasteful to the birds. I have found a mixture of lime and soot very useful, this also helping to cleanse the bushes of moss and Other insects. In many gardens the gooseberry caterpillar is a great scourge, quite defoliating the bushes. Where this has been the case all the prunings should be gathered up and burned. Then re- move some three inches or so of the soil under- neath the bushes, wheeling it away and burn- ing, it, substituting some fresh soil from another part of the garden. After this smother the ground with soot and newly slaked lime, which will destroy ,any caterpillars that may have been 1,ft.,.--Wick, in "Farm and 'Lome."

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKING MEN'S ASSOCIATION.

Locally there has been little done this last fortnight, but if the elements are favourable we see no reason why there should not yet be a specimen or two put on the board, as the weeds are now practically done with and fish should feed better after the frost. Several members have not yet given up hope of bringing one or two from the Shropshire Union Canal and the Gowy before the season ends.

div.head: N.A.A. GENERAL MEETING.
div.p: N.A.A. GENERAL MEETING.

Tht general meeting was held at the Earl of Crewe Hotel, Crewe, Mr. R. 0. Atherton pre- siding. The General Secrettiry, Mr. T. Redford, said he was sorry there was a great falling off of members this year. At the same time he ;was pleased to inform them that most of the mem- bers who had left the. ranks of angling had joined the ranks of the British Army, and there were now over three thousand fighting for their King and country. As the balance sheet showed, there was no need to fear as to the 'future of the N.A.A. At the same time they did not know what the coming summer would bring, and they must prepare to meet whatever conditions might arise. He was pleased to in- form them of the successful case, the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, that was gone into by the F.F.p.L., by obtaining £4O damages for tar running into the water and poisoning fish to a considerable extent. Mr. Fletcher, of Preston. added that it was owing to the vigorous protest of the N.A.A. and guaranteeing the F.F.P.L. £2O to go on with the case that success was achieved.
The total membership is 6.505; balance in bank, £l4O 7s. 10d. Auditors, G. T. Moore and NV, C. Seabrook. _

Officers for 1916:—President, Mr. W. Brown, Crewe; Vice-President, Mr. J. Arnett, Preston; Treasurer, Mr. D. Cuedon, Bolton; Secretary, Mr. T. W. Redford, Bolton; Solicitor, Alderman P. A. Horridge, Bolton.

div.head: DELEGATES' REPORT.
div.p: DELEGATES' REPORT.
Delegate meeting, held at Earl of Crewe Hotel, Crewe, Saturday, November 27th.

It was reported to the secretary that persons had been using night lines in the S.U. Canal. also taking undersized fish. The matter had been fairly dealt with and the persons found proved to be non-centre members. The Boatman's Arms Club, near Wigan (un- attached), had fished a raatcn in the Haigh Canal, contrary to the ruling of the Wigan Centre, and they objected to paying to stock this length, but Wigan pointed out ,to them they had the ruling of this particular length from the N.A.A., and all moneys received had been spent in stocking, and more, and they were not going to be told by the Boatman's Arms in what part of the length they were to turn the fish in. A letter of apology was re- ceived by the general secretary from the club, ' rind the matter was allowed to drop and Wigan is to give them another trial. Mr. W. D. Phillips, of the North Staffordshire Railway, proffered £lO towards stocking the Trent and Mersey Canal between Wassail Green and Brochen Cross. The matter was left in the hands of the general secretary of Crewe Centre.

The F.F.P.L. was advised to • write to the Surrey Trout Farm Nr fish to stock the L. and L. Canal, as Walkden had a fine consignment, that came from there the same day. There will be no matter in connection with railway travelling during 1916 in the N.A.A. cards, but cheap fares are under consideration. Wigan Centre has put 800 perch in the Haigh Canal, and expects fair sport during next sum- mer for the match anglers.

div.head: CREWE CENTRE.
div.p: CREWE CENTRE.

Crewe Centre entertained the delegates to a fine tea, for which the General Secretary pro- posed a vote of thanks, Mr. Arnett, of Preston, seconding. Mr. Browne, of Crewe, now presi- dent, invited the delegates to their club room, he remarked it was one of the largest Individual clubs in England. It is named The Crewe Pioneer Angling Institute, and has a refresh- ment bar, committee room, reading room, billiard room (three tables), shooting range, general offices and kitchen, in billiard room. There are 28 cases of specimen fish set up, some that we noticed in particular are a case of four chub caught at Welshpool, in the Severn, 41b. 41b. 240 z., 31b., 15t0z., 31b. 111-oz. Trout ! caught in the river Audlem 41b. 10Ioz.; chub caught in the river Audlem 41b. Gloz.•, bream, 41b. 7toz.; pike, 181 b. Goz.; rudd, 21b. lioz.; eel. 2ft. Sin. long, 21b. 11-Soz.; besides many othms that we had not time to take particulars of. Surely this is a fine collection, and very in- teresting to anglers visiting the Crewe Centre. Mr. Browne assures us that at any time War- rington anglers are Crewe way be will be pleased to show them round their club and give them all the advice possible. - A. S.

div.head: FOOD FOR ATHLETES AND
div.p: FOOD FOR ATHLETES AND
OTHERS.
Change Of Opinion As To Nutritive Properties.
COOKING ERRORS.

The recent investigations of Dr. Chitten- den, head of the Physiological Department of Yale University and of Professor Folin of Cologne, have so modified the scientific opini- on as to the comparative values of different kinds of food that many of our current ideas wilt have, to be set on .one side, and test
books above a few years old looked on as out of date. Indeed the whole theory of nutrition has been altered, not tentatively or timorous-
ly, but with an array of fact; and figures, put forward in such a logical and eonc...usive fashion that there is no appeal.

Briefly, what the investigations of Pro- fessors Chittendeu and P--Vdt have proved is that the proteid or sc,t_ J!..sl 4lesh-forming foods, otherwise nitrogetutatt are but of small value in nutrition, and that in select- _ _
ing his dietary the man who desires to be healthy and strong should avoid the proteids as much as possib.e. The old theory was that about fourteen ounces of the tissues ox
man's bf>dy are broken up every day, and that, to supply this waste, at least an equal weight of nitrogenous food fi..tould be used.
UNSUITABLE FOODS. The analysis of the uriro provided the data for this calculation, but now it has been

proved, if anything ever can be proved, that the nitrogen emitted by the body has never Yormed part of the tissues at all, that it is, in fact, the rejection by the system one day of unsuitable food eaten the day before. This at once places the beefsteak, and lean meats of all kinds, as well as cheese, to say- nothing of the pulses, peas, beans, etc., on a far lower level, as far as their place in the nutrition of man is concerned. It had occurred not only to Folin and Chittenden, but to others, that such a large daily waste of the body, as the excreted nitrogen suggested, was scarcely in accordant* with the ordinary simplicity of nature...By experiments on themselves, they
were able to se-e that the quantity of nitroge-n passed out was always in proportion to the quantity eaten on the previous day, and that this could be reduced to a minimum without
11;-_-th-e least decreasing the weight of the

body. There was clearly some flaw in the old theory: if the body required fourteen ounces of nitrogen a day, how was it that it did not lose weight after being served for' a length- ened period with only one or two ounces a day? And not only did the body appear not to call out for the larger quantity, but the whole system seemed to work better, and the spirits to be lighter and freer when only the small allowance was used. Dr. Chittendeu got some of his fellow professors at Yale to re- duce the weight of the proteids they had been in the habit of using, and the result was still the same—a very much better condition of the body.

div.head: NEW THEORY TESTED.
div.p: THE NEW THEORY TESTED.

Though satisfied of the falsity of the old theory, he was anxious to prove to the world the truth of the new, and for this purpose, with the consent of the Government of the United States, he selected twenty men from the Army Medical Corps, who agreed to sub- mit to the test; and experimented with them for a period of nine months. Their weight and strength were tested at the beginning, a certain number of marks being assigned for particular feats, such as running, 'Jumping, climbing up ladders, expansion of the mus- cles, etc., and the same tests applied at th 4 end. The transition from the ordinary quan- tity of nitrogen to almost no nitrogen at all was fairly quick, but the men did not seem to suffer any inconvenience. On the contrary, most of them were able to say that they haA never before felt so well, a,ncf at the end of the nine months their strength had practical- ly doubled. But Doctor Chittenden did not stoT here. The fact that the men were living more regular lives, and put in more practice is the gymnasium, than they had been aeonstomed to do might, he thought, have had at appreciable effect on the results obtained. So he went to the athletes of the University, all of them trained up as far as training could go, and got several of them to submit to the same dietary and tests that had beer used in the case of the soldiers. For anothei nine months this went on, such foods as lean
meats being almost entirely eliminated from the menu, and at the end the same result Ink

shown. The athletes had practically doubled in strength, and not only so, but many oi them declared that they felt far less fatigue under the new system than they had been in the habit of feeling under the old, and were altogether in better condition. Professor Chittenden argues reasonably enough that the expulsion of so much useless food every day imposes on the system a bur- den which must involve a considerable waste of energy, whilst the fact of eating it at all cannot but prove deleterious, and may easily account for the prevalence of such a disease as appendicitis. • HOW TO BEEP IN CONDITION.

But if we are not to eat lean meat, etc., what then should be the food of the athlete, or for that matter of any person who wishes to keep his body in the best possible condi- tion, and consequently to get the greatest en- joyment out of life ? The answer is. all star- chy foods, such as bread, rice, oatmeal, and fats, such as butter, oil,, and the ordinary fats of the various flesh meats. All these come iinder the general name of carbo-hydrates, and it is their burning up in minute particlee all over the body that produces both energ3 and heat. As a rule,‘ the starches are to be preferred to the fats, as they have a less ten• dency to remain in the body, and the person who wishps to be slender should not touch fats at all. Such plants as cabbages are of very little use as food, though the salts which they contain are very excellent for the blood. Unfortunately, however, these salts are al: lost by our method of cooking, being thrown away with the water, and what remains is an almost useless fibre. Some people, and among others the writer, have taken to drinking the cabbage water and discarding the rest. Po- tatoes, however, being a starchy food are valuable enough, but even here some portior of the nutriment is lost by our manner of cooking them. They are beet of all roasted, but failing that, they should. bp steamed, or at least boiled in their jacket& THE VALUE OF ME.

Not very long ago it was the fashi9n decry rice as an almost useless article of food, owing to the small proportion of nitrogen which it contains, but curiously enough it is now found that even rice contains as mud. of the proteid element as the body needs. And even if the theory did not fit in, some ex- planation would have to ba found for the fact that many strong races live almost entirely -on that cheap ,grain. I military writer, (Colonel Murray, I think, who followed the Russo-Japanese war as attaché, has declared in his book that the Japanese soldier, living almost exclusively on rice, could carry a Brit- -1511 soldier on his back and run further in day than the ordinary British soldier Could march. It is all very well to put this down to race and to climate; no race can get out of a food properties which it does not contain, and as for climate I do not think that many of us in Great Britain are called upon to en- dure more rigours of cold than thi Japanese had to bear during their winter campaign in Manchuria. I have been told by one of them- selves that the only war correspondent wlic was able to treat the cold of that winter with indifference was one who lived as the Japan. ese lived, that is, mainly on rice.
The road to success Is embellished with mighty few signposts.
The man who fails is worth two of the men who never try.
A: man never makes a mistake in dccepting advice. It's acting upon it that counts.
A Rough Guess. The other-people's-business man persigted in trying to extract information from a prosperous. looking elderly man next him in the Pullman smoker.
. "How many people work m your office?" he asked.
C 4,741., ••• • "Oh," said the elderly man, getting up and throwing away his cigar, "I should say, at a rough guess, about two-thirds of them."
Frost Stops Matches In Lancashire.

The frost interfered with the Northern Union fixtures last Saturday, with the conse- quence that not a single game was played in Lancashire. and only four in Yorkshire.. The results of these were as follows :
Batley, 6 points; Brighouse, 0. Dewsbury, 29; Featherstone, 0. Halifax, 8; Braniley, 5. Hull Kingston R., 14; Bradford, 0.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. THELWALL.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. THELWALL.
The above clubs were engaged in a friendly fixture on Saturday on the Hood-lane ground.

Warrington: Fearnley; Glover and Leah; Heywood, Siddall- and Kelley; Illidge, Whit- field, Aspinall, Foster and liillward. Thelwall : P. Kite; Millington and Bromilow; J. Kite, J. Millington and Payne; Welsby, Davies, M. J. Kite, Barrow and Banner. Referee, H. Smith;. Latchford. The visitors won- the toss and decided to de- fend the lane goal, having the sun at their backs. Aspinalf set the ball rolling and the game at once became very fast and evenly con- tested. None of the players took unne*ssary risks on the frost-bound ground. The ball travelled very quickly from end to end, but the lhome forwards were better at shooting at the target, and Kite had most shots to deal with. At the end of twenty minutes' play Aspinall re- ceived the ball from a clearance from Kite and had not much difficulty in placing in the net. After a short spell of midfield play the same player notched a second point. The visitors in- creased the efforts to reduce the arrears, but were easily checked. Half-time: Warrington, 2 goals; Thelwall, nil. The second half opened in favour of the visitors, but Fearnley and his backs would not yield to. the charges on them, and play was transferred to the visitors' end, where the home forwards dallied with the ball and allowed the backs to • clear. A few minutes- later the Warrington front rankers returned to the attack and Millward sending the ball across the mouth of the goal, T. Whitfield added the third point. A few minutes later Aspinall registered a fourth. Th.) visitors now made a rally and warmly attacked the home goal, where Fearnley was cheered for the way in which he cleared his lines. F. Millington missed scoring from a free-kick just outside the penalty area. •Millward made a fine centre, which -Kite made two grand efforts to clear, but finally Whitfield placed in the net. The visitors forced a couple of fruitless corners, and were then forced to defend th.ir own goal. 'Heywood scored from a penalty. Further goals were added by Aspinall and Tllidge. The result at the call of time being: Warrington, 9 goals; Thelwall, nil.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT
LEAGUE.
PADDINGTON UNITED v. WARRINGTON
CENTRAL.
On the ground of the former in their return fixture. _ _ _ _
Paddington United: Fforrocks; Holmes and Holden; Sherratt, Marsh and Pritchard; Green- wood, Taylor, Darbyshire, Hardman and Gar- nett.
Warrington Central: T. Knight; Williams and Robinson; 'Brown, Gilbert and Stevens; W. Warburton, T. Warburton, Hands, Emery and Hindes.

Referee, Mr. S. C. Essenhigh. Darbyshire set the ball rolling before a fair number of spectators. Owing to the hard and rough surface of the ground play was not very keen, and for a while long kicking was indulged in. The defence of both teams proved too good for the opposing forwards. Offside against Grtr- nett spoiled a good opportunity for the United, and good tactics by Gilbert and Stevens trans- ferred play to the home goal, where Sherratt made a timely clearance. , The visitors returned to the attack, but Stevens shot wide. Good play by Greenwood Placed the visitors' goal: in danger, and after Gilbert had cleared the home forwards returned to the attack, and Hardman opened the score. From the centre-kick the visitors assumed the offensive, and after several efforts had been repulsed Stevebs equalised with a splendid long shot, which fairly beat Hr- rocks: Half-time Paddington United, 1 god; Warrington Central. 1 goal. _

, On resuming the home team were nuicklv at- tacking, but Stevens. Gilbert and Williams de- fended grandly and forced play to midfield. The United forwards again attacked the visitors' goal and gained a free-kick just outside the uenalty area. from which Darbyshire gained the lead for the home team. From the centre-kick. Gilbert made an effort to break through the home defence, but the frost-bound ground spoiled his efforts. and the Central were again put on the defensive. Darhyshire. shooting hard. hit the post and the ball went into the net. After this reverse the visitors rallied and Gilbert, with
the goal at his mercy, shot straight at Trorreeks. who conceded an unproductive corner. Play continued even until the call ef time. Result: Paddington United, 3 goals; Warrington Central, I goal.
