MERSEY JUNIORS v. HOWLEY UNITED.

On the Arpley ground. The game opened very evenly and some keen play was witnessed, Smith opened the score for the Juniors, and a few minutes later Davies equalised. Even play followed until the interval, when the score was one goal each. The second half opened with some keen tack- ling on both sides, but eventually the United gained the upper hand, when Miller sent in a high shot which completely beat Walters and gave the United the lead. The Juniors tried hard to get on equal terms, but the United defenders proved too good and kept their goal intact. Glassey increased the lead With a good shot. Final score :—Howley United, 3 goals; Mersey Juniors, 1 goal.

div.head: LATCHFORD CADETS v. STOCKTON HEATH SCOUTS.
div.p: LATCHFORD CADETS v. STOCKTON HEATH SCOUTS.
In Victoria Park. Cadets: Hart; Plumpton and Newall; Ash- ton, Rainford and Walker; Jones, smith, Cart- wright, Davenport and Roberts. Scouts: Hampson; Farncll and Foster; John-

son, Ford and Manuel; Smith, Bennett, Haslam, Williams and Baguley. Referee, Mr. H. Berry. The Cadets won the toss and Haslam kicked off, for the Scouts who at once attacked the Cadets' citadel, but failed to pierce it. The Cadets broke away, and after several futile shots at the Scouts' custodian. they gained a corner-kick, but failed to improve upon it. From the goal-kick Smith, on the visitors' extreme right, made a grand individual effort, and with a splendid centre placed the home goal in danger. The other forwards failed to get up in time and Newall effected a fine clear- ance. The Scouts' centre-forward broke away, beat the opposing backs, and sent in a shot which gave Hart no chance to save. After this reverse the Cadets replied strongly, when Jones, after getting past the backs, hesitated in front of goal and allowed the ball to be cleared away. Another corner-kick was gained just be- fore the interval, but Cartwright placed on the wrong side of the uprights. Half-time :—Scouts, 1 goal; Cadets, nil. The Cadets in the second half at once became aggressive, and the Scouts' defence were very busy, but Foster and Farnell played a good de- fensive game and kept their lines clear. The Scouts were only able to make occasional raids into the Cadets' lines, and these were initiated by Smith, who received poor support from his partners. Newall bit the upright with a good long shot, and directly a penalty was given for hands against Johnson, Newall took the kirk and Hampson effeeted a very good save. Result :—Scouts, 1 goal; Cadets, nil.

ST. ELPHIN'S v. FAIRFIELD UNITED RESERVES. On the Arpley ground; before a good number of spectators. Both teams were at full strength, but, unfortunately, the ground was in a bad con- dition owing to the frost, and was a disadvantage for so important a match. The opening ex- changes were very keenly contested and the United being smarter on the ball, made a strong 'attack on the Saints' goal. England opened the score .for the United by heading a splendid goal after ten minutes' play. This reverse put the "Saints" on their mettle, and they retaliated very strongly, when Boyle had the misfortune to see a splendid shot hit the crossbar, but directly after Hough equalised the score with a hard drive. Both teams were now on level terms, and both were playing keenly, but the Saints were combining better and gradually put the United on the defensive. Shakeshaft scored the second goal for the "Saints." Half-time :—St. Elphin's, 2 goals; United Reserves, 1 goal. The second half opened very fast. Wood house made the scores equal with a long shot from near the half-way line. The " Saints " put more vigour into their game and were quicker on the ball than their opponents, and Boyle, receiving from the wing, eluded the at- tentions of Lockhart and placed the ball be- tween the uprights and gave the " Saints " the lead. The remainder of the game was in favour of the "Saints," but no further scores were made. Result :—St. Elphin's, 3 goals; Fairfield United Reserves, 2 goals.

div.head: ORFORD JUNIORS v. BEWSEY.
div.p: ORFORD JUNIORS v. BEWSEY.

On the Longford ground, before a fair crowd of spectators. For a few minutes play was in front of the home goal, but .the defence eventually cleared and midfield play followed. The home team were now settling down to their game and transferred play to the visitors' goal, where a splendid centre was put in from the touch-line, and the ball was quickly put past the visitors' custodian. For a few minutes play was not very interesting. Then the home lot appeared to wake up and the visitors' defence was hard pressed, but they managed to survive the attack. Half-time :—Orford, 1 goal; Bewsey, nil. On changing ends the Bewsey captain made several alterations in the players' positions, and the visitors were seen to better advantage. They played hard to get the equalising point, but the home defence stuck to their work and gradually , drove them back. Hands against Dickinson gave the home team a free-kick, from which they increased their lead. After this reverse the visitorr, appeared somewhat disheartened; but Hassall• got past the home tams and reduced the arrears with a rattling shot. Encouraged by this success the Bewsey lads played keener, and in a few minutes Edwards put them on equal. terms. Now came the tug-of-war, and only a few minutes left to gain the lead by either team. Some exciting struggles were crowded in. The visitors gained a penalty- kick, and this was entrusted to Smallman who, to the dismay of his colleagues, shot over the bar. At the opposite end the home team gained a corner-kick, which was well placed, but in the struggle was again , played out for another corner-kick. Time was called before this could be taken. Result :—Orford Juniors, 2 goals; Bewsey, 2 goals.
GIRL'S TERRIBLE END.
Fatally Burned In Enamelling
Shop.
A DANGEROUS PRACTICE.

An inquest was held at the Warrington Police Station on Wednesday, by Mr. S. Brighouse, on the body of Edith Forster, aged 19 years, who lived at 73, Cartwright-street, Warrington, who met her death whilst employed as an enameller by Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., Ltd. Present at the inquiry were Messrs. H. R. Brothers (H.M. Inspector of Factories) and Mr. T. S. Steel, solicitor—who was instructed by Messrs. Greenall and Co.—represented Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. Mrs. Forster, the girl's mother, said that she was the widow of the late James Forster, iron- worker, of 73, Cartwright-street. Her daughter said that when she was coming out of one of the stoyes a flash caught her clothes and "burned them oil." A HOPELESS CASE. Nurse Burton, a sister at the Warrington Infirmary, said that the deceased was admitted to that institution at 12.30 on Saturday. Her case was hopeless and she passed away on Mon- day morning at 3.15. HOW THE TRAGEDY OCCURRED.

Alice Higley (19), of 10, Wakefield-street, deposed that she was employed by Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. 'as an enameller. She and the girls who worked with her " dipped " parts of bedsteads into the enamelling pan, and then placed them into a stove for the enamel to dry. On Saturday, when she had nearly finished her work, she went to get in a kettle some spirit which they used for cleaning off the enamel. She placed the kettle just inside the stove door so •as to get the spirit warm. She used the spirit to clean her arms before leaving work. She got some more parts of bedsteads and put them into the stove. Edith Forster came be- hind her and as soon as she entered, the witness heard her scream and saw that her clothes were on fire. Edith collapsed on to the floor and a workman came and put his coat over her. Questioned by the Coroner, the witness said that she did not know that she was doing wrong in putting the kettle in the stove; she ha.l done it before. None of the officials knew that she had done so. She had been enamelling bedsteads for nearly a year.

div.head: WHY THE SPIRIT WAS REQUIRED!
div.p: WHY THE SPIRIT WAS REQUIRED!

In reply to Mr. H. R. Brothers, the witness said that the kettle was three-parts full of spirit. The other girls knew that she had brought it. The spirit was in the stove for about five minutes. The deceased was carry- ing part of a bedstead at the time of the acci- dent. In answer to Mr. Steel, the witness said that the heat of the stove came from plates at the bottom. As soon as the kettle was knocked over—as it must have been—the spirit burst into flame. Saturday was a very cold day and her object in putting the kettle into the stove, was to warm the spirit. The Coroner: If that is the irregular practice, what is the regular practice? Mr. Steel replied that it was for the employes to dip their hands in the spirit outside the stove. The witness admitted that she had never seen anybody put the spirit in the stove, except dur- ing the past fortnight, whilst Mrs. Weston, the forewoman, was away ill. • Mr. Steel informed the Coroner that when a workman came to the two girls, the witness told him to attend to Edith.

div.head: SUMMING-UP AND VERDICT.
div.p: SUMMING-UP AND VERDICT.

The Coroner said that a point for the jury was whether the girls put the spirit into the stove with the knowledge of the firm or not; and then the point arose as to whether the firm had taken the necessary steps to warn the girls. Evidence was also given by Mr. E. Williams; the assistant works manager, after which Mr. Brothers observed that apparently the fatality was the result of one of those accidents which it was impossible to foresee. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," expressing the opinion that a notice should be put up warning the girls against heating the spirit. Mr. Steel said that the firm could not foresee that anybody would do a thing like this; but now they had decided to put notices up regard- ing the matter. On behalf of the firm he ex- pressed sympathy with the relatives of the un- fortunate girl.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 4, 1915.
Situations Vacant.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
GAME OF CHANCE.

div.head: Nominal Fine On Man Who Had
div.p: Nominal Fine On Man Who Had
Ileliwd Police.

At Tuesday's Borough Police Court, Gilbert Chadwick, whose address was given as ".a van, off Flag-lane' was summoned for inducing persons to indulge in a game et chance, on the Warrington Pair Ground, on November 27th.— He pleaded " Guilty ; but I did not know that I ‘vii4 (loing wrong."

div.head: Detective Wins.
div.p: The Detective Wins.

Detective-Sergeant Reddington deposed that al: 9.30 bn Saturday night he was on the Fair' ottial with Detective Skelton.. They saw a large stall of which the defendant had charge, and on which there. were a number ,of small discs, somewhere about the 'size of a shilling; indeed, there must have been , about two hundred of the discs. Defendant had ,a supply of wooden rings—considerably larger than the discs—and he was inviting people to " buy " the rings at three a 'penny and attempt to throw them or roll them on the stall in such a man- ner that they all, or any one of them, dropped over a de, so- as to .encircle it. The players hod to stand four or five feet away from the st9ll ard. of course. it Was a Question of chance
as. to Allether the rings with which they were supplied rolled .over a disc or were throim over one. I
The Modus Operandi.

If a ring fell over a disc defendant paid the player threepence, or he could take twopence and have three further tries with the rings. Witness and his companion saw several men and boys, and a few women' " have It shot" at the game. He tried it himself. (Laughter,) En fact he had. seven goes and he was successful twice. (Renewed laughter.) Witness had *never tried the game before in all his life. Each time he " ringed " a disc defendant gave him twopence and three more rings. After he had experimented witness called the defendant aside and told him who he was, adding that the game was purely one of, chance, and that it child of seven had the same chanee of winning as a man of forty or fifty. Defendant admitted that that was so, and Said that as 'witness con- sidered the'game one of chance he would stop it.
Defendant told the Bench he did not think he was contravening the law. Defendant's U ndertaking.

The Chief Constable said that the defendant had given an undertaking that he would im- mediately cease the game, and he said that he would never have started it had he known that it was illegal. He had an idea that it was every bit as legal as the game of houp-la, but the fact that he used discs—or dummy three- penny pieces—made the game, in a legal sense, one of chance. In the past defendant had been Of assistance to the police, and in vi.2w of that fact, and' others, he (the Chief) was prepared to say in the man's favour that he believed he would not have carried the game on had he known that it came within the definition of games of chance. _ _ _
The Bench fined defendant , ss. and ordered him to pay 2s. 6d. to a witness, who was in at- tendance, but was not called.

div.head: PREVENTED AN ASSAULT.
div.p: PREVENTED AN ASSAULT.
Woman Who "Vent For" Constable With Umbrella.
Before the Borough Bench on Tuesday morn- ing, Mary Jane Jenks pleaded, in answer to a charge of having been drunk and disorderly on the Central 'Station on Monday, that she "had had a drink or two."

P.C. Clarke stated that at 10.45 at night he saw the prisoner and a young woman come on to the station. Prisoner was obviously in a drunken state and she became Very disorderly and made use of. obscene language. When wit- ness asked her whether she was travelling by train she. said What's that to do with you? Find out !" She was then requested to leave the platform, but she refused to go and, lifting her umbrella, tried to • Strike witness, P.C.' Joynson, who was standing by, warding off the blow. .
Prisoner: Oh, I say; it's not so bad as he puts it!
P.C. Joynson corroborated the evidence of the previous witness, adding that lit had never be- foro heard a woman make -4,iste ot such bad language as that used by the'pisoner., - - -
frisoner assured the Bench that she had never used bad language in her, life. She had been drinking, , but she was quite capable of going home had the police officers left her alone.

The Chief Constable Said that when the woman was arrested she had in her possession a flask of whisky three-parts full. • There were two previous convictions against her, the last being dated May, 1914. Prisoner was fined 205., fourteen days' hard labour being the alternative. Prisoner: Can I have time to pay? • The Chief Constable: You can pay with the £1 note, you have got in your possession.-

div.head: STOLE FROM THE DRILL HALL.
div.p: STOLE FROM THE DRILL HALL.
Boy Who Is "Totally Neglected" By
Parents.
At a Juvenile Court held at the Borough Police Court on Wednesday a boy, aged 'about ten or twelve years, was summoned for stealing a lock and staple from the Drill Hill on November 25th.

The Chief Constable said that the lock had been forced off a box by the military authori- ties and placed in another box, from which it was taken by the boy. For the defence, it was urged that the boy did not realise the seriousness of his act. It was suggested that if the Bench dealt leniently with the case, the boy would be sent to Canada in about six weeks' time. The Chief Constable said that the boy was not looked after properly by the mother, and, if possible, the father was worse. Mr. J. Moore Murray, the Director of Educa- tion. also said that the boy's condition waq due to the total neglect of his father and mother.
, The case was adjourned for four weeks. If in the meantime the boy was not sent to Canada the BenCh intimated that further measures would be taken.

div.head: Intermediate Rugby League.
div.p: Intermediate Rugby League.
At a meeting of the loc' al In—termeiliate Rugby Football League held on Thursday even- ing, Mr. W. Bibby, of 112, Lovely-lime, was appointed hon. secretary and Mr. B. Hawkes- worth hon. treasurer.

div.head: COMMERCIALS ASTIR.
div.p: COMMERCIALS ASTIR.
General Secretary of Association Speaks To-night.

Mr. Fred Coysh, the general and Parliamen- tary secretary of the United Kingdom Commer- cial Travellers' Association, will to-night pay a visit to the Warrington and district branch, and at the Lion Hotel deliver an address on the effect of the war on travellers, and the associa- tion, accident insurance and uniform subscrip- tion. Mr. W. Peter Rylands, who will occupy the chair, has been an active president of the local branch for several years, and the vice- presidents include leading gentlemen connected with the works in the district.

The Warrington branch, which was formed about nine years ago, and is recognised as one of the most progressive in the country, has about 100 members, representative of all our principal industries. Its members have done good work for the various charitable institu- tions belonging to the association. A • short time ago 30 guineas was handed to the Com- mercial Travellers' Schools at Pinner, where 335 children of deceased or incapacitated com- mercial travellers are at present being educated free of charge. This excellent institution is now being enlarged, and the members of the branch are collecting 100 guineas to endow a bed in the new building, which will be known as the "War- rington bed." Another very deserving charity for which the members do all they can is the Commercial Travellers' Benevolent Institution. which provides annuities for incapacitated travellers or their widows when left in reduced circumstances. The branch has also helped the Infirmary and other local charities at various times.

There are many benefits to be obtained by membership in the branch, and it is to the in- terest of all 'commercials to become members; and it is hoped all those, interested will be present. The chair will be taken at 6.45. Arrangements have been made to have a smoking concert after the meeting, when Mr. J. Itabbitt, Mr. J. Poole and Mr. L. Auckland will be amongst the singers.

div.head: MR. KITCHINGMAN'S WILL.
div.p: MR. KITCHINGMAN'S WILL.
Compromise Sanctioned In Chancery Court.

In the Chancery Court, London, on Thursday, before Mr. Justice Peterson—the newly- appointed judge—sanction was given to the compromise of an action relating to. the will of the late Mr. Joseph Kitchingman, who, for- merly, practising as a ,solicitor in Liverpool, was at one time connected with Warrington. By his will the testator, after certain bequests— including a legacy of £l,OOO to the Warrington Infirmary—devised his house known as "Sea- bank Nook," Liscard, to his _trustees upon trust, to allow the same to be used, by the Cor- poration of Warrington for the purposes of a convalescent home; and he directed the trustees to permit the whole or part of the income of the residuary estate to be applied in main- taining, supporting and keeping up the con- valesgent home. In the event of the Corpora- tion being unwilling or unable to use and run the house for the purpose named the testator directed that it be sold, the proceeds of the sale to be divided betvceen the Warrington Infirm- ary and the Victoria Hospital, Liscard, and the whole of the residuary estate to go to the Victoria Hospital. How The Proceedings Arose.

Certain questions upon the construction of the will having arisen—and more 'particularly the question as to whether having regard to ,certain cdvenants restricting the use of the house for private purposes only, it would be legally possible for the Corporation to use the same as a convalescent home—the trustees took proceedings for the administration of the estate by the Court. An Agreement Reached.

There being a very serious doubt as to Whether the restrictions mentioned could be got over without great expense, the Warrington Corporation, the Warrington Infirmary and the Liscard Hospital came to an agreement whereby the Corporation was to receive the sum of £3,000, with interest at 4 per cent., free of legacy duty; the WarringtOn. Infirmary was to. receive, in addition to its legacy of £l,OOO, the further sun). of £6OO with like interest, and also free of legacy duty, and the. Liscard Hospital was to receive the balance of the residuary estate. It was also agreed that the sum of £3,000 to be paid to the Corporation was to be devoted to charitable purposes, in accordance with a scheme to be sanctioned by the Court. Mr. Courthope Wilson (instructed by Messrs. Jones, Sephton and Hughes) on behalf of the trustees of the Will, stated the facts, and sub- mitted that,., according to the Weir Hospital case the Court had no power to sanction the agreement that had been arrived at by the beneficiaries, as it had been decided, in the case cited, that such an arrangement could not be legally upheld. - - _

div.head: Legal Point.
div.p: A Legal Point.

Mr.' Austin Cartm;ll (instructed by Messrs. Forshaw and Hawkins, Liverpool), on behalf of the Attorney-General, said that the Weir Hos- pital case had no bearing at all on the agree- ment in this case: for, in that case the trustees were trying to do something entirely different from the wishes of the testator, and something which the Attorney-General could not agree. to; whereas in this case the agreement was .a com- promise by beneficiaries and it had the com- plete approval of the Attorney-General. Mr. Nuttall (instructed by Mr. Hallaway, deputy town clerk), on behalf of the Corpora- tion; Mr. John Rutherford (instructed by Messrs. Forshaw and Forshaw) on behalf of the Warrington Infirmary, and Mr. Harold Mather, on behalf of the Liscard Hospital, all expressed their concurrence in the terms agreed upon, and considered that they ought to be sanctioned by the Court. The Judge said that in his opinion the case quoted by Mr. Courthope Wilson did not apply to a case like this, where a very fair compromise had been made by the beneficiaries, and he should therefore sanction the terms of settle- ment.
Concert for Fighters' Christmas Boxes.

As the result of a concert held in the Wycliffe Memorial Buildings on Monday evening, a sum of nearly £lO will be handed to the fund for providing Wycliffe men on active service with Christmas gifts. ' Mr. 'Joseph, Monks kindly defrayed- the expenses of the -concert, and Mr. W. IL Payton acted as conductor and accom- panist.

div.head: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
div.p: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
Entertainments At The
Hospitals.
SCOTTISH NIGHT AT WINWICK.

An exceedingly successful concert took place! at the Lord Derby War Hospital on Saturday; evening. The Warrington Caledonian Associa- tion, in view of the fact that there were a large number of wounded Scottish soldiers in the hos- pital, arranged with the Hospital authorities to provide a concert with a strong Scottish flavour. The large hall was well filled by a most enthu- siastic audience of convalescents. The various items were evidently very midi to their taste, and they proved unmistakably that if their limbs were temporarily hors ,de combat, their lungs were in splendid order. 'There was un- stinted applause, and the Way the choruses of the well-known favourites. were taken up was refreshing. Mr. Toni Barlow, Of Liverpool, was at the top of his form, and his rendering of "Mary o' Argyle" and "Kind and gentle is she" fairly got hold of the " Tommies." Mr. W. Atkinson's fine baritone voice was heard, to perfection, his singing of "Annie Laurie" being specially effective, and very much to the taste of the audience. Messrs. Barlow and •Atkinson also contributed two or three duets, whiehawere highly appreciated. Mrs. Alec Chrystal is the possessor of a contralto voice of great range and power, and she fairly captured all hearts with her spirited rendering of "Angus Macdonald," and a delightful interpretation of "My am n folk" and "Loch Lomond." 'Mr. Alec Chrystal was responsible for the humorous element, and. whilst he was in possession of the stage it was a continuous time of merriment, the audience being kept in a constant ripple, breaking out re- peatedly in roars of laughter at some original joke. In a duet, "Growing older every day," in which he was assisted by Mrs. Chrystal, some satirical allusions to the Kaiser were hugely enjoyed. Mr. W. H. Payton' accompanied in his usual finished style. During the concert Piper. D. Laidlaw, V.C.. played selections which were much appreciated by those who were 'anxious to see the gallant piper. • _
Several members of the • Caledonian Associa- tion., including the President, were entertained by the Hospital authorities, and will retain a very pleasant recollection of their visit to Win- wick. •

div.head: MISS MARIE HOUGHTON AT WHITECROSS
div.p: MISS MARIE HOUGHTON AT WHITECROSS

Miss Marie Houghton again visited the White- cross Military Hospital, and in company with Miss Doris Read and Mr. Chas. Lambert a very delightful concert was given. One of the features of the evening was the appearance on the programme of Lance-Corporal Knowles and Private Bew, two gallant warriors under treat- ment in the hospital. Their efforts to entertain their fellow comrades were greeted with tre- mendous applause. Altogether, a very pleasant evening was spent, and one that was thoroughly appreciated by all. Miss Houghton and Mr. Lambert have prom- ised Mr. Loxham to entertain the soldiers on Christmas Day.

div.head: DISMISSED 1.
div.p: DISMISSED 1.
Appeal To General Munitions
Tribunal Fails.

At the first sitting of the General Munitions Tribunal for the Warrington . District of ,the North-West Coast (No. 2 Division), held at. the Labour Exchange, Sankey-street, on Tuesday afternoon, a local firm, who are a controlled establishment, were summoned at the instance of a Sheffield firm for having, on November 15th and other dates, infringed the provisions a an Order .dated July 14th, 1915, made by the Minister of Munitions, by employing a sorkman without a certificate of discharge.—Mr. James F. Wing, solicitor, Sheffield.. waS fcr e,4n- plainants. an Mr. T. S. Steel, of Warrington (acting for Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co.) for the 'defendants, on whose behalf he entered a plea of not guilty.

div.head: Voints At Issue.
div.p: The Voints At Issue.

In opening his ease, Mr. Wing read corre- spondence which had taken place between his clients and the defendant, with the object of showing that the former did not desire to lose the services of the man—who was engaged as a turner-in" in the rod mill—and that they had given the defendants notice that owing to the extraordinary position Of affairs which prevailed in connection with both skilled and unskilled. labour, they could not do without his services. The defendants, on the other hand, contended that they had done nothing in contravention of the Act, and that they had taken the workman back again on a promise which had been made to him that he could return if he was dissatisfied with his work at Sheffield. • •
Considerable evidence having been called for the complainants, Mr. Steel contended for the defence -that the complainants' work did not comp within Section 7 of the Order made by. the

Minister of Munitions. There was no evidence that the Sheffield factory was a factory or work- shop where the business carried on consisted "solely or mainly in engineering, shipbuilding, or the production of arms, munitions or ex- plosives." There wa* no evidence that the establishment came within the class specified in the Order, and even if the Court held that it did there was no evidence that the man was employed "on or in connection with" munition work.

div.head: President's Finding.
div.p: The President's Finding.

In giving the decision of the Tribunal, the Chairman (Mr. A. J. Ashton, K.C., Recorder of Manchester), said that with the assistance of his assessors—Messrs. F. G.' GoOdbehere for the employers and MT. Peter Phythian for the workers—he had come to the conclusion that the complainants had not satisfied him that they carried on business "solely or mainly" in the production of arms, &c., or that a particular workman concerned was employed. "on or in connection with" munitions. Consequently the application was dismissed.
NAT CARE in
Partners.

par as regards quality and attractiveness with the many which have in the past given un- bounded delight to patrons. "Partners," a brilliant ' American burresque, featuring the celebrated Jewish comedian, Nat Carr, tops a tine bill. The production is presented by a company of thirty, and is noteworthy . for its clever wit, classical dancing and effective stage pictures. In addition to the outstanding feature, a number of excellent artistes have been booked, including Dorothy Leigh (in comedy songs), Keir and Kempton (a Scottish vocal duo), and the Record Quartet (in a novely banjo act).
Pearl Girl" will doubtless prove one of the greatest successes ever staged at Warrington's popular playhouse. •
GOOD ALL-ROUND " BILL " AT THE HIPPODROME,.

"Another bill of all-round excellence!" is the popular verdict of visitors to the Hippodrome this week, for, indeed, the programme on offer is one that is pleasing and. entertaining. That versatile comedian, George D'Albert, with his bright and breezy songs, has been delighting large audiences, singing and pattering in a style that is to the liking of his many old admirers. A new song with a patriotic_ flavour was enti- tl4d "The girl I left :behind me," and judging from the applause which greeted it on Monday, 'augurs well or becoming one of the most popu- lar songs of the day. This novelty is quite in keeping • with the record of this famous comedian, for no matter how often he visits our local variety house he always has in the mean- time added fresh songs to his ever-increasing repertoire. One of the hits of the evening's en- tertainment is the sketch entitled "A Scotch 'Wedding," played capitally : by Miss 1,. Houston, Mr. J, Houston and Mr. A. Kerr. The scene is laid in a typical Scotch kitchen, and, merry trifle meets with whole-hearted applause. Another popular "turn" on the programme is •that Provided by Adam Tomlinson, the dialect comedian. As a policeman •he is exceedingly funny and original, and during the whole. time he occupies the boards he keeps the audience in one continual roar of „laughter. Some of his jokes are as clever as they are humorous, and on the occasion of our visit, •when the curtain fell, after the performance of this popoular comedian, the applause took some minutes to subside. Another special item of note is that presented by the OlracS--a quintet of clever acrobats, who appear in a sketch, "Tun in a Drawing-room." _ Exceedingly smart as bal- ancers and knockabouts, they perform their tricks with a degree of rapidity and ease which leaves one breathless. Other contributions to a notable programme come from Les Napier Trio, in a singing., dancing,' gymnastic and juggling display; Nellie Nova, in a brilliant instrumental speciality; and Marjory Dawson, "the Crinoline Girl," in old4ashioned, illustrated sons. MISSING. PRIVATE R. H. ALLEN. Local Swimming Champion Drowned In Anglia Disaster. It is feared that when the Hospital Ship Anglia went down in the English *Channel she took with her one who was well-known in local natatory circles—Private Robert Henry Allen, one time swimming champion of Warrington. Gave Up Good Berth To Volunteer. The missing man is the son of the lafe Mr. William Allen, a stonemason—who died fifteen years ago—and of Mrs. Allen, late of 33, Allen- street, Warrington—who died on February 11th, 1911. Formerly Private Allen was a wiredrawer in the employ of the Firth Mattress Co., Howley. LANCE-CORPORAL J. DANDY. At Present An Inmate Of A Sheffield Hospital. Lance-Corporal J. Dandy, son of Mrs. Dandy, 3, Cherry-lane, Lymm, is at present an inmate of the Northern General Hospital, Sheffield, *here he is convalescent. A short time ago Lance-Corporal Dandy contracted fever whilst out in France, and, unfortunately, the after- effects caused influenza. He is, however, at present making satisfactory progress towards recovery. Lance-Corporal Dandy joined His Majesty's Forces in January last, and after a few months' training in Lincolnshire was drafted to France. He was slightly wounded

Holiness, of course, is .a greater word, but we cannot pro- duee that in others. What is put in our power happiness, and for that each man is his brother's keeper.—Henry Drummond. • The Spinal Column. The subject for the hour was physiology. I was explaining the nature of the spinal column. to a class of twelve-year-olds. After" finishing the discussion I said to a little Irish boy:— "Now, Michael, what is the spinal column?" Scratching his head thoughtfully for a minute, he smilingly replied, "Well, ma'am, 'tis the thing that runs up and down your back. Yer head sits on one end and you sit on the other."--" Hospital News."

LOCAL AMUSEMENTS. • !lOMANTIC. . DRAMA AT ROYAL • .. . • COURT. Long ago Charles Garvice won his spurs a-. ,1 novelist, and now he is winning them as a play- wright, for his dramatic effort "A Heritage of Hate," which is being presented at the Royal Court Theatre this week, is a decidedly promis- ing essay into the realm of_ stageland. From first to last the piece rivets the attention, and it runs along somewhat original lines, having for its hero the sole inhabitant of a Pacifk island who until the heroine was, with her mother, washed up on the shores of his ocean eerie had gone one better than Robinson Crusoe, in that he had never before seen a woman. How he succumbs to feminine charms and 1, eventually restored to his rightful position in life, after villainy has been vanquished and virtue nas been proverbially triumphant, forms an enthralling story, which is most capably and effectively told by that sterling actor, Mr. Sant Livesely and his company. " The Pearl Girl " Next Week. Royal Court devotees are to have another great treat next week, when one of the famous Robert Courtneidge companies will present "The .Pearl Girl," one of the latest, up-to-datest and .most enchanting of all the musical comedies that ever captivated great London, and the still bigger public in Lae provinces. The company which is to present the sparkling production to Warrington includes some well-known artistes, including Miss. Eva Brickwell (whose portrait we give), Miss- Phyllis Hughes, Miss Ethel Gardener, Miss Mary Tomlinson (who may be remembered as the principal bOy in one of last year's Liverpool pantomimes), Mr. Raymond Gascoyne, Mr. Lamont Dickson and, Mr. Aniiry Millwall.
